docs.title: VINEYARD
docs.text:
Build the graph, pull in the intelligence, work on the project together.

VINEYARD is an open investigation workbench for CTI and OSINT. You map entities and the relationships between them, enrich them with packs you install from the Marketplace, and share the project with the people working on it — with plugins running in your own session, never on a server.

docs.text:
Set up a project, build the graph, install packs and run them. Share a project and follow collaborators live.

docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text: Build for Vineyard by authoring a Plugin Pack, Type Pack, or Skill Pack in your own GitHub repo, then publishing a one-line pointer to the registry.

docs.title: The model in one paragraph
docs.text:
You author a pack in your own repository. To distribute it, you open a pull request that adds a single metadata entry — a pointer, not code — to the Marketplace registry. When a user installs your pack, the Vineyard app fetches it from your repo at a pinned commit. The server never executes plugin code, never stores plugin bytes, and never records the runs a plugin produces.

flowchart LR
    A[Author repo on GitHub] -->|PR: one metadata entry| B[(Registry<br/>metadata only)]
    B -->|fetch reference| C[Marketplace<br/>docs.vineyard.run]
    C -->|install reference| D[Vineyard app]
    D -->|fetch pack @ pinned ref| A
    D -->|run on the client| E[Your graph]
    style B fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#4c1d95
    style D fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#4c1d95

docs.title: Key principles
docs.text:
• Client-side execution — the server never executes plugin code.
  • Ephemeral — a run is never written to the database; it lives in the browser tab, and only the graph changes you approve are saved.
  • Least authority — plugin JS runs in a Web Worker sandbox with only the scopes you approve. Its graph writes are staged and applied only after you review and approve them.
  • Distribution = GitHub + a metadata-only registry — pointers, never code.

See Architecture & principles for the full design.

docs.title: The three content types
docs.text:
Every Vineyard pack carries a content_type discriminator, and identifiers are reverse-DNS:

Content type content_type Identifier form What it is Plugin Pack vineyard:pluginpack <namespace>.pluginpacks.<name> One or more bundled JS modules exporting definePlugin({ manifest, run }) that read the graph and stage changes to it for the analyst's review. Type Pack vineyard:typepack <namespace>.typepacks.<name> JSON that defines node entity types (icons, colors, properties, validators). Skill Pack vineyard:skillpack <namespace>.skillpacks.<name> JSON text: an investigation playbook the agent follows. No code, no permissions.

<namespace> is your own reverse-DNS prefix, two labels or more: com.acme, io.github.yourname, dev.yourdomain. run.vineyard.* is Vineyard's own and is not yours to publish under. A submission under a namespace you do not own is refused at review.

The three systems are designed to work together — a plugin's io references Type Pack types by their qualified category.name form, and a Skill Pack's steps call plugin packs declared in its requires — but each can be published independently.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Plugin Packs need JavaScript or TypeScript, the SDK (a single sdk.ts you copy into your repo), and a bundler (esbuild, Vite, Rollup, or similar). A plugin ships as a single bundled module referenced from your manifest's platforms.web.entry.
  • Type Packs and Skill Packs are plain JSON — author them in any editor, no toolchain.
  • A GitHub repository. Push a version and pin its commit SHA in a one-entry registry PR. The registry stores only that pointer; your repo hosts the actual pack content that clients fetch directly.

Initial scope is browser + desktop

The sandbox-js runtime (platforms.web.runtime: "sandbox-js") ships today, in the browser and in the desktop app: both run the plugin's platforms.web entry. A platforms.desktop block is accepted by the schema but not read. The web-proxy and native/subprocess runtimes are accepted by the schemas but not built yet.

docs.title: Architecture & principles
docs.text: Vineyard executes plugins and Type Packs in the user's app, never on a server.

docs.title: Design facts
docs.text:
• Client-side execution. Plugins (JS) and Type Packs (JSON) run in the user's app, in the browser or in the desktop app. The server never executes plugin code; it stores pointers and serves the ordinary graph API.
  • Per-plugin platform flags. A plugin declares where it runs in platforms. The browser and the desktop app both run its platforms.web entry (sandbox-js); a platforms.desktop block is accepted but not read. A plugin that needs a capability the browser cannot provide (web_probe) sets platforms.primary: "desktop" to mark itself desktop-only.
  • Metadata-only registry. Distribution is GitHub + a registry of pointers, not code. The client fetches the bundle (via jsDelivr, pinned to the immutable commit SHA), checks it against the digest the registry recorded, and runs it in the sandbox worker. See distribution.
  • Ephemeral by default. A plugin-run task lives in the current tab's memory, except a run whose changes wait for review: what it staged is kept on this device for 7 days after its last change and is waiting for review again after a reload, including what a run cut short had staged. AI conversations (and their task rows) are kept on this device too. None of it is sent to the server — only applied changes reach the project's graph. See lifecycle and Tasks.
  • Least authority. Plugin JS runs in a Web Worker sandbox with only its declared scopes — graph verbs, network, network_configurable, web_probe (desktop), services, config; the worker has no DOM, no access to the site's storage, and no network of its own. Graph writes are staged, not live: they are applied only after the analyst reviews and approves the change set. See scopes and security.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Author<br/>repo + pushed version<br/>(commit SHA)"]
    R["Registry<br/>metadata-only<br/>pointer: repo @ ref"]
    H["App / Host bridge<br/>main thread"]
    W["Web Worker sandbox<br/>plugin main.js<br/>no DOM, no own network"]
    S["Staging store<br/>captured writes<br/>awaiting review"]
    G["Graph<br/>REST + WS"]

    A -- "one-entry PR<br/>(identifier, repo, ref, path, version)" --> R
    R -- "resolve pointer" --> H
    A -. "fetch bundle per run<br/>(jsDelivr, CORS-open)" .-> H
    H -- "Comlink proxy<br/>= granted scopes only" --> W
    W -- "ctx.graph" --> H
    H -- "capture write" --> S
    S -- "analyst reviews + approves" --> G
    H -- "reads" --> G

  1. Author → registry. The author pushes the version to their repo, then opens a one-entry pull request adding packs/<identifier>.json — { identifier, repo, ref, path, version, … }, where ref is the commit SHA of that version. The registry stores the pointer (repo @ ref), never the code.

  2. Registry → app. When a user installs, the app resolves the pointer and fetches the bundle directly (via jsDelivr, pinned to the immutable commit SHA). No server-side content copy exists.

  3. App → sandbox. The host loads the fetched main.js into a dedicated module Web Worker and exposes ctx as a Comlink proxy whose shape is exactly the granted scopes — a ctx member is absent unless its scope was granted.

  4. Execution → staging → graph. The plugin calls ctx.graph. Reads are served from the project's in-memory graph; writes are captured into the staging store rather than sent. They are applied only once the analyst opens the change set and clicks Apply (N), which applies every row left checked (a run the AI agent launched under Apply automatically is the exception; see security). Outbound ctx.net.fetch requests are matched against the plugin's declared endpoints by origin and whole path segments, never as a string prefix. The worker has no network of its own, so a direct fetch fails; go through ctx.

See SDK for the ctx interface, lifecycle for how a run moves through the task states, and security for the sandbox boundary.

docs.title: In scope now vs. deferred
docs.text:
Implementation scope

The browser and desktop Electron shell both ship today. Items listed as deferred below remain in the schemas as forward-looking design but are not built yet — do not treat them as shipped.

docs.title: Ships today
docs.text:
• Browser runtime — platforms.web.runtime: "sandbox-js": author JS runs in a Web Worker.
  • Desktop app — the Electron shell runs the same platforms.web sandbox-js entry in the same worker sandbox and adds the anonymous HTTP probe (web_probe capability). It does not read platforms.desktop.
  • Metadata-only registry with GitHub-hosted bundles fetched via jsDelivr, pinned to an immutable commit SHA.
  • Staged graph writes + analyst review — captured node/edge changes, applied only on approval — plus the egress allowlist.
  • Client-side task execution, one dedicated Web Worker per run.
  • Secret config — config.secret:true values kept per signed-in account (in the OS keychain on desktop, for the tab session in the browser) and read by the declaring plugin (BYOK).
  • Vineyard-operated services — scopes.services (rdap, telegram), called by name through ctx.service.
  • The packs listed in the Marketplace — Plugin Packs (the six Chaos reference plugins among them), Type Packs such as Infrastructure and Threat, and Skill Packs.

docs.title: Deferred (designed, not built)
docs.text:
• native/subprocess desktop runtimes — platforms.desktop.runtime: "native" and "subprocess" are allowed by the schema but not yet implemented.
  • web-proxy runtime — the single-endpoint CORS escape hatch for web plugins that need a third-party API.
  • Type Pack version pinning — see Type Packs.

When targeting platforms that ship today, give the plugin a web block using sandbox-js: its entry is what runs in both the browser and the desktop app, and a pack member without one inherits the pack's. To mark a plugin desktop-only, set platforms.primary: "desktop" — in the browser the Run plugins dialog then greys it out (does not hide it) with the reason "Desktop only — …". The per-platform fallback hint is not read by the app. See plugin manifest.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text: What the app loads is decided by the registry entry — repo, ref and path — and, for plugins, by platforms.web.entry. A pack document does not describe where it is published; the registry entry that points at it does.

docs.title: The pinned pointer
docs.text:
A registry entry (packs/<identifier>.json) names the content repo (repo, as owner/name), the commit to load (ref) and the document's path within that commit (path). The client fetches https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/{repo}@{ref}/{path}. The full field-by-field reference lives in the registry schema.

ref must be immutable — branches and tags are rejected

The registry entry's ref must be a commit SHA, 40-hex or 64-hex. Branches and tags are rejected by the entry schema and by verify_pinned.py, because they can be moved after review. See updates for how a new version becomes an offered update.

docs.title: The code module: platforms.web.entry
docs.text:
A plugin's platforms.web.entry names the module the plugin worker imports: a path inside the repository, relative to the repo root (for example dist/pack.mjs), resolved against the same pinned commit as the manifest. A pack member without its own platforms.web block runs the pack's module. A plugin with no entry to run is not listed as runnable, and registry CI refuses an entry of inline, which names no module.

The entry cannot name code outside that commit, because the commit is what was reviewed. It must be /-separated segments made only of ASCII letters, digits, ., _ and -, and no segment may be . or ... Anything else fails registry CI: an absolute URL, a leading /, a backslash and a percent-escape, but also a name such as dist/pack@1.2.0.mjs or dist/vt+community.mjs. When a project opens, the app does not load a published pack whose entry, the pack's own or a member's, does not resolve to such a path inside the pinned commit: none of its plugins load, and the project shows a notice naming the pack.

docs.title: One self-contained file
docs.text:
The worker does not import the module from its URL. The app fetches it, checks it (see verification), and hands the worker those bytes as a blob: URL, so the module cannot reach a file next to it. It must be one self-contained ES module:

  • no static or dynamic import of another file, relative or absolute, and no import.meta.url to find assets by;
  • no WebAssembly, and no eval or new Function: the worker refuses them;
  • everything else bundled in, for example with esbuild --bundle --format=esm.

Every published pack's dist/pack.mjs is such a file. A new Blob([...]) built at run time works; turning one into a URL (URL.createObjectURL) does not.

Packs loaded for development

A pack loaded from Settings → Plugins → Development → Load a pack from a URL is not held to this rule, since it reaches only this device: its entry may be an absolute URL, such as your dev server's. See quickstart.

docs.title: Storage: metadata only
docs.text:
• The registry holds path/metadata only (plus, in its approved-ref lists, a SHA-256 of each approved document and of each code module a Plugin Pack runs). There is no server-side copy of the bundle content.
  • The client fetches pack content via jsDelivr, pinned to the entry's commit SHA: the pack document each time a project opens, and a plugin's code module each time it runs. There is no persistent local cache.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The client loads a pack only if its repo@ref/path is listed in registry/approved-{plugin,type,skill}packs.json and the fetched document matches the SHA-256 recorded there. If the registry is unreachable, a pointer this device has verified before still loads, checked against the digests this device kept the last time the registry listed it, and any other is held. CI checks that the plugin code module (platforms.web.entry) is inside the pinned commit and declares the same version and licence as the manifest (see publishing).

The code is checked the same way. A Plugin Pack's approved row also records the SHA-256 of each code module the pack runs, the pack's and any member's own (bundle_sha256). Each time a plugin runs, the app fetches its module from jsDelivr, refuses bytes that do not match, and gives the plugin worker only the bytes it checked. A pack whose row records these digests but not one for a module the pack runs is not loaded at all, with the same notice as an entry outside the commit. Both digests are of the bytes GitHub holds at the pinned commit, never of what the CDN served the registry: the registry fetches each file from GitHub and from jsDelivr, records GitHub's digest, and fails its build when the two differ. A row approved before code digests were recorded, or whose code GitHub could not serve when the registry was built, has none, and its code is checked by its listing alone; a pack the catalog lists today always has them, because the registry does not publish a list in which one lacks them. While the registry is unreachable, a pack is held to the digests this device kept for it; one this device has not seen listed since it began keeping them is checked by its listing alone. The app runs plugin code only from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/, including a pack loaded for development, except in the frontend's own npm run dev build.

docs.title: Where it fits in the install flow
docs.text: Installing a Plugin Pack fetches the document at the entry's repo@ref/path (via jsDelivr) for the permission view in the install dialog (a Skill Pack's is fetched for its overview), then stores a {identifier, url, version} pointer on the project. When the project opens, each pointer is verified against the registry as above, and a plugin's platforms.web.entry is resolved against the same pinned commit and loaded in the sandbox worker. For the submission/review gates, see publishing.

docs.title: Task lifecycle
docs.text: Every plugin run and every AI agent turn in Vineyard is a task, tracked client-side. A plugin run the AI agent launches gets no Tasks row of its own: it belongs to the agent's conversation, where each such run that staged something appears as its own change set.

docs.title: States
docs.text:
A task is created directly in running and ends in one of these terminal states:

running → succeeded | failed | cancelled | incomplete
State Meaning running Executing. succeeded Completed normally. failed Completed with an error. cancelled Stopped: the Tasks panel's Stop button, or leaving the project (a run the agent launched is also cancelled when its turn is stopped). A run that a reload or a crash cut short while it was still staging also comes back cancelled when the project is opened again, marked Cut short by a reload. Changes it had already staged stay available for review. incomplete AI agent only — the turn ended before the agent finished. While the app is open, that means the turn ended holding tool calls it never got answers for. When the project is reopened, a turn that ran out of steps or was cut off by the app closing also comes back as incomplete, and so, usually, does a turn you stopped; its last answer then offers Continue. What it did is kept and can be continued.

Each run gets one dedicated Web Worker, spawned directly — there is no worker pool or queue.

docs.title: Cancel is cooperative
docs.text:
Stopping a task is cooperative, built on the Web AbortController / AbortSignal pair:

  • The host aborts the controller; the plugin observes ctx.signal (an AbortSignal) or registers ctx.onCancel(handler).
  • A well-behaved plugin checks ctx.signal.aborted between units of work and unwinds cleanly, preserving any partial results.

See the SDK for a ctx.signal checkpoint example.

Stop gives the plugin 3 seconds

Stop does not kill the worker at once. The host aborts ctx.signal and gives the plugin a 3-second grace period to unwind and return; only a worker still running after that is terminated. A plugin that returns in time finishes like any other run, with what it staged held for review; one that throws after Stop, whatever the error, or is terminated ends cancelled, and the changes it had already staged still stay available for review. The host decides this from its own Stop, not from the error's type. Design run() to be interruptible — see SDK and lifecycle controls in the manifest.

docs.title: manifest.lifecycle.timeout_ms
docs.text:
The one lifecycle hint the host actually enforces is a wall-clock budget for one run. Past it, the host terminates the sandbox and fails the task — the backstop for a plugin that stops yielding to its event loop and so can never see ctx.signal.

Every run has a budget. Without timeout_ms it is 10 minutes, and a declared value is capped at 60 minutes, so a pack may raise its budget but cannot opt out of having one. A timed-out run fails with "plugin exceeded its time budget (…s) and was terminated". Like every failed run, whether it timed out, its sandbox did not start or the plugin threw an error, it discards the changes it had staged. Only a Stop keeps them, or a reload or a crash that cuts the run off: what it had staged by then was already kept on the device, and comes back for review.

"lifecycle": {
  "timeout_ms": 30000
}

The manifest schema accepts long_running, controls, progress, persistence, and states under lifecycle (it does not list timeout_ms), but nothing in the host reads them today — see plugin manifest.

docs.title: Other limits
docs.text:
These end a run as failed, separately from the budget:

  • Loading. The sandbox and the pack's code, including its top-level code, must load within 60 seconds, or the run fails with the plugin's code did not load within 60s from <host>.
  • Starting. If the sandbox's own script fails to load, or throws before the pack has loaded, the run fails at once with the plugin sandbox did not start: ….
  • Messages. A reply from the sandbox that the app cannot read fails the run with the plugin sandbox sent a reply the app could not read.
  • Storage. In a browser where the sandbox cannot block site storage, the pack is not loaded and the run fails with the plugin sandbox could not block site storage in this browser (see the sandbox).

docs.title: Plugin manifest
docs.text:
The plugin manifest is a vineyard:plugin document that fully describes one plugin: who made it, where it runs, what graph types it reads and writes, the form it shows before running, and the authority it needs. It is the single source of truth.

This page walks through the manifest blocks using two real, shipped plugins as examples: RDAP IP (from the IP Recon pack) and Wayback Snapshot History (from the Wayback Machine pack). For the exhaustive, field-by-field schema — every type, pattern, and default — see the plugin schema reference.

The required top-level keys are identifier, content_type, name, version, description, platforms, io, scopes, and lifecycle.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
The identity block names and attributes the plugin: identifier (a reverse-DNS <your-namespace>.plugins.<slug> string that the marketplace and update checks key off), the constant content_type of vineyard:plugin, the display name, a SemVer version, a one- to two-sentence description, and the optional author, license, and icon. icon is a kebab-case lucide icon name (e.g. network); anything else renders as the default puzzle icon. The optional thumbnail_url is a repo-relative path to the card image (not a URL); the app resolves it only against the pinned commit via cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/{repo}@{ref}/{path}, with raw.githubusercontent.com/{repo}/{ref}/{path} as fallback. marketing_url and latest_url are in the schema reference (the update check does not use latest_url: an update is offered when the catalog's version is newer than the installed one, compared as SemVer — see Updates).

The AI agent chooses a plugin by its description, so say what the plugin takes and what it adds. It also reads each parameter's description (or title). In its plugin list, a parameter description longer than 300 characters is cut to its first sentence until the agent asks for that plugin, so put the essential rule first.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text:
platforms declares where the plugin can execute. It requires at least one of web or desktop; primary names the preferred target. There are two web runtimes:

web (sandbox-js)web (web-proxy) 
"platforms": {
  "primary": "web",
  "web": { "runtime": "sandbox-js", "entry": "dist/pack.mjs" }
}

sandbox-js runs the author's bundled JavaScript inside a dedicated module Web Worker that has no network of its own; it reaches out only through the host: ctx.net.fetch (limited to the declared scopes.network endpoints and the addresses the analyst sets for scopes.network_configurable), ctx.service (scopes.services), or, in the desktop app, ctx.net.probe (scopes.web_probe). This is what RDAP IP uses (ctx.net.fetch).

"platforms": {
  "primary": "web",
  "web": {
    "runtime": "web-proxy",
    "entry": "dist/client.js",
    "proxy_endpoint": "https://api.example.com/run"
  }
}

web-proxy is designed as the CORS escape hatch: the worker would be a thin client calling exactly one author-controlled endpoint, with proxy_endpoint required to equal the single scopes.network entry (no fan-out). The schema accepts this value, but no runtime dispatches it yet — do not ship a plugin that depends on it.

Desktop: the app runs the web entry; native/subprocess deferred

The schema accepts a desktop block (with runtimes sandbox-js, native, or subprocess), but the host does not read it: the Electron shell runs the plugin's platforms.web sandbox-js entry in the same sandbox worker, not a separate desktop runtime. native and subprocess runtimes are forward-looking design — do not rely on them executing yet.

The host executes platforms.web (runtime sandbox-js) on both the web and the desktop app — the desktop block and both fallback fields are accepted by the schema but not read, so every plugin needs a web block. primary: "desktop" marks the plugin desktop-only: in a browser it stays listed in the Run plugins panel under Desktop only, greyed out and not runnable, rather than hidden. The marketplace labels such packs Desktop only but still installs them in the browser.

docs.title: io — consumes and produces
docs.text:
io ties the plugin to the graph by referencing entity types from Type Packs. Both consumes and produces are required arrays (either may be empty), and each entry is a type reference of { typepack, category, name, as? } — category and name together form the qualified runtime type, so Node.type equals <category>.<name>.

"io": {
  "consumes": [
    { "typepack": "run.vineyard.typepacks.infrastructure", "category": "infrastructure", "name": "ip_address" }
  ],
  "produces": [
    { "typepack": "run.vineyard.typepacks.infrastructure", "category": "infrastructure", "name": "netblock" }
  ]
}

This is RDAP IP's io: it takes an infrastructure.ip_address node and adds the owning infrastructure.netblock.

consumes shapes the UX:

  • consumes decides where a plugin is offered in the Run plugins… panel (opened from a node's or the canvas's right-click menu, the toolbar, or the menu bar): a plugin is listed under Matches selection / Matches project data when any consumed type is present in the chosen scope (Selected or Whole project). RDAP IP is offered whenever an infrastructure.ip_address node is in scope.
  • A type reference also accepts an optional as binding alias (to pre-bind the consumed node's value into params under that key); the schema accepts it, but the run form does not read it yet.
  • A plugin with an empty consumes array is a whole-graph plugin: it is listed in the panel's Whole-graph / input via form section instead. A whole-graph plugin with at least one parameter is also offered to the AI agent as a query tool: the agent runs it with no nodes and fills params itself.

produces is informational: the Marketplace shows it as type chips next to the plugin, and the Run plugins… panel's filter box matches it along with the name, description and consumed types. It does not limit what the plugin may create. See Type Packs (develop) for how these types are defined.

docs.title: params — the pre-run form
docs.text:
params is a JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) describing the form shown before the plugin runs. The submitted object is passed to run as ctx.params (and kept on the run's task row). The form reads title (label), description (help text), type (text / number / switch), enum (a select) and required (Run stays disabled until filled); default, pattern, minimum and maximum are not applied, so validate and default inside run. A property with "format": "file" renders a local file picker (accept filters it; "type": "array" allows several files) and the plugin receives the File object(s). Wayback Snapshot History's form:

"params": {
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "from": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^\\d{8}$", "description": "Earliest capture date, YYYYMMDD. Empty = no lower bound." },
    "to": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^\\d{8}$", "description": "Latest capture date, YYYYMMDD. Empty = no upper bound." },
    "limit": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 500, "default": 50, "description": "Maximum captures to fetch per node, 1–500. Default 50." },
    "drop_duplicates": { "type": "boolean", "default": true, "description": "Keep only the newest capture of each content digest. On by default." }
  }
}

No secrets in params

params MUST NOT carry secrets (API keys, tokens, passwords, and similar) — submitted values are recorded with the run. Declare credentials as a scopes.config entry with "secret": true instead — those are collected in the plugin's own settings form and never written to any record. See Secret handling.

docs.title: scopes — the authority surface
docs.text:
scopes is the only authority a plugin receives. A capability that is not declared here is simply absent at runtime. RDAP IP reads the source node, writes its result, and fetches from one endpoint:

"scopes": {
  "graph": ["node:read", "node:create", "node:update", "edge:create"],
  "network": [
    { "endpoint": "https://rdap.org/", "methods": ["GET"], "purpose": "Look up each selected IP's netblock and owner in RDAP." }
  ]
}

Two rules worth repeating here: for a web-proxy plugin, network must be exactly one entry equal to platforms.web.proxy_endpoint; a sandbox-js plugin's network entries are checked instead against the host's egress allowlist (see security). config entries with "secret": true are masked in the form, kept per signed-in account (in the OS keychain on desktop, for the tab session in the browser), and handed to the plugin that declared them. Things like reading this run's params, reporting progress, writing to log, and the cooperative cancel signal are not scopes — they are always available.

For the full scope vocabulary, the scope families, and the enforcement model, see the scopes reference.

docs.title: lifecycle
docs.text:
lifecycle declares the run's timeout budget. RDAP IP:

"lifecycle": {
  "persistence": "opt-in",
  "controls": ["progress", "cancel"],
  "progress": "determinate"
}

The one field the host actually enforces is timeout_ms — a wall-clock budget for the run, past which the host terminates the sandbox and fails the task. When timeout_ms is omitted the host applies a 10-minute default, and a declared value is clamped to 60 minutes — a manifest can raise its budget but not opt out of one. controls, progress, and persistence are accepted by the schema but not read by the host today. See Lifecycle and the user-facing Tasks page.

docs.title: Where it is loaded from
docs.text: What the client runs is decided by the registry entry — it fetches the manifest from repo@ref/path via jsDelivr, verifies it against the digest the registry recorded, and loads platforms.web.entry from the same commit. The registry entry's ref must be a full commit SHA (40- or 64-hex) — registry CI rejects tags and branches. See Distribution.

docs.title: Bundling many plugins
docs.text: A single bundle can carry more than one plugin. The default export may be one plugin, an array, or a pack (definePluginPack) — for example the Chaos Reference Pack ships six graph-manipulation plugins together. The host flattens packs into individually addressed plugins. See Plugin Packs.

docs.text:

  • Scopes reference
  • Security & secret handling
  • Lifecycle · Distribution · Publishing
  • Quickstart and the SDK

docs.title: Plugin Packs
docs.text: A Plugin Pack is one bundle that ships many plugins — the plugin-side analog of a Type Pack carrying many types.

docs.title: One file, many plugins
docs.text:
A plugin bundle's default export does not have to be a single plugin. It may be:

  • a single plugin — export default definePlugin({ manifest, run }),
  • an array of plugins — export default [definePlugin(...), definePlugin(...)], or
  • a pack — export default definePluginPack({ ..., plugins: [...] }).

The host accepts all three shapes and normalizes them. This lets one author repository, one build, and one registry entry deliver a family of related plugins — for example the six graph-manipulation tools in the Chaos reference pack.

docs.title: definePluginPack
docs.text:
A pack is declared with definePluginPack from the SDK (sdk.ts, copied into your repo — see SDK). The pack-level fields describe the bundle, while each entry in plugins is a full plugin definition with its own manifest and run.

import { definePlugin, definePluginPack } from "./sdk";

export default definePluginPack({
  identifier: "run.vineyard.pluginpacks.chaos",   // the pack id
  content_type: "vineyard:pluginpack",
  name: "Chaos Reference Pack",
  version: "1.0.0",
  plugins: [
    definePlugin({ manifest: {/* … */}, run: koreanRoulette }),
    definePlugin({ manifest: {/* … */}, run: russianRoulette }),
    /* …more… */
  ],
});
Field Notes identifier The pack id, a reverse-DNS string <your-namespace>.pluginpacks.* (e.g. run.vineyard.pluginpacks.chaos). It names the bundle, not any one contained plugin. content_type vineyard:pluginpack — the bundle's own kind. Each contained plugin still carries vineyard:plugin. name Pack name in the bundle (not shown by the host; the marketplace card uses the registry entry's name). version SemVer for the bundle as a whole. plugins The array of definePlugin(...) entries. Each carries its own identifier, scopes, io, and lifecycle.

docs.title: How the host flattens a pack
docs.text:
When the client loads a bundle, it calls flattenPlugins on whatever the module default-exported.

default export (pack | array | single)
        │  flattenPlugins(...)
        ▼
run.vineyard.plugins.korean_roulette
run.vineyard.plugins.russian_roulette
run.vineyard.plugins.thanos_snap
run.vineyard.plugins.black_hole
run.vineyard.plugins.dumb_ai_optimizer
run.vineyard.plugins.schrodingers_node

After flattening there is no special "pack" runtime object — there are just plugins. Korean Roulette runs in its own sandboxed Web Worker with only its declared scopes (node:read, node:delete, edge:read, edge:delete), independent of the other five, even though all six shipped in one file.

docs.title: How a pack appears in the registry
docs.text:
The Marketplace registry is metadata-only (it stores pointers, not code), and each entry is a lean projection of the full manifest that lives in the author's repo. A pack still occupies a single registry entry, keyed by the pack identifier. Two derived fields make a pack legible from the listing:

  • plugin_count — the number of plugins bundled (6 for the Chaos pack; omitted or 1 for an ordinary single-plugin entry). The marketplace uses it to label the card ("6 plugins") and to signal that installing once adds all of them together.
  • scopes_summary — a roll-up of the contained plugins' authority (e.g. graph_write: true) so the card can summarize what the whole pack does without fetching each manifest.

The plugins a pack offers are read from its JSON manifest at repo@ref/path (content_type vineyard:pluginpack, with identifier, name, version, summary and description, platforms.web.entry pointing at the bundle, and a plugins array of member manifests). summary is the pack's one line and description its page — see A pack's line and its page; each member keeps its own description, which is what the agent chooses that plugin by. The Plugin Pack schema gives a member the fields of a plugin manifest except latest_url and the pack's own author, thumbnail_url and marketing_url, which the pack states once for all of its members, and allows no other key; a member's description, like a plugin's, is at most 1,024 characters. When a member runs, the client fetches the bundle, checks it against the registry's digest, imports it in a fresh worker, flattens its default export, and picks the member whose identifier matches — so every member in the JSON must exist in the bundle under the same identifier. A member without its own platforms.web.entry inherits the pack's; registry CI refuses an entry of "inline", which names no module, and any entry that is not a path inside the pinned commit (see distribution). The exact registry-entry shape — plugin_count, scopes_summary, and the lean projection — is documented in Publishing.

The client holds every identifier in the document to its shape before it loads the pack, for a registry pointer and a dev override alike: the pack's is <reverse-DNS>.pluginpacks.<name>, and each plugin's and member's is <reverse-DNS>.plugins.<name>. No plugin may use an id the app's own writers stage under — run.vineyard.agent (the AI agent), run.vineyard.merge (a merge), run.vineyard.retest (a re-verification) and run.vineyard.value (the value menu's New node) — since the app tells its own writes from a plugin's by that id. A document with any identifier that breaks this is refused whole: none of its plugins is listed or run, and the analyst gets a red notice naming the pack and asking for a corrected release. The schemas already forbid these ids by their shape. Registry CI refuses a pinned document that breaks this rule too, so an author hears of it when the entry is reviewed (see Publishing), and the client checks it anyway, because a dev override is reviewed by no one and a document approved before this check was never held to it.

docs.title: When to use a pack
docs.text: Reach for a pack when several plugins share a repo, a build pipeline, a theme, or a release cadence — like a demo/validation set or a coherent toolkit. If two plugins are genuinely unrelated, ship them as separate entries instead so users can install only what they want.

docs.title: Publishing to the registry
docs.text: Publishing a Plugin Pack, Type Pack, or Skill Pack to the public Vineyard marketplace is a single pull request against the registry repo. You add one file, CI validates it, a human merges it, and your entry goes live on the next registry fetch — no app release required.

docs.title: The registry repo holds metadata only
docs.text:
Submissions go to Vineyard-Intelligence/registry. The repo carries pointers and derived facets, never code and never copies of your manifest or bundle. Your full manifest/Type Pack JSON, README, screenshots, and bundle all stay in your author repo at the pinned ref; the marketplace detail page hydrates from there lazily. The app and the marketplace fetch that pinned content through https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/{repo}@{ref}/{path}, and any GitHub owner is served: the app runs plugin code from the CDN's /gh/ path, not from one organization, so a Plugin Pack in your own repo runs like any other. What decides whether a pack is loaded is the registry's approved-ref list — the app loads only a repo@ref/path on it, checks the fetched document against the SHA-256 recorded there, and checks a plugin's code module against the SHA-256 recorded for it before running it. The reviewed, immutable commit is the unit of trust.

Path Role packs/<identifier>.json The source, and the only thing a submission adds. One file per pack, named for its identifier. registry/community-pluginpacks.json Published index of Plugin Packs — generated, one lean entry per pack: identifier, name, author, summary, repo, ref, path, version, platforms, scopes_summary, verified. registry/community-typepacks.json Symmetric for Type Packs; carries categories/type_count instead of scopes (no code executes). registry/community-skillpacks.json Symmetric for Skill Packs; carries applies_to/section_count/requires instead of scopes (text only, no code executes). registry/approved-*.json Generated from the history of packs/ by scripts/build_approved.py. Lists every repo@ref/path the registry has ever approved, with a SHA-256 of that document and, for a Plugin Pack, of each code module it runs (bundle_sha256). The app loads only pointers on this list whose bytes match the digest, and runs only code whose bytes match its own. schemas/ The published meta-schemas CI validates entries against. verified-authors.json Who may show the verified badge, the namespaces each owns, and the GitHub numeric id their pack repository must be owned by. Operator-owned — a submission never edits it. SPEC.md The registry contract in full — entry format, the pinning rule, what CI enforces.

Do not edit registry/community-*.json or registry/approved-*.json

The three catalogs are built from packs/ by scripts/build_registry.py, and the three approved-ref lists by scripts/build_approved.py. Both are rebuilt and committed on merge, so a hand edit is overwritten. Your content_type decides which catalog your entry joins — you never pick one.

docs.title: Submission workflow
docs.text:
1. Fork Vineyard-Intelligence/registry.
  2. Pin an immutable ref — the commit SHA of the release in your author repo. Tags and branches are mutable and rejected; resolve a tag/branch to its commit SHA with python scripts/resolve_ref.py owner/repo <tag-or-branch>. The commit must be on a branch or tag of the repository named in repo — push or merge your release there before you pin it, and keep it there.
  3. Add one file, packs/<identifier>.json, holding your entry. The filename must match the entry's identifier exactly.
  4. Open a PR. The validate workflow posts its result as a status check.
  5. Fix any failures, then wait for a human merge.
  6. After green CI + merge, the catalogs are rebuilt and your entry is live on the next registry fetch — clients pull the static JSON.

A few things worth knowing going in:

  • The identifier in the entry must equal manifest.identifier (or typepack.identifier) and uses the reverse-DNS form <your-namespace>.pluginpacks.* / .typepacks.* / .skillpacks.* — see the three content types. Inside a Plugin Pack, every plugin and member is <your-namespace>.plugins.<name>, and none may be one of the ids the app's own writers use (run.vineyard.agent, .merge, .retest, .value): the app refuses the whole pack otherwise, whatever the registry accepted (see Plugin Packs).
  • ref is the only thing pinning your code. To ship a new version, edit your pack's file in place with the new ref and a higher version — see Updates.
  • Derived fields (platforms, scopes_summary, categories, type_count, …) are projections of the full manifest/Type Pack so the browse page renders without fetching every manifest. CI recomputes scopes_summary, platforms, services, plugin_count, desktop_only, icon, section_count and type_count from the pinned document and rejects the entry if any it carries disagree. categories and a Skill Pack's applies_to/requires are not recomputed, so keep them accurate yourself.

docs.title: A pack's line and its page
docs.text:
A Plugin Pack, a Type Pack and a Skill Pack each carry two texts at pack level, the way a browser extension store shows a short line under the name and an About section below. Both are required.

Field What it is Limit Who reads it summary The line under the name: what the pack does, standing on its own. 250 characters, one line Every card, picker and the agent's lists description The pack's page, its About section, in Markdown: what it is for, what each plugin adds, what it costs, what it needs, what it exposes. 16,000 characters The marketplace drawer when a pack is opened, and the agent only when it asks for that one pack by id

The page is rendered as Markdown with its headings, lists, tables and code, and with nothing that acts: an image is never loaded (its address is shown instead, so opening a pack never tells its author who looked at it), a link is not clickable (its text is shown with the full address beside it), and raw HTML is dropped.

Write the page for the analyst deciding whether to install the pack. The agent does not read it when it lists plugins or skill packs; it gets a pack's page from list_plugins with pack_id only when a plugin's own entry does not say enough, and it treats the page as data, never as instructions. A Skill Pack's page is never sent to the agent at all: the overview and the sections are the text written for it. Individual plugins keep their own description unchanged.

Documents from before the page. A document without summary was written before the page existed, and there description is the one line. The app still reads one, so every project pinned to such a commit keeps loading it, but the registry lists none: move the old line into summary, write the page into description, and re-pin. A lone vineyard:plugin document cannot carry both, because its description is the plugin's own; list it as a Plugin Pack of one.

docs.title: What CI enforces
docs.text: Every check below is blocking — a pull request cannot merge until they all pass. They run in .github/workflows/validate.yml.

docs.title: The entry
docs.text:
• Filename matches identifier, and content_type is one of the four known kinds. (build_registry.py)
  • Registry-entry schema. The entry validates against schemas/registry-plugin-entry, registry-typepack-entry, or registry-skillpack-entry. (validate.py)
  • Declared dependencies resolve, and are still live. A Skill Pack's requires and a Plugin Pack's typepacks must name packs that are in this catalog — the marketplace builds its co-install offer from those lists. A pack added in the same pull request counts, so a Type Pack and the plugin that uses it can land together. A dependency that has been delisted is also rejected. (validate.py)
  • Namespace and authorship. A namespace listed in verified-authors.json may only be published under by its owner, and an author name listed there may only be worn inside its own namespaces — so neither run.vineyard.* nor author: VINEYARD can be claimed by anyone else. (validate.py) verified is derived, not submitted. build_registry.py sets it to true when the identifier's namespace is claimed in verified-authors.json by the handle in author, and discards any value in the submission. Each author listed there also carries github.id and github.handle: validate.py resolves the pack repository's owner and requires owner.id == github.id, so an entry cannot borrow VINEYARD's namespace and author while pointing at someone else's repository. The handle is display text; verification never compares it.

docs.title: The pin
docs.text:
• Immutable ref. Must be a commit SHA (40-hex or 64-hex). Tags and branches can be moved and are rejected. (verify_pinned.py)
  • The commit belongs to repo. Some branch or tag of the repository named in repo must contain the pinned commit. A commit that no branch or tag contains is refused — one that exists only in a fork, for example, or a pull request's own commit after a squash merge (pin the commit the merge created instead). Push or merge it into repo (or tag it there) and pin that; resolve_ref.py gives you the commit a branch or tag points at. A commit on the default branch, or the one a tag or branch points at, is found. This applies to every entry, verified or not, and is checked when your pull request adds the entry or changes its repo or ref. Keep that branch or tag for as long as the entry is listed — tagging each release is the simplest way — and do not rewrite its history: a commit nothing in repo holds any more is not guaranteed to stay available. (validate.py) The November 2026 rewrites of the Vineyard-Intelligence pack repositories broke this rule on purpose, once to remove machine hostnames from commit identities and once to remove Claude co-author trailers and Claude identities: each moved ref has a twin row in approved-baseline.json (the frozen input to registry/approved-*.json) with the same tree and digest, and the old row stays approved, so a project pinned to the old commit keeps loading it and the new commit is approved for the same content.
  • The pinned document matches the entry. The document at repo@ref/path is fetched and its identifier, content_type, and version must equal what your entry advertises. An entry whose metadata was bumped without re-pinning the ref fails here.
  • The pack states both texts, and the card line is the document's own. The pinned document must have summary and a non-empty description, and your entry's summary must equal the document's exactly — the entry mirrors the line the document states. The page stays in the document; the marketplace reads it from the pinned commit when the pack is opened. (verify_pinned.py)
  • The line and the page are well formed. summary is one line of at most 250 characters; the page is text of at most 16,000 characters with no control characters but newlines and tabs; a lone vineyard:plugin document is refused. See A pack's line and its page. (verify_pinned.py)
  • Every plugin is named in its schema's shape, and none as one of the app's own writers. In a Plugin Pack document the pack's identifier must be <reverse-DNS>.pluginpacks.<name> and each member's <reverse-DNS>.plugins.<name>, matched against the patterns the schemas themselves give, and none may be run.vineyard.agent, run.vineyard.merge, run.vineyard.retest or run.vineyard.value, the ids the app stages its own writes under. The entry's pattern admits either kind segment and names no member, so this is checked on the pinned document. The app refuses such a document whole (see Plugin Packs), so such a pack, were it listed, would fail to load for everyone who installs it. (verify_pinned.py, test_plugin_ids.py)
  • Every summary field is recomputed, not trusted. scopes_summary, platforms, services, plugin_count, desktop_only, icon, section_count and type_count are derived from the pinned document and compared to what you wrote. scopes_summary.network is true when a member declares network, network_configurable or web_probe.
  • A configurable endpoint reads the plugin's own address setting. Every network_configurable entry of the pack and of each member must name a scopes.config key of type: "url" that the same plugin declares, list its methods from GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE (upper case, each once), list only https and http in schemes when it has one, and carry no field but config_key, methods, purpose and schemes. The app grants nothing for an entry that does not read such a setting, and matches methods exactly, so such a pack would install and then have every request refused. (verify_pinned.py, test_scopes.py)
  • The bundle is in the pinned commit and matches the manifest. For Plugin Packs, platforms.web.entry of the pack and of each member must be a path inside the repository, relative to its root (dist/pack.mjs). Each segment of that path may use only ASCII letters, digits, ., _ and -, and may not be . or ... Anything else, such as an absolute URL, a leading /, a backslash or a %, fails here before anything is fetched. The module it names is fetched at the pinned commit, and the version and license it declares for the pack and for each member must equal the manifest's. A manifest edited without rebuilding dist/ fails here, and so does an entry that 404s. (verify_pinned.py)
  • The approved list records your code's digest. After merge, the SHA-256 of each module your pack runs is recorded on its approved row, read out of the pinned manifest, and the app refuses a module whose bytes do not match it. The digest is taken from GitHub at the pinned commit, and the build also fetches the same file through jsDelivr and fails if the bytes differ. Every pack the catalog lists must have one: the build fails, and nothing is published, when a listed pack's document or modules cannot be hashed, so the pinned commit has to be on GitHub when your entry merges. The module must be one self-contained file. (build_approved.py, test_approved.py)

docs.title: The type graph
docs.text:
Every io.consumes / io.produces entry is resolved against the Type Packs published in this catalog:

  • the category.name must be a type some published Type Pack actually defines;
  • the typepack field must name the pack that really defines it;
  • that Type Pack must appear in your entry's typepacks list.

A Type Pack the registry does not carry is not acceptable. Publish the Type Pack first, then the plugin that uses it.

Type Packs get four checks of their own here. A category.name may be defined by only one published Type Pack. Every identity_properties key must name an existing property of that type that is not array, object or json. Every normalize must be one of crypto_address, hex, hostname, ip, cidr and url, may sit beside "case_insensitive": true only for hostname, ip and cidr, and must be on a property that is not array, object or json, because an app that does not know a rule falls back to the flag without a word. Every duplicate_key must be a boolean on such a property, outside the identity.

docs.title: What a human weighs
docs.text:
There is no automated static analysis of your bundle; a person reads it and weighs the following. None is an automatic rejection:

  • Breadth of requested scopes against what the pack plausibly needs.
  • node:delete / edge:delete usage (graph-destructive verbs).
  • network + node:read together (data leaves the graph, and there is egress).
  • network_configurable: it reaches whatever server the analyst names, often one on their own network. The reviewer reads what the bundle sends there, and whether anything it reads there leaves for a fixed network endpoint.
  • Minified-only bundles — no readable source to inspect. Ship readable code if you want a fast review.
  • Secret-looking params keys. Credentials belong in scopes.config with secret: true, never in user-facing params.
  • A native or subprocess desktop runtime, which the app does not run today.

Destructive ≠ rejected

The Chaos pack — Korean Roulette, Russian Roulette, Thanos Snap, Black Hole, Dumb AI Optimizer, Schrödinger's Node — leans entirely on node:delete/edge:delete. It publishes fine.

docs.title: Sample submissions
docs.text:
A Plugin Pack, filed as packs/run.vineyard.pluginpacks.chaos.json. Note plugin_count marks a pack with multiple plugins (one file → many plugins):

{
  "identifier": "run.vineyard.pluginpacks.chaos",
  "content_type": "vineyard:pluginpack",
  "name": "Chaos Reference Pack",
  "author": "VINEYARD",
  "summary": "Six graph-manipulation plugins for demos and validation.",
  "repo": "Vineyard-Intelligence/pluginpack-chaos",
  "ref": "024c36cf17011abb4a7fc6004ced208751c13473",
  "path": "plugins/chaos-pack.manifest.json",
  "version": "1.0.3",
  "platforms": ["web"],
  "scopes_summary": { "network": false, "graph_write": true, "secret_config": false },
  "plugin_count": 6,
  "icon": "boxes",
  "typepacks": []
}

A Type Pack, filed as packs/run.vineyard.typepacks.infrastructure.json (no scopes; categories/type_count drive the facets):

{
  "identifier": "run.vineyard.typepacks.infrastructure",
  "content_type": "vineyard:typepack",
  "name": "Infrastructure",
  "author": "VINEYARD",
  "summary": "Network-infrastructure and web OSINT entities (IPs, domains, URLs, hosts, ASNs, netblocks, DNS/WHOIS records, TLS certificates, SSH host keys, technologies, web fingerprints and tracking/ad-account identifiers) and their relationships.",
  "repo": "Vineyard-Intelligence/typepack-basic",
  "ref": "721e3fdab2bdcace019cd9329b47b1014d8acdbb",
  "path": "typepacks/infrastructure.json",
  "version": "4.0.0",
  "categories": ["infrastructure", "web"],
  "type_count": 15,
  "icon": "network"
}

Field reference

The required fields are identifier, content_type, name, author, summary, repo, ref, path. content_type is the literal vineyard:plugin, vineyard:pluginpack, vineyard:typepack, or vineyard:skillpack. The full field list and constraints live in registry-schema.

docs.title: After merge
docs.text: Merging triggers a rebuild of the three catalog files and the three approved-ref lists from packs/, committed straight back to main. The next time a client fetches the registry your entry appears in the browser with its derived badges.

docs.title: Taking a pack down
docs.text:
Deleting your entry is not how a pack is retired: the pack disappears from the browse page, but every project that already has it goes on loading it from the pinned commit. Instead, the row stays and gains a status block:

"status": {
  "state": "deprecated",
  "reason": "Unmaintained since the API it collects from shut down.",
  "since": "2026-08-09",
  "replacement": "com.acme.pluginpacks.recon"
}
State In the catalog In a project that has it deprecated Still browsable and installable, badged Loads normally; the analyst is told once per project open withdrawn Hidden from browse unless the project has it; install refused Not loaded — the reason is shown instead

reason reaches analysts verbatim, so write it for them: what happened, and what to do. replacement must name a live pack of the same kind.

Deprecating your own pack is an ordinary pull request. Withdrawal is the operator's call, reserved for content that turned out to be harmful or has disappeared.

Two things to expect:

  • Fix the dependants first. A live pack may not list a delisted one in requires (or typepacks), so CI will name every pack that depends on yours. Update them, or delist them in the same pull request.
  • A withdrawn entry is not pin-verified, so its content may be gone. A deprecated pack is still pin-verified, so it must still resolve.

Removing the row outright is only for an entry nobody could have installed: a mistaken submission, or a duplicate.

docs.text:
• Distribution — how pack content is actually fetched and verified.
  • Updates — shipping a new version by re-pinning to a new immutable ref.
  • registry-schema — full field-by-field schema reference.
  • scopes — scope strings and the endpoint allowlist rule.
  • Marketplace — the static marketplace browser your entry lands in.

docs.title: Quickstart — your first plugin
docs.text: Build, test, and locally load a working Vineyard plugin end to end. By the end you will have a single main.js bundle that does export default definePlugin({ manifest, run }), a unit test that runs run(ctx) with no app at all, and the plugin loaded in the app through the dev loader.

docs.title: What a plugin is
docs.text: A plugin is a bundled main.js whose default export is the result of definePlugin({ manifest, run }). At runtime (web) it executes inside a dedicated module Web Worker with no DOM, no window, no localStorage, and no network of its own. The site's other storage is blocked too, in every build including a local dev build: IndexedDB, Cache Storage, BroadcastChannel, navigator.storage and Web Locks are undefined or throw a SecurityError, so keep a run's state in memory. Everything it can do flows through the ctx object passed to run — and a ctx member is absent unless its scope was granted. See Architecture and Security for the full model.

docs.title: 1. Set up a repo and bundler
docs.text:
You ship one JavaScript file. Use any bundler that can produce a single ESM file — esbuild and Vite are both first-class.

mkdir my-plugin && cd my-plugin
npm init -y
npm i -D esbuild typescript vitest

There is no SDK package to install: the SDK is a single file. Download sdk.ts, the app's own copy (its first line gives the date), into src/ and import from ./sdk. Copies vendored in published pack repos can be older and lack newer fields such as SafeRequestInit.timeoutMs, so use this one.

esbuildVite 
// package.json (scripts)
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "esbuild src/main.ts --bundle --format=esm --outfile=dist/main.js",
    "watch": "esbuild src/main.ts --bundle --format=esm --outfile=dist/main.js --watch --servedir=. --cors-origin=http://localhost:3000"
  }
}

Vite needs library mode to emit a single ESM file (npm i -D vite):

// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    lib: { entry: "src/main.ts", formats: ["es"], fileName: () => "main.js" },
    emptyOutDir: false, // lets the dev server see each rebuild of dist/main.js
  },
});

// package.json (scripts)
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build",
    "watch": "vite build --watch",  // rebuilds dist/main.js on every save
    "dev": "vite"                   // serves this folder (manifest and dist/main.js) for the dev loader
  }
}

Run watch and dev side by side.

The build output (dist/main.js) is what the entry field in your manifest points at, and what the dev loader imports when the plugin runs.

docs.title: 2. Write definePlugin({ manifest, run })
docs.text:
Here is a minimal whole-graph plugin, a simplified copy of Korean Roulette from the Chaos reference pack under an example namespace (com.example; use your own): it keeps one random node and deletes everything else. (consumes: [] means it operates on the whole graph: it appears in the Run plugins… panel's "Whole-graph / input via form" section, whether the panel was opened from a node, the canvas, the toolbar or the menu bar.)

// src/main.ts
import { definePlugin } from "./sdk";

export default definePlugin({
  manifest: {
    identifier: "com.example.plugins.korean_roulette",
    content_type: "vineyard:plugin",
    name: "Korean Roulette",
    version: "1.0.0",
    description: "Keep one random node; delete everything else.",
    platforms: {
      primary: "web",
      web: { runtime: "sandbox-js", entry: "dist/main.js" },
    },
    io: { consumes: [], produces: [] },
    scopes: { graph: ["node:read", "node:delete", "edge:delete"] },
    lifecycle: { persistence: "ephemeral", controls: ["progress", "cancel"] },
  },
  async run(ctx) {
    const { nodes } = await ctx.graph!.list!();           // node:read
    if (nodes.length === 0) return { summary: "empty graph" };

    const survivor = nodes[Math.floor(Math.random() * nodes.length)];
    const doomed = nodes.filter((n) => n.id !== survivor.id).map((n) => n.id);

    await ctx.graph!.deleteNodes!(doomed);                // node:delete (edges cascade)
    return { summary: `survivor: ${survivor.id}`, counts: { deleted: doomed.length } };
  },
});

Why the ! operators?

ctx.graph and each method on it are optional in the type — they exist only when the matching scope is granted. Because this manifest declares node:read and node:delete, ctx.graph.list and ctx.graph.deleteNodes are present at runtime. The non-null assertions document that contract; a scope-[] plugin like Dumb AI Optimizer would correctly see ctx.graph === undefined.

run returns an optional RunResult ({ summary?, counts? }). All graph effects happen through ctx — the return value is just a summary surfaced in the task UI.

docs.title: 3. Manifest essentials
docs.text:
Every field below is required unless noted. The full schema is documented in plugin-schema; the manifest authoring guide is plugin-manifest.

Field Notes identifier Reverse-DNS, <your-namespace>.plugins.*. content_type Must be the literal vineyard:plugin. name, version, description version is SemVer. platforms.web { runtime: "sandbox-js", entry: "dist/main.js" }. sandbox-js runs your JS in the worker — it is the only runtime the host executes. (web-proxy is accepted by the schema but not dispatched; see plugin-manifest.) Installed code is fetched from the registry entry's pinned commit, dev code from the URL you load in the dev loader (see distribution). io { consumes: [], produces: [] } — empty consumes = whole-graph plugin. Non-empty entries are qualified types like infrastructure.ip_address and decide where the plugin is offered in the Run plugins… panel. See Type Packs. scopes The only authority your plugin gets. Here, scopes.graph lists node:read, node:delete, edge:delete. See scopes. lifecycle persistence: "ephemeral" plus the controls you support (progress, cancel, …). See lifecycle.

Never put secrets in params

Never put a secret-looking key in params — those values are recorded. Declare secrets as scopes.config with secret: true: they are entered in the plugin's settings form (masked), kept per signed-in account (in the OS keychain on desktop, for the tab session in the browser), and handed only to the plugin that declared them via ctx.config — see Security. Korean Roulette needs no secrets and no network, which is exactly why it's a clean first plugin.

docs.title: 4. Unit test with createMockContext
docs.text:
The SDK ships a test harness so you can exercise run(ctx) with no app, no GitHub, no server. createMockContext({ nodes, edges, grantedScopes }) builds a HostContext whose graph member (and each write method on it) exists only for the granted graph verbs; net.fetch/net.probe exist only when you pass netHandler/probeHandler, and config comes from the config option. It records what the plugin did under ctx.mock for assertions.

// test/korean_roulette.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { createMockContext } from "../src/sdk";
import plugin from "../src/main";

describe("Korean Roulette", () => {
  it("keeps exactly one node", async () => {
    const nodes = [
      { id: "a", type: "infrastructure.ip_address", data: {} },
      { id: "b", type: "infrastructure.ip_address", data: {} },
      { id: "c", type: "infrastructure.ip_address", data: {} },
    ];

    const ctx = createMockContext({
      nodes,
      grantedScopes: { graph: ["node:read", "node:delete", "edge:delete"] },
    });

    const result = await plugin.run(ctx);

    // n-1 nodes were deleted; exactly one survives.
    expect(ctx.mock.deletedNodeIds.length).toBe(nodes.length - 1);
    expect(result?.counts?.deleted).toBe(nodes.length - 1);
  });
});

Useful ctx.mock fields for assertions: deletedNodeIds, deletedEdgeIds, createdNodes, createdEdges, updatedNodes, and progress. All six reference plugins (Korean Roulette, Russian Roulette, Thanos Snap, Black Hole, Dumb AI Optimizer, Schrödinger's Node) are testable exactly this way.

Test the scope boundary, not just the happy path

Pass grantedScopes: {} (or omit graph) and assert your plugin degrades gracefully when ctx.graph is undefined. This catches the most common runtime surprise: assuming a capability you didn't declare. It does not prove your read scopes: the mock provides get, list, edges and neighbors whenever any graph verb is granted, while the app requires node:read / edge:read for them. See Testing with createMockContext.

docs.title: 5. Load it in the app (dev loader)
docs.text:
GitHub and the registry are a distribution layer; during development the app loads your plugin from a URL you serve. The dev loader reads a JSON manifest document, not the bundle, so first write one next to src/ — the manifest from step 2, as JSON:

// plugin.manifest.json
{
  "identifier": "com.example.plugins.korean_roulette",
  "content_type": "vineyard:plugin",
  "name": "Korean Roulette",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Keep one random node; delete everything else.",
  "platforms": { "primary": "web", "web": { "runtime": "sandbox-js", "entry": "dist/main.js" } },
  "io": { "consumes": [], "produces": [] },
  "scopes": { "graph": ["node:read", "node:delete", "edge:delete"] },
  "lifecycle": { "persistence": "ephemeral", "controls": ["progress", "cancel"] }
}

Open Settings → Plugins → Development → Load a pack from a URL, choose Plugin Pack, and enter the absolute URL of your plugin's manifest document (a JSON file with content_type: "vineyard:plugin", or a vineyard:pluginpack document, whose platforms.web.entry points at your bundle, e.g. dist/main.js, relative to the manifest's folder). The frontend's own npm run dev (web) build takes plugin code from any http(s) URL, so a dev-server URL (esbuild --watch --servedir or vite) works there, as long as the server sends CORS headers and serves the bundle as JavaScript; the desktop dev build follows the packaged rule. The released app runs plugin code only from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/, so point the dev loader at a pinned commit there instead; a localhost URL loads the manifest, but the run fails with "plugin code is loaded only from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/" (see §6). The bundle must be one self-contained file. The URL is kept on this device per signed-in account and loads into every project you open — reopen the project after adding it. The identifier in the JSON manifest must match the one in definePlugin, or the run fails with plugin not loadable: <identifier>.

Try Korean Roulette on a throwaway project

Because it deletes nearly everything, run it against a scratch project first. Watch the task panel show the run, review and apply the staged deletions, then see the survivor node standing alone in the canvas.

docs.title: 6. Integration testing in the app
docs.text:
When unit tests pass, exercise the plugin end-to-end against a real graph. On app.vineyard.run and in the packaged desktop app, plugin code is loaded only from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ — any GitHub repo, at a pinned commit, through jsDelivr. So the dev loop does not need a local app build: push your manifest and bundle to your repo, add https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/<you>/<repo>@<commit>/<manifest> in the dev loader, trigger a run on a throwaway project, watch it in the Tasks panel, then open its staged change set and apply it. A localhost URL is refused: the manifest is fetched, but the run fails before any code loads. The frontend's own npm run dev (web) build takes code from any http(s) URL, so a dev-server URL does work there — that build needs the frontend repository, which is not public, and the packaged desktop app is not that build. Wherever it runs, the packaged app also blocks a plugin's own fetch/XHR: go through ctx.net/ctx.service only.

Debugging

console.log output from your plugin's worker shows in the browser DevTools console of the local dev build. ctx.progress.log is discarded, so use ctx.progress.set({ message }) to show status: the message appears after the plugin's name in its Tasks row. The packaged desktop app has no DevTools.

The dev loader relaxes two protections

To keep the loop fast, the dev loader may auto-approve scopes and skip the integrity check (no registry digest, no commit pin — see Distribution and Updates). Use the dev loader only for code you wrote or trust, and re-test the published artifact through the normal install path before relying on it.

docs.title: 7. Going live
docs.text: When the plugin works locally, publish it: push the version to your repo, then pin its commit SHA in a one-entry registry PR. The full process — repo layout, immutable refs, and the registry pull request — is in Publishing. Shipping more than one plugin from a single bundle? See Plugin Packs (the Chaos pack ships all six reference plugins from one bundle this way).
