docs.title: SDK & host context
docs.text: The plugin SDK is the small author-facing TypeScript surface you build a plugin against. It gives you two define helpers, the typed HostContext (ctx) your run function receives, and an in-process mock for unit tests. The SDK is a single TypeScript file, sdk.ts, which matches the app as of this release. Copy it into your repo and import from ./sdk. Copies vendored in published pack repos can be older and lack newer fields such as SafeRequestInit.timeoutMs.

docs.title: The two define helpers
docs.text:
A plugin's bundle does a default export through one of two factory functions. Both are identity functions — they exist purely to give you type-checking against the SDK shapes.

import { definePlugin, definePluginPack } from "./sdk";

// A single plugin
export default definePlugin({ manifest, run });

// Or a pack — one bundle carrying many plugins (see plugin-packs.md)
export default definePluginPack({
  identifier: "run.vineyard.pluginpacks.chaos",
  name: "Chaos",
  version: "1.0.0",
  plugins: [koreanRoulette, russianRoulette, thanosSnap /* ... */],
});
Helper Signature Shape it validates definePlugin (p: VineyardPlugin) => VineyardPlugin { manifest, run } definePluginPack (pack: VineyardPluginPack) => VineyardPluginPack { identifier, name, version, summary?, description?, plugins[] }

A bundle's default export may be a single plugin, an array of plugins, or a pack (PluginEntry); the host flattens them with flattenPlugins. See Plugin Packs for the packaging rules.

VineyardPlugin.run is the entrypoint:

run(ctx: HostContext): Promise<RunResult | void>;

Graph effects happen through ctx; the return value ({ summary?, counts? }) is only a human-readable summary surfaced in the task UI.

docs.title: HostContext (ctx)
docs.text:
ctx is a Comlink proxy to the host. The worker that runs your code has no DOM and no network of its own — only the members its scopes granted. Your graph writes are staged: they are applied only after the analyst reviews and approves the change set, except for a run the AI agent launched under Apply automatically (see the security model). Network requests are checked by the host against the endpoints your manifest declared. See the security model.

A member is absent unless its scope was granted

ctx.graph, ctx.net, and ctx.config are optional and only exist when the corresponding scope was declared and granted. A no-scope plugin like Dumb AI Optimizer correctly sees ctx.graph === undefined. Guard with optional chaining or feature-test before use. Within ctx.graph, each method is likewise present only if its specific verb (node:delete, edge:create, …) was granted.

docs.title: Always present
docs.text:
These members exist on every run, regardless of scopes.

Member Type What it gives you ctx.run { runId, projectId, pluginId, grantedScopes, platform } Identity of this run; grantedScopes is the manifest's scope set as approved at install; platform is "web" or "desktop". ctx.input { selection: string[] } The node ids this run targets. From the Run plugins panel: for a plugin with consumes, the selected nodes of a consumed type (scope Selected) or every node of those types in the project (scope Whole project); for a consumes-less plugin, the current selection. run is called once with the whole list — iterate all of it. Black Hole reads ctx.input.selection[0]. When the AI agent runs a plugin, selection holds the live node ids the agent passed. They are not filtered to your consumed types, and the agent is asked, but not forced, to pass none to a plugin with an empty consumes. Check each node's type, and have a whole-graph plugin ignore selection. ctx.params Readonly<Record<string, unknown>> This run's user input from the pre-run form (only required is enforced — pattern/minimum/maximum/default are not applied, so validate and default in run). File fields arrive as File objects. Nothing is enforced when the AI agent fills params, not even required, so validate and default every value in run. ctx.progress { set?, log?, status? } Drives the continuously-managed task UI (details below). ctx.signal AbortSignal Cooperative cancellation — you must observe it. ctx.onCancel (handler) => void Register a cleanup handler invoked on cancel.

Cancellation is cooperative

Cancellation is cooperative but bounded. Poll ctx.signal.aborted, pass ctx.signal to long awaits, or register ctx.onCancel(...): after Stop the host waits 3 seconds for run to return, then terminates the worker. Whatever the run staged before stopping is kept for review. Independently, every run has a wall-clock budget (lifecycle.timeout_ms, default 10 minutes, max 60) after which the worker is terminated and the run fails. A run that fails, for this or any other reason, discards what it had staged; only Stop keeps partial results.

docs.title: Progress, status, and logging
docs.text:
These live under ctx.progress (each method optional but always available on the object):

ctx.progress?.set?.({ percent: 40, message: "Scanning neighbors", phase: "expand" });
ctx.progress?.log?.("found 12 candidate nodes");
ctx.progress?.status?.("waiting");   // "running" | "waiting"

Only set is surfaced: percent drives the Tasks row's progress and message is shown after the plugin name (phase is ignored). log and status are accepted but currently discarded — to show a rate-limit pause, report it through set({ message: "waiting for rate limit…" }). The SDK has no built-in backoff helper.

docs.title: Scope-gated members
docs.text: Each of the following is undefined unless its scope was granted.

docs.title: graph (graph:* scopes)
docs.text:
Present iff at least one graph verb was granted. Each method present iff its verb was granted.

// reads — node:read
ctx.graph?.get?(nodeId): Promise<GraphNode | null>
ctx.graph?.list?(opts?: { type?: string }): Promise<{ nodes: GraphNode[] }>

// reads — edge:read
ctx.graph?.edges?(): Promise<GraphEdge[]>
ctx.graph?.neighbors?(nodeId): Promise<{ nodes: GraphNode[]; edges: GraphEdge[] }>

// single writes — node:create / node:update / node:delete / edge:create / edge:delete
ctx.graph?.createNode?(draft: EntityDraft): Promise<GraphNode>
ctx.graph?.updateNode?(nodeId, data): Promise<void>
ctx.graph?.deleteNode?(nodeId): Promise<void>
ctx.graph?.createEdge?(edge: EdgeDraft): Promise<void>
ctx.graph?.updateEdge?(edgeId, patch: { label?: string; data?: Record<string, unknown> }): Promise<void>   // edge:create
ctx.graph?.deleteEdge?(edgeId): Promise<void>

// bulk
ctx.graph?.deleteNodes?(ids: string[]): Promise<{ deleted: number }>
ctx.graph?.deleteEdges?(ids: string[]): Promise<{ deleted: number }>

list({ type }) filters by node type over the whole graph in one call — it is not cursor-paginated (used by whole-graph plugins like Thanos Snap). neighbors returns the 1-hop neighborhood (used by Black Hole). updateNode and createEdge take a delta/draft and stage it for review rather than returning the resulting record, so both resolve void — re-read via get/list if you need the applied state. updateNode merges: values you pass replace those fields and every other field is kept, including on a node your run just created. Empty strings and null are ignored, so it cannot clear a field. It throws on an id that is not in the project. createNode de-duplicates by identity — the canonical type plus that type's identity_properties (else its label property, else value): if a live node (or one this run already created) has the same identity, it is reused and your fields are merged in, and that node is returned. It throws if type is not defined by an installed Type Pack. Both createNode and updateNode throw when the data fails the type's property checks; see What the app checks on node data. EdgeDraft.from/to are node ids — live ids or the ids createNode returned. label is free text describing the relationship; edges have no type.

Six fields merge differently, in updateNode and when createNode reuses a node, and again when the review is applied, against the node as it is then:

  • tlp is never lowered. A TLP label already on the node is replaced only by a stricter one, in the order TLP:CLEAR (TLP 1.0 WHITE), TLP:GREEN, TLP:AMBER, TLP:AMBER+STRICT, TLP:RED, read in any case, with or without a TLP prefix, which any run of characters other than letters and digits separates from the label (TLP:RED, TLP-RED, TLP=RED, TLP/RED), and with AMBER+STRICT also written AMBER STRICT or AMBER_STRICT. A value that starts with a bare label in brackets, such as (RED) or [AMBER], is read as that label too. A value with a label and other text, such as TLP:RED (Case 7 only) or RED - do not share, counts as the strictest label in it, so it keeps its text against a label of the same rank. A value with no label in it does not replace one that is.
  • source_report, created_by and markings (separated by ;), tags (by ,) and references (one per line) are lists. The parts you pass are added after the ones already there, each once, so a second source does not replace the first. An array is a list of its elements, and a string and an array meet the same way: the result keeps the shape already on the node.

updateEdge is gated by edge:create (the edge:update scope currently grants nothing). Omit label to leave the wording and its grade alone. EdgeDraft/updateEdge accept an optional data object that is merged into the edge; confidence, confidence_source, label_source and corroborated_by are host-owned and rejected. There is one edge per ordered node pair, so createEdge on a pair that is already linked proposes a relabel of that edge instead of adding one. A call that would change nothing stages nothing: no new wording, and data whose every key the edge already holds with that value, a null matching a key the edge does not have. The one exception is createEdge with the edge's own wording from a writer other than the one that drew it: that writer is recorded in corroborated_by once, in the same change as any data it brings. A plugin can therefore write a whole summary on every run, and the review lists only the edges whose summary changed. The analyst sees the edge's data read-only, in the Review dialog before applying and in the edge's Properties panel under Recorded with this link, so it is the place for where and when your source observed the link (source, first_seen, last_seen, …).

Nodes read back through get, list and neighbors, and the node createNode returns, carry a copy of their data, nested lists and objects included, so changing it changes nothing in the project or in what the run staged; write with updateNode.

Edges read back through edges and neighbors carry id, from_node_id, to_node_id, label and the edge's data as the project holds it: what its writers recorded and the host's own keys, such as confidence, confidence_source, label_source and corroborated_by. The data is a copy, so changing it changes nothing in the project; write with updateEdge. An edge that holds no data comes back without data, and so does every edge in older versions of the app, so read a missing data as not known rather than as no keys. updateEdge replaces each top-level key you send whole: to add to a list the edge holds, such as its recent rows, merge it with what you read and send the result.

docs.title: net (network scope)
docs.text:
Present iff a network or network_configurable scope is declared (or, in the desktop app, web_probe — then only probe exists). fetch is limited to the manifest.scopes.network endpoints, the addresses the analyst set for network_configurable, and their declared methods. While a configurable address is not set, a request for it rejects with an Error that names the setting. Requests are sent without cookies and pass your request headers, including Authorization, through unchanged. A request that carries any header or a body does not follow a redirect: a 3xx answer rejects with an Error whose message starts with redirect not followed. A request with neither follows redirects as the browser does. The six reference plugins use no network.

ctx.net?.fetch?(input: string, init?: SafeRequestInit): Promise<SafeResponse>

Each request has a deadline covering the whole response, body included: 60 s by default. Set init.timeoutMs to change it (at least 1 s, at most 10 minutes); 0, a negative number or a value that is not a number gives the 60 s default. A request that misses it rejects with an Error named TimeoutError, whose message names only the method and origin, e.g. GET https://api.example.com did not answer within 60s; an AbortError means the run was stopped. The run's wall-clock budget still applies on top.

The host remembers which origins did not answer in time, so a plugin that catches TimeoutError can still return normally and the gap is reported for it. If the run succeeds without staging anything, its notification turns yellow and ends (no answer from <origins>); for a run the AI agent launched, the agent is told which hosts did not answer, whatever the outcome.

There is no built-in retry/backoff helper — handle HTTP 429/Retry-After yourself and report the pause with ctx.progress?.set?.({ message: "waiting for rate limit…" }) while you wait.

docs.title: net.probe (web_probe scope, desktop only)
docs.text:
Present iff scopes.web_probe is declared and the plugin is running in the desktop shell — it stays absent in the web build even when the scope is granted. Performs ONE anonymous request to an arbitrary public host, for plugins that cannot know their target hosts in advance: no cookies, no Origin, redirects are not followed (the caller sees the true status), and private/loopback hosts are refused. Only the default ports (80/443) and methods GET/HEAD/POST are allowed; cookie, authorization, host and forwarding headers are dropped; unless you set User-Agent, a desktop-browser one is sent. maxBytes defaults to 512 KiB (max 2 MiB). timeoutMs bounds the connection and response: 8 s by default, at least 1 s and at most 20 s. The shell runs at most 48 probes at once, and the clock starts only once a probe has a slot and its host name has been checked (DNS has its own 3 s deadline, tried twice), so a probe can take longer than timeoutMs. Up to 2048 probes wait for a slot; past that a probe resolves at once with error: "too many queued probes". A refused or failed probe resolves with status: 0 and error set rather than throwing.

Two options change what comes back:

  • bodyEncoding: "base64" returns the body base64-encoded, for binary content such as a favicon. Check response.bodyEncoding === "base64" before decoding.
  • headerNames: true (GET or HEAD only) makes the request over HTTP/1.1 and returns headerNames: the response header names exactly as the server sent them — order, case and repeats. The body is not read.
ctx.net?.probe?(input: string, init?: SafeProbeInit): Promise<SafeProbeResponse>

docs.title: service (scopes.services)
docs.text:
Present iff scopes.services names at least one Vineyard-operated service (currently rdap, open to any pack, and telegram, reserved for run.vineyard.pluginpacks.telegram — other packs calling it get an error). Calls throw in a build running without a Vineyard account (local mode). The destination is a NAME, not a URL — the host resolves it and attaches the analyst's credential; an Authorization header you pass cannot override it.

ctx.service?(name: string, path: string, init?: SafeRequestInit): Promise<SafeResponse>

init.timeoutMs and the request deadline work as for net.fetch.

path is resolved against the service's root: a leading slash is dropped, so "/8.8.8.8" and "8.8.8.8" reach the same place. A path that would leave the root, through a .. that climbs out or an absolute URL, throws service path '<path>' escapes the '<name>' service root. Because a service request always carries the analyst's credential, it never follows a redirect: a 3xx answer rejects with an Error whose message starts with redirect not followed. A 401 means the analyst's Vineyard session has ended, not that the service is broken.

docs.title: config (scopes.config)
docs.text:
Present iff scopes.config is declared and the analyst has set at least one of its keys. Read-only, declared values only.

ctx.config?: Readonly<Record<string, string | number | boolean>>

Secrets reach only the plugin that declared them

secret: true only changes how the value is entered (a masked field) — the value is still handed to the plugin that declared it, as ctx.config.<key>; only keys your own manifest declares ever reach you. Members of one pack that declare the same key and call the same network origins share one value, so the analyst enters it once. Values are kept per signed-in account — in the OS keychain on desktop (for that session only on a desktop that cannot encrypt them), in that tab only in the browser. See secrets handling.

There is no publish scope

A plugin cannot post into the project chat/feed — there is no ctx.message. publish is not in the scopes schema; the app ignores it and grants nothing, so remove it. Report what you found by writing it into the graph instead.

docs.title: Bulk ops
docs.text: deleteNodes(ids[]) and deleteEdges(ids[]) are each a single bridge call that stages one delete per id in one batch, rather than hundreds of round trips. The whole call is refused (no node <id> in this project / no edge <id> in this project) if any id is unknown, so pass only ids you read from the graph. Prefer the bulk forms for whole-graph mutations (e.g. Korean Roulette wiping the whole graph). Each affected node and edge still appears as its own line in the change set the analyst reviews.

docs.title: A complete run(ctx) example
docs.text: For a full worked example (Korean Roulette) and a createMockContext unit test, see quickstart.

docs.title: Testing with createMockContext
docs.text:
createMockContext lets you unit-test run(ctx) with no app, no GitHub, and no server. It builds a HostContext over an in-memory graph: graph exists when any graph verb is granted and its write methods only for their verbs (the read methods are always present in the mock — production also requires node:read/edge:read); net.fetch/net.probe exist when you pass netHandler/probeHandler; config is whatever you pass (default {}). updateEdge and identity de-dup are not mocked. The returned context carries a mock record you can assert against.

The mock differs from the app in ways a passing test can hide:

  • Writes land in the mock's graph at once, so get, list, edges and neighbors see what the run created or changed and stop seeing what it deleted. In the app these reads come from the live graph, where staged changes do not show until they are applied; only get also finds a node the run created.
  • list({ type }) ignores type and returns every node.
  • get, list, edges and neighbors return the very node and edge objects you passed in, so changing one changes the mock's graph; the app returns a copy of each. An edge the run creates in the mock carries no data.
  • ctx.signal is undefined unless you pass signal, so code that reads ctx.signal.aborted needs one in tests; onCancel handlers are never called.
  • ctx.config is {} when you pass no config; in the app it is absent until the analyst sets one of the declared keys.
  • There is no ctx.service. net.fetch hands every request to your netHandler, with no check against your declared endpoints and methods, no deadline and no redirect rule.
  • createNode does not check the type against installed Type Packs, nor the data against the type's property checks.
  • updateNode writes "" and null over a field; the app ignores them. It also replaces tlp and the list fields like any other, where the app keeps the stricter tlp and adds to the lists.
  • createEdge stores no data on the edge (the draft you passed, data included, is recorded in mock.createdEdges), does not refuse the host-owned data keys, and always adds a new edge instead of relabelling an already-linked pair.
  • updateNode, deleteNode, deleteEdge and the bulk deletes do not refuse unknown ids.
  • run.platform is always "web".

MockContextOptions accepts nodes, edges, params, config, selection, grantedScopes, projectId, pluginId, signal, netHandler, and probeHandler. The ctx.mock record exposes nodes, edges, createdNodes, createdEdges, deletedNodeIds, deletedEdgeIds, updatedNodes, and progress. See quickstart for a full test example.

Reference implementation

createMockContext is implemented in sdk.ts itself; treat the names above as the stable contract.

docs.title: Sandbox & security
docs.text: How Vineyard contains plugin JavaScript: graph writes that are staged for the analyst's review instead of applied, a Web Worker sandbox with no ambient authority, a host-side egress allowlist, and secret-handling rules that keep API keys out of the graph and out of task history.

docs.title: What a plugin can reach
docs.text:
A plugin is third-party code the installing user chose to run. It can only touch what its scopes declare, on the project it was launched in. A ctx member is absent unless its scope was granted: a plugin with no graph scope has ctx.graph === undefined.

The whole authority a plugin can ask for is six manifest keys: graph verbs, network, network_configurable (an address the analyst sets), web_probe (desktop only), services, and config. services names a Vineyard-operated service (rdap, telegram) the plugin calls through ctx.service by name, never by URL: the host fixes the destination and attaches the analyst's own credential.

Plugins cannot post chat messages

There is no ctx.message, and there is no publish / message:post scope: publish is not in the scopes schema, the app ignores it and grants nothing, so remove it.

docs.title: Graph writes are staged, not applied
docs.text:
ctx.graph's write methods do not call the API. Reads come from the live graph, so the plugin sees the real graph, while its creates, updates and deletes accumulate as a change set belonging to that one run (ctx.run.runId).

By default, nothing reaches the project until the analyst opens that change set and approves it — per item, with anything they uncheck excluded. The approved items are then applied under the analyst's own account. Other runs and collaborators may have changed the graph since the edits were staged, so each item is applied independently and ends as applied / skipped / failed — "delete an already-deleted node" is a recorded skip, not a failed batch.

The exception is a run the AI agent launched while the analyst has the agent set to Apply automatically (see Review and apply in the AI agent settings). Its change set is applied at the end of the agent's turn without the analyst opening it. What still waits for review: a change set that removes or overwrites something, together with every change set staged after it in that turn, while Stop and ask before anything is removed or overwritten is on (the default); and the items the independent check holds back, when Have an independent check test each inference is on. Whatever the settings, a change set the server could not write in full waits too, and so does a later change set in that turn that links to one of its new nodes that was not created, and a change set whose links point at nodes another change set still waiting for review would create. Runs started from the Run plugins panel always wait for review.

A plugin can never do more than the analyst who approves its changes is allowed to do.

Bulk ops and review

Whole-graph plugins (e.g. Korean Roulette, Thanos Snap) call ctx.graph.deleteNodes(ids[]) or ctx.graph.deleteEdges(ids[]). Each affected node or edge is staged as its own reviewable item, so a mass-delete arrives as one change set the analyst can trim item by item before approving.

docs.title: The Web Worker sandbox
docs.text:
Plugin main.js runs in a dedicated module Web Worker, not on the page. Inside that worker there is:

  • no DOM and no window,
  • no localStorage / sessionStorage,
  • no IndexedDB, Cache Storage, BroadcastChannel, navigator.storage (including the origin-private file system), Web Locks or service-worker registration,
  • no account token, cookie, or session of any kind,
  • no network of its own: fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket, EventSource and a nested new Worker are all refused,
  • no code but its own module: an import() of any other module, eval, new Function, compiling WebAssembly and URL.createObjectURL are all refused.

The worker runs exactly the code the registry reviewed. Before a plugin runs, the app fetches the plugin's code module, checks its bytes against the SHA-256 the registry recorded for that module, and hands the worker those bytes and nothing else. Code whose bytes do not match is not run, and the run fails with <plugin> was not run: its code does not match the registry's digest. The digest is of the bytes GitHub holds at the pinned commit, so the CDN cannot vouch for itself. A pack approved before the registry recorded code digests is checked by its listing, as its document is. While the registry is unreachable, the app checks against the digests this device kept from the last time the registry listed the pack (see distribution).

The storage block is applied before the pack's code is imported and, unlike the network block, holds under vite dev too: indexedDB, caches and BroadcastChannel are undefined, and the methods of navigator.storage and navigator.locks, and service-worker registration, throw a SecurityError (not available to plugins). In a browser where it cannot be applied the plugin does not load, and the run fails with "the plugin sandbox could not block site storage in this browser". URL.createObjectURL is refused the same way, in vite dev too; Blob itself works. Keep a run's state in memory.

Staging, egress, progress and notifications live on the main thread, in the HostBridge. The worker reaches it through a Comlink proxy shaped exactly like the granted scopes, so every request goes through ctx.net.fetch, ctx.service, or ctx.net.probe on desktop. Desktop runs the same plugin in the same worker.

Direct fetch and import() work in dev only

The dev server (vite dev) does not enforce the worker's network block or its code block, so a pack that calls fetch or import() directly works in dev and fails in production. Use ctx.net.fetch, and bundle everything the pack needs into its one module.

// Inside the worker, ctx is a Comlink proxy of the main-thread HostBridge.
// No fetch, no DOM, no token. graph/net exist only if their scope was granted.
export default definePlugin({
  manifest: { /* … */ },
  async run(ctx) {
    // ctx.run.runId  -> groups every write into this one reviewable change set
    // ctx.graph?.list?() present only because node:read was granted
  },
});

docs.title: Egress is allowlisted on the host side
docs.text:
Every ctx.net.fetch is checked on the host against the manifest's declared network endpoints, and the addresses the analyst set for its network_configurable entries, before the request is made:

Rule Effect The parsed origin must match — protocol, host and port a different host, protocol or port is refused, even if the URL starts with the declared one A path prefix matches on a segment boundary a scope of https://h/v1 covers /v1/search, and does not cover /v1beta The method must be in the scope's methods list a GET-only endpoint cannot be POSTed to; an empty methods list allows every method A URL that will not parse denies — A configured address must be usable it is a URL setting the same plugin declares, set by the analyst, with a scheme the entry allows (https by default) and no user name, password, query or fragment. It is not the Vineyard backend's origin, and in the web app it is not an http address off localhost, which the browser would block from the https page. Until then the entry grants nothing, and the refusal names the setting. The plugin cannot write its own settings A URL on the Vineyard backend's origin is refused whatever the manifest declares or the analyst configures, and on any path of that origin. Graph writes reach the backend only through staging. A redirect to that origin or a ctx.net.probe of it is not refused, and carries none of the analyst's credentials

Requests are sent without the analyst's cookies, and cancelling the run aborts anything still in flight. Headers you set, including Authorization, reach the endpoint as written.

A sandbox-js plugin may declare several network endpoints; each is checked this way. The schema's one-entry proxy_endpoint rule belongs to the deferred web-proxy runtime and is not enforced (see scopes and plugin manifest).

docs.title: Desktop
docs.text:
On desktop, declared endpoints are reachable even if they send no CORS headers. That stops at the analyst's own network:

  • An endpoint addressed as localhost or by a loopback or private-network IP address (e.g. http://127.0.0.1:9200) is left out and still needs the server's own CORS headers.
  • A name that resolves to such an address is judged on each response, by the address the connection reached. The response is refused unless the server itself allows app://vineyard or *. The request carries no Origin here, so a server that only answers CORS when it sees one does not qualify. The analyst can add the endpoint's origin, as the manifest wrote it, under Additional trusted origins in Desktop Settings.
  • An address the analyst sets for a network_configurable entry is treated exactly the same way: it is waived for the open project while it is the address, and not for the analyst's own network. For a server there, such as an internal MISP or OpenCTI, the plugin's settings field offers to add its origin to Additional trusted origins, behind the same confirmation dialog. That list is not per project: an origin on it is waived in every project, for the app and for every plugin whose endpoints include it, until it is removed in Desktop Settings.

Judging a response takes one from the network, so a plugin's requests to an endpoint that gets this treatment skip the HTTP cache, whatever Cache-Control the plugin sets, and a plugin that repeats a request pays for it each time, rate limits included. An origin that is also a built-in AI provider or on the analyst's list keeps the cache.

This limits what a plugin can read, not what it can send: a request may already have reached the server by the time its response is judged. Behind a proxy the app sees the proxy's address and not the target's, so names are not judged there. IPv6 unique-local addresses (fc00::/7) do not count for a name, because some proxy tools answer every name from that range.

ctx.net.probe (the web_probe scope) exists only on desktop: an anonymous cross-origin request made by the desktop app itself, for reading sites that decline CORS. It follows no redirects and is capped in size and time. In the web build ctx.net.probe is absent, so the plugin must fall back.

docs.title: Secret handling
docs.text:
API keys and secrets must never land in a task record or in AI-conversation history.

  1. A secret goes to the plugin that declared it. A config value with secret: true reaches the plugin as ctx.config[key] at run time — a plugin only gets the keys its own manifest declared. The flag masks the field wherever the value is entered: the plugin's Settings (x/y set) block in the Run plugins panel, or Settings → Keys & Secrets under Plugin keys. Members of one pack that declare the same key and call the same network origins share one value, entered once; each plugin still receives only the keys it declares. The value is encrypted by the OS keychain on desktop; in the browser it is kept in that tab only and has to be re-entered after the tab closes; on a desktop that cannot encrypt it is kept for that session only. Both places say whether the value will be kept.
  2. Secrets are not params. Never put credentials in params: the run form's values are recorded in the task. Declare credentials as scopes.config with secret: true instead — those are never written to a task record or an AI conversation.
  3. Type Packs may not declare secret property types. A secret / credential property type is a hard schema rejection (see Type Packs).
  4. Kept per account. Config values and keys are kept separately for each account on the device: another account signing in on the same device does not get them, signing out keeps them, and deleting the account removes them. This separates accounts inside Vineyard; it is not protection against someone with direct access to the computer.

docs.title: Skill Packs
docs.text:
A Skill Pack is text: a reusable investigation playbook the agent can consult.

A Skill Pack runs no code and requests no permissions of its own. It is guidance the agent follows, surfaced through the list_skills / load_skill tools. Its only dependency surface is the Plugin Pack(s) its steps call, declared in requires.

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
A Skill Pack is a single JSON document, content_type: "vineyard:skillpack", living in an author repo at a pinned commit (exactly like a plugin manifest or Type Pack):

{
  "content_type": "vineyard:skillpack",
  "identifier": "run.vineyard.skillpacks.account_identity_pivot",
  "name": "Account & identity pivoting",
  "summary": "Turn one account or handle into the person's other accounts, and know when a shared username is NOT the same person.",
  "description": "## What it is for\n\nYou hold one handle or email and want the person's other accounts…\n\n## What it needs\n\nThe WhatsMyName plugin pack…",
  "author": "VINEYARD",
  "version": "3.1.2",

  "applies_to": ["identity.handle", "identity.account", "identity.email_address", "identity.person"],
  "triggers": ["account", "username", "handle", "email", "same person", "sock puppet", "persona", "계정", "핸들", "아이디", "동일인", "부계정"],

  "requires": ["run.vineyard.pluginpacks.whatsmyname"],

  "overview": "Account & identity pivoting — from one handle or email to the accounts behind the same person…\nLoad the section for the lead you are holding:\n  - \"from-handle\"  - a username: spreading it across platforms\n  - \"from-email\"   - …\n  - \"corroborate\"  - deciding whether two accounts are one person\n…",

  "sections": [
    { "id": "from-handle", "summary": "From a username: spreading it across platforms.", "body": "JUDGE THE CROWD BEFORE THE SWEEP — …" },
    { "id": "from-email", "summary": "From an email address: the handles, keys and documents behind it.", "body": "…" },
    { "id": "from-profile", "summary": "From one profile page: every pivot it carries.", "body": "…" },
    { "id": "discriminate", "summary": "A candidate pair with a gap: the check that would settle it.", "body": "…" },
    { "id": "corroborate", "summary": "Judging whether two accounts are one person — how narrow is the population?", "body": "…" }
  ],

  "starters": [
    {
      "id": "deep-dive-handle",
      "label": "Deep-dive one handle",
      "category": "Find accounts",
      "summary": "Spread a single username across platforms, then work out which hits are the same person.",
      "prompt": "I want to deep dive on the user account \"{{handle}}\". For your information: {{context}}. …",
      "variables": [
        { "key": "handle", "label": "Handle or username", "placeholder": "example", "required": true },
        { "key": "context", "label": "What you already know (optional)", "placeholder": "looks South Korean, software developer", "multiline": true }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
Field Role identifier Reverse-DNS primary key, <your-namespace>.skillpacks.<name>. One manifest = one identifier (no member expansion, unlike a plugin pack). applies_to Node types (category.name) the playbook is about — a hint for when it is relevant. triggers Keyword hints the agent sees when it lists skill packs. requires Plugin pack identifiers the playbook's steps call. A skill is only available when every one is installed in the project and can run on this build (the marketplace co-installs them; at runtime a required pack that is blocked on the current platform, such as a desktop-only pack on the web, hides the skill even though it is installed). Empty or absent = the playbook leans on built-in graph tools only. overview The router, not the procedure: what the pack is for and what sections it holds. The agent reads this first. sections The actual steps. Each has an id (addressed by load_skill(id, section)), a one-line summary (so the agent can pick a section without loading them all), and the body. Loaded on demand — progressive disclosure. starters Ready-made ways to start a run: a prompt with {{key}} blanks and a variables list (key, label, placeholder, required, multiline). category groups them in the picker, rendered in first-appearance order.

docs.title: Writing good sections
docs.text:
• The overview is a router. Tell the agent what the pack is for, when to reach for it, and which section to load for which situation. Keep it short — the detail lives in sections.
  • One section, one situation. A section should be loadable on its own: the agent is going to read it instead of the others, not after them.
  • Say what evidence looks like. The best playbooks state what actually ties two things together (a shared verified email, a reused cert) versus what does not (a common handle, shared hosting) — and tell the agent to label edges for the evidence, never for a conclusion the evidence does not carry.

docs.title: The safety model
docs.text:
Skill text is read by the agent on demand as a tool result, not injected into the prompt, so it costs nothing when unused.

  • The app's own rules outrank the playbook. Text telling the agent to ignore its rules, skip the analyst's review, or treat untrusted text as an instruction is refused.
  • The page is for the analyst, not the agent. summary is what list_skills gives the agent; description is the pack's page in the marketplace and is never sent to it — the overview and the sections are. See A pack's line and its page.
  • Fields are trimmed. One-line fields (names, summaries, labels, ids and list items) are collapsed to one line and stripped of control characters; the overview, section bodies and starter prompts keep newlines and tabs and lose every other control character. Each field is then cut to its limit: a starter prompt stops at 1,200 characters, because a starter is a paragraph, not a document.
  • A per-turn load budget bounds context. Each turn may read at most 12 (skill, section) documents and ~40,000 chars total; a re-read is charged like any other read.

docs.title: Loader limits
docs.text:
The loader applies these limits to every pack, whether installed from the registry or written in a project:

Field Limit identifier 200 characters name, each section summary, each applies_to / triggers / requires item, and a legacy one-line description 240 characters summary 250 characters description (the page, when summary is present) 16,000 characters overview, each section body 8,000 characters applies_to, triggers, requires 32 items each sections 64; each id 120 characters starters 48; each id 120, label 80, summary 200, category 40 and prompt 1,200 characters variables of one starter 8; each key 40, label 80 and placeholder 120 characters

None of this is reported. Text over a limit is cut, entries past a count are dropped, a section without an id and a starter without an id, label or prompt are dropped, and when two sections or two starters share an id only the first is kept.

Check your starters before you publish. The loader does not compare a starter's prompt with its variables. A {{key}} the starter does not declare gets no input field, and a line whose blanks are all empty is left out of the prompt; a declared variable the prompt never uses is a field the analyst fills for nothing. The app fills only blanks whose key uses ASCII letters, digits, _, . and -. The reference pack's CI, validate.yml, fails on undeclared and unused variables, on a repeated starter id, and on a category that is empty, has spaces at either end or is over 40 characters; copy it into your repo. The registry does not run these checks.

docs.title: Drafting a pack in the app
docs.text: A project owner can also write a pack inside Vineyard, with Run ▸ Skill packs ▸ New skill pack or Make a copy of an installed pack, and download it with Export JSON (see Your project's own skill packs). The export is the same document this page describes. Before you publish it, change its local.project.skillpacks.* identifier to your own namespace, in the editor's Details or in the file. The editor refuses what the loader would cut or drop, as well as unknown fields and undeclared or unused starter variables, so a pack that saves there reaches the agent exactly as written.

docs.title: Publishing to the registry
docs.text:
Skill Packs are distributed exactly like Plugin Packs and Type Packs: the document stays in your author repo, and the registry holds a single lean entry in community-skillpacks.json:

{
  "identifier": "run.vineyard.skillpacks.account_identity_pivot",
  "content_type": "vineyard:skillpack",
  "name": "Account & identity pivoting",
  "author": "VINEYARD",
  "summary": "Turn one account or handle into the person's other accounts, and know when a shared username is NOT the same person.",
  "repo": "Vineyard-Intelligence/skillpack-account-identity-pivoting",
  "ref": "77e1444b3422cb41c2a1d382730489b745ade5a6",
  "path": "skillpacks/account-pivot.skill.json",
  "version": "3.1.2",
  "applies_to": ["identity.handle", "identity.account", "identity.email_address", "identity.person"],
  "section_count": 5,
  "requires": ["run.vineyard.pluginpacks.whatsmyname"]
}

You write applies_to, section_count and requires into the entry so the browse page can render without fetching every document. CI recomputes section_count from the pinned document and rejects a mismatch. It checks that every requires identifier is a live pack in the catalog. applies_to is not checked, so copy it from your document. The full workflow — fork, pin an immutable commit ref, add one packs/<identifier>.json, open a PR — is identical to Publishing to the registry.

docs.title: Type Packs
docs.text: A Type Pack is a vineyard:typepack document that defines the node entity types your graph and plugins work with. For the field-by-field contract see the Type Pack schema reference.

docs.title: What a Type Pack is
docs.text: Plugins do not invent their own data shapes. They consume and produce node types that a Type Pack declares, addressed by a qualified string. Edges carry no type: a relationship is stated in the edge's free-text label. The shipping reference packs are Infrastructure, Threat, Identity, Financial, Cryptocurrency, Endpoint, Geospatial, Social Media, and Telegram.

docs.title: Top-level fields
docs.text:
{
  "identifier": "run.vineyard.typepacks.infrastructure",
  "content_type": "vineyard:typepack",           // const
  "version": "1.0.0",                             // SemVer of the PACK CONTENT
  "name": "Infrastructure",
  "summary": "Network infrastructure entities.",     // the card's one line
  "description": "## What it models\n\n…",       // the pack's page, Markdown — see publishing.md#pack-page
  "authors": [{ "name": "Vineyard", "url": "https://vineyard.run" }],
  "license": "Apache-2.0",                        // SPDX expression
  "marketing_url": "https://vineyard.run/packs/infrastructure",
  "thumbnail_url": "https://vineyard.run/img/infra.png",
  "types": [ /* entity types — at least one required */ ]
}

types[] requires at least one entity type. The full required/optional field table is in the Type Pack schema reference.

The reference packs are valid templates

The nine reference packs (infrastructure.json, threat.json, identity.json, financial.json, endpoint.json and geo.json in typepack-basic, social.json in typepack-social, telegram.json in typepack-telegram, cryptocurrency.json in typepack-cryptocurrency) follow this schema — explicit property types, structured validators, and the required top-level fields — so you can read any of them as a working template. telegram.json leaves optional out on some properties; write it on every property of your own pack (see Property types). New authoring MUST follow the schema below.

docs.title: Entity types
docs.text:
{
  "category": "infrastructure",        // snake_case identifier segment
  "name": "ip_address",                // snake_case identifier segment
  "display_name": "IP Address",        // optional human label
  "description": "IPv4/IPv6 network address with geo and ASN context.",
  "icon": "network",                   // see Visuals
  "color": "#60a5fa",                  // see Visuals
  "label_property": "ip_address",      // a key in properties; MUST exist and be non-optional
  "properties": {                      // at least one property
    "ip_address":   { "type": "ip", "optional": false },
    "country_code": { "type": "string", "validator": { "regex": "^[A-Z]{2}$" }, "optional": true },
    "asn":          { "type": "integer", "validator": { "min": 1, "max": 4294967295 }, "optional": true },
    "organization": { "type": "string", "optional": true }
  }
}
  • category and name are snake_case identifier segments (^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$, ≤31 chars).
  • properties MUST be non-empty; each property key is also a snake_case segment.
  • label_property names the key used as the node's display label. That key must exist in properties and be non-optional ("optional": false).
  • identity_properties (optional) lists the keys — together — that identify one entity for de-duplication; defaults to [label_property]. Display and identity are different questions: identity.account has username as its label_property but is identified by (username, platform), since the same username on two platforms is two different accounts. Every listed key MUST exist in properties.
  • label_template (optional) builds the display label from several properties, e.g. "{username} · {platform}". Falls back to label_property when a referenced field is empty, so a partially-filled node never shows a dangling separator. Display only — de-duplication always uses identity_properties.

docs.title: Property types
docs.text:
Every property MUST declare an explicit type from the enum (see the schema reference for the full list). Write optional on every property, too. "optional": false makes the key required: a plugin or the agent creating a node without it is refused. "optional": true lets the key be absent from Node.data. A property that leaves optional out is marked required (*) in the Properties panel, but a create without it is accepted, so do not rely on the absent flag. You may supply a default (its value should match type), but the app never applies it: nothing fills an absent key from it, so it is documentation only. Three of the types need extra keys:

enumreferencevalidated string 
"malware_type": {
  "type": "enum",
  "enum": ["trojan", "ransomware", "worm", "rootkit"],   // required when type=enum
  "optional": false
}

A reference property links to another node type. Provide a reference.target as a qualified category.name (or * for any):

"observed_on": {
  "type": "reference",
  "reference": { "target": "infrastructure.ip_address" },
  "optional": true
}

"cve_id": {
  "type": "string",
  "validator": { "regex": "^CVE-\\d{4}-\\d{4,}$" },
  "optional": false
}

A Type Pack may not declare a secret or credential property type — there is no such enum value, so the schema hard-rejects it. API keys and tokens are not graph data; secrets are handled exclusively through plugin config with secret: true (see security).

docs.title: The structured validator
docs.text:
validator is a structured object, not a raw regex string. Its keys (regex, min/max, min_length/max_length, format) are tabulated in the schema reference.

"cvss_score": { "type": "number", "validator": { "min": 0, "max": 10 }, "optional": true }

A regex is tested as written, so a match anywhere in the value passes: [A-Z]{2} accepts xxUSyy. Anchor it with ^…$ when the whole value must match, as every reference pack does.

docs.title: What the app checks on node data
docs.text:
A Type Pack's property declarations are checked when a plugin or the AI agent calls createNode or updateNode, and when an analyst saves an edit in the Properties panel. A write that fails is refused with a message naming each problem (a plugin's call throws). Only the keys being written are checked, plus, on create, the required keys. The agent's updateNode hands over the whole node, so for it only the values that differ from the node as it stands are checked: a value written before a pack release added a pattern does not block an edit to another field. The checks are:

  • type: a string, text, hash, url, email, ip, date or datetime value must be a string; integer a whole number; number a finite number; boolean a boolean; array an array; object an object that is not an array. A reference value is not checked.
  • enum: the value must be one of the listed values.
  • validator.regex: applied to string values as written (see above). It is skipped for values longer than 4,096 characters, for a pattern that does not compile, and for a pattern with a backtracking-prone shape such as (a+)+. A refused value's message quotes the property's description (up to 280 characters), because the message never shows the pattern and the agent sees field names only. Write that description as what to enter, for example "Account number without spaces or hyphens".
  • validator.min / validator.max: applied to number values.
  • "optional": false: on create only, the key must be present and not blank.

Not checked: validator.min_length, max_length and format, which are hints; keys the type does not declare; and blank values (null, ""), which count as absent. A node created from the Types panel starts as an unchecked placeholder (New <type>); its values are checked as the analyst edits them. How the Properties panel edits each declared type, and what an analyst sees when a value is refused, is in The Properties panel.

docs.title: Visuals: icon and color
docs.text:
Both are per-entity-type and optional.

  • icon is polymorphic, resolved in order:

    1. a data: / http(s): image URI → drawn as the node icon;
    2. otherwise a kebab-case lucide icon name (e.g. shield-alert) → serialized to an SVG and tinted to color;
    3. otherwise a literal glyph/emoji.

    When icon is absent, the node renders with color only. lucide is the default icon set: the host bundles the complete set, so any kebab-case lucide name resolves; a name that is not a lucide icon falls back to color. - color is #rrggbb. When absent, a stable color is hashed from category.name.

The Threat pack, for example, uses lucide names like bug (malware), shield-alert (vulnerability), and venetian-mask (threat actor).

docs.title: Type identity & storage
docs.text:
A node type is addressed as the qualified string "<category>.<name>" — e.g. infrastructure.ip_address or threat.malware. This qualified form is what Node.type stores and what a plugin's io.consumes / io.produces and emit reference. Edges have no type field; the relationship is stated in the free-text Edge.label.

De-duplication keys on the exact qualified type. When a plugin or AI task adds a node, the host de-duplicates by "<category>.<name>" + the identifying value, resolved in order: identity_properties (joined, when the type declares it), else label_property, else value, else name. Values are compared exactly unless the property sets "case_insensitive": true, which folds case for de-duplication only (display and storage keep what was written). Set it where case carries no meaning, such as handles, domains, hostnames, emails and hex digests. Never set it on Base58 crypto addresses, URL paths or case-sensitive file paths, where two different entities can differ by case alone. A property whose values mix the two kinds sets "normalize" instead, naming a rule that decides per value: a crypto address is Base58 on some chains and hex or bech32 on others, and an EIP-55 address's mixed case is only a checksum, so "normalize": "crypto_address" folds the hex and bech32 spellings and leaves Base58 exact, and "hex" does the same for a 64-hex hash with or without 0x (see the schema reference). Neither re-encodes a value, so whatever writes one must write it in a single canonical form. normalize also names the DNS, IP and URL rules: "hostname" for a domain, host or record name (a trailing dot and an internationalised spelling fold into the plain punycode name), "ip" and "cidr" for addresses and ranges, and "url" for a URL, whose path keeps its case. Set "case_insensitive": true beside hostname, ip and cidr, so an app that predates the rule still folds case, and never beside the other three. The agent's common_ground and aggregate_values apply a normalize rule by property name across every installed type, so declare it only on a name that means the same thing in every pack that uses it: another type's property of that name follows the rule too, and a name two packs give different rules is compared exactly as written. A property marked "duplicate_key": true holds a canonical form filled after the node was made, such as a phone number's e164: two nodes sharing it are reported as duplicates, and nothing merges them on write. The type is resolved by its exact qualified key only — a node whose type is not defined by an installed pack keeps its raw type string, so a pack that moves a type to another category (e.g. url from infrastructure to web) never merges old nodes with the new type's creates. Creating a node with a type no installed pack defines is refused outright. (Each io.consumes/io.produces typeRef resolves to the Type Pack that defines it. The plugin's registry entry must list those packs in typepacks, which CI enforces. The marketplace installs the packs in that list alongside the plugin.)

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
version is the SemVer of the pack content.

  • MAJOR = a breaking change: a renamed or removed type. Nothing remaps existing nodes when a new MAJOR is installed; they keep the old type string. A node whose stored type no longer exists renders through any installed type with the same bare name (the first in pack-identifier order), so a type moved to another category still draws with its new definition, though it never merges with new creates. Only a node whose bare name matches no installed type renders unresolved. Nodes record, at write time, the pack revision that resolved their type as Node.type_pack ("<identifier>@<version>"), so a later remapping can tell which revision produced them.
  • MINOR / PATCH = additive or fix-level changes that don't break existing Node.type values.

Open issue: Type Pack version pinning

A plugin's typeRef does not carry a Type Pack version or range, so a MAJOR Type Pack bump can silently break a plugin's io. Treat MAJOR bumps conservatively.

docs.title: Validation checklist
docs.text:
Nothing validates a Type Pack against this checklist at install time: the app loads any document with content_type: vineyard:typepack. Treat it as an authoring checklist, and validate your document against typepack.schema.json in your own CI, as the reference pack repos do. Registry CI enforces only these: the pinned document's identifier, content_type and version match the entry; type_count matches; icon, when the entry carries one, equals the first type's lucide icon; every identity_properties key names an existing, scalar (not array/object/json) property; every normalize is one of the six rules, beside case_insensitive: true only for hostname, ip and cidr, on a scalar property; every duplicate_key is a boolean on a scalar property outside the identity; and no category.name is already defined by another published Type Pack.

  • [ ] content_type is vineyard:typepack.
  • [ ] identifier is a valid <your-namespace>.typepacks.* reverse-DNS string.
  • [ ] At least one entity type; every entity type has ≥1 property.
  • [ ] Each property declares an explicit type from the enum (no secret/credential).
  • [ ] validator, when present, is the structured object — not a raw regex string.
  • [ ] label_property exists in properties and is non-optional.
  • [ ] Every property writes optional explicitly; each required one says "optional": false.
  • [ ] Every validator.regex that must match the whole value is anchored with ^…$.
  • [ ] enum properties supply enum; reference properties supply reference.target; any default matches type.
  • [ ] A property that sets normalize to crypto_address, hex or url does not also set "case_insensitive": true; one that sets hostname, ip or cidr does.
  • [ ] A duplicate_key property is not one of the identity fields.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text: How Vineyard detects and applies a new version of an installed Plugin Pack, Type Pack or Skill Pack.

docs.title: The registry entry is the latest pointer
docs.text:
Vineyard does not poll author repos for updates. The registry entry is the canonical latest pointer: each row in community-pluginpacks.json (or community-typepacks.json) carries the current version, the immutable ref, and the repo/path that resolve to the manifest at that ref. When the marketplace fetches the registry, the app already knows the newest published version of everything you have installed.

A manifest's latest_url field is accepted but not used; the app has no update check outside the catalog. A pack loaded from a URL during local development is not installed. It is re-fetched from that URL on every load, so it is always the current build.

What an update actually is

A ref is immutable: a commit SHA (40-hex, or 64-hex for SHA-256 repos). Tags and branches are rejected because they can be moved (see publishing). You never update in place. A new version is a new ref published as a new registry entry projection, and applying it is a full re-install at that ref.

docs.title: How the app detects an update
docs.text:
The app holds an install record per project of the form { identifier, url, version } — no ref field is stored. To find updates it compares the installed version with the registry entry's version for the same identifier, as SemVer: only a newer catalog version is offered (1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.0, and a release is newer than its own pre-releases). An equal or lower version, or one that is not SemVer, offers nothing.

When a newer version is in the catalog, the marketplace shows an Update button on the card and Update available in the detail drawer.

The check compares version, not ref: re-pinning a new ref without raising version never reaches projects that already have the pack.

docs.title: Applying an update
docs.text:
Choosing Update opens the same approval dialog as a fresh install, and nothing changes until the analyst confirms. For a Plugin Pack, every permission the new version adds is marked New. Packs the new version needs and the project does not have yet — Type Packs for a Plugin Pack; Plugin Packs and their Type Packs for a Skill Pack — are listed under Also installs and added in the same step. If one of them, at either level, is missing from the catalog or withdrawn, the update is refused. Confirming re-points the project's pointer to the new entry's { identifier, url, version }.

publish is not in the scopes schema; the app ignores it and grants nothing, so remove it if your manifest declares it.

docs.title: Gating: which version is even offered
status (deprecated / withdrawn)
docs.text: There is no separate deprecation file. Delisting a version is the registry entry's own status block — { state, reason, since, replacement } — set by editing the pack's row in packs/ (see Taking a pack down). A withdrawn ref is never offered as an update, cannot be freshly installed, and a project that already has it refuses to load it on the next run — the analyst sees the reason instead. A deprecated ref keeps installing and updating normally; the analyst is just shown the notice once per project open.

docs.title: Type Packs update the same way
docs.text: Type Packs follow the identical model: the community-typepacks.json entry is the latest pointer, and the update check is the same SemVer comparison described above. Type Packs declare no scopes. status (deprecated/withdrawn) exclusion applies the same as for Plugin Packs. Skill Packs do too: the community-skillpacks.json entry is the latest pointer, and Update re-points the project's skills pointer. A project's own skill packs, including copies of registry packs, are stored on the project rather than installed from the catalog, so they never receive registry updates. See Type Packs for the schema and registry schema for the entry projection.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: VINEYARD is an open investigation workbench for CTI and OSINT. You build a graph of entities and relationships, then extend the app with packs that you browse, install, and run entirely in your own session.

docs.title: What packs give you
docs.text:
There are three kinds of pack:

  • Plugin Packs — JavaScript actions that read, create, or modify your graph's nodes and edges (and, with permission, call the network).
  • Type Packs — JSON definitions of the entity types your graph understands, giving nodes their properties, validation rules, icons, and colors.
  • Skill Packs — investigation playbooks the AI agent can follow when working on your project. Text only — no code, no permissions. Besides the ones in the Marketplace, a project can have skill packs of its own, written or imported in the app.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text: You browse the Marketplace for a pack, install that reference into the app, and then the app runs it client-side on your graph. The Vineyard server never executes plugin code and by default never records your runs.
