docs.title: The Properties panel
docs.text: The Properties panel shows what you have selected on the canvas: one node, one link, or how many nodes. It is where you read a node's values, edit them, add and remove fields, read it as one page, and see what a link is worth and who drew it. It sits on the right, above Tasks (7 in the workspace picture). Like the other panels it can be dragged elsewhere and resized, and Reset panel layout puts it back.

docs.title: What the panel shows
docs.text:
You have selected The panel shows Nothing No node selected One node Its name, its type and its fields (A node) Several nodes N nodes selected and Show in node table, which opens the node table on them A link (an edge) Its two ends, its label, its evidence grade and what was recorded with it (A link)

The panel shows the selection as it is stored now, not as it was when you clicked. When you or someone else deletes the node it shows, the panel goes back to No node selected; a selected link that is deleted leaves This link no longer exists.

docs.title: View only
docs.text:
When you can view a project but not edit it, through its public link or as a collaborator without edit access, the panel opens with View only at the top. Hovering it says Only people who can edit this project can change these values. In local mode the panel always edits.

  • Values are shown, opened under their row and found in the same way, and cannot be changed.
  • The value menu copies, searches the graph, goes to nodes and opens URLs, and offers no new node.
  • + Field is not shown, no field can be removed, and the JSON view's Edit is disabled.
  • In a link's panel, relation and confidence cannot be changed. Re-verify is there, because it writes nothing itself; applying what it proposes takes edit access.

The server decides every write. If you lose edit access while the project is open, the panel can still look editable until the project is read again, and a value you change there is refused with Not saved: you do not have write access to this project. and goes back to what is stored.

docs.title: A node
docs.text:
The top of the panel names the node:

  • The icon and colour of its type, and its name as the canvas shows it.
  • ID, and Type as stored (infrastructure.domain).
  • Last written by … and how long ago, when this tab has seen someone write the node since it opened. Hover it for the session the write came from, when there is one. It is empty after a reload; the Document view reads who created and changed the node from the activity log.
  • Table, Document and JSON, which change how the panel shows the node. The choice is remembered on this device.

docs.title: The grid
docs.text:
Table shows the node's fields in a grid, one row each, the name on the left and the value on the right.

  • The fields the node's type declares come first, in the order its Type Pack lists them, whether or not they hold anything. A * after a name marks a field the type requires.
  • The fields the node holds and its type does not declare come after them, under Added fields and the name of the type that does not declare them. A plugin, an import, the AI agent or + Field wrote them, and the type does not check their values.

  • Before each name, a small marker says what the value holds now, which is not always what the type declares: a field declared a number that holds text shows T.

    Marker The value is a dash nothing: no value is stored T text. URLs, dates, hashes and addresses are text too. # a number a switch true or false {} an object [] a list

  • Point at a name to see it whole with the type's description of the field. Point at a value to see all of it: a list one entry per line, a structure as indented JSON. A long value is cut after 16 lines, with how much is left (… 2,340 more characters). The value's tip stays closed while you are editing it.

  • Drag the line between the two columns to give the names more room.
  • A node whose type declares nothing and that holds nothing shows No properties defined for this type.

When the node's Type Pack is not installed or did not load, the grid still shows every field the node holds, each read by its value. Nothing then says which fields the type declares or requires, the Added fields heading is not shown, and no value is checked when you save it.

docs.title: Finding a field
docs.text:
Above the grid, Find a field or value and Hide empty narrow what it shows. Neither changes the node, and both are there in a panel marked View only.

  • Find a field or value keeps the fields whose name or value contains what you type, ignoring case. first seen finds first_seen. A list is matched entry by entry and JSON by its values, not its keys, and AS64496 also finds a field that holds the number 64496. Esc or × empties it. What you type stays when you select another node, so you can look at one field across several nodes.
  • Hide empty leaves out the fields that hold nothing: no value, an empty text, an empty list or {}. 0 and false are values. A field the type requires (*) stays. The choice is remembered on this device.
  • The field you are in stays on screen until you leave it, even when you clear it or what you type no longer matches.
  • A field you changed stays after you leave it, whatever the finder and Hide empty say, until the change is saved. When the value is refused or the server cannot be reached, it stays with what you typed, so you can correct it.
  • Enter or F2 on the canvas opens the field the node's label shows even when the finder or Hide empty leaves it out: its row is shown while you are in it.
  • While fields are left out, a line under the grid says how many are shown, how many do not match (Clear empties the finder) and how many are empty (Show turns Hide empty off).

docs.title: Reading values
docs.text:
The grid shows each value by what it is, not only by the type that declares it: a URL with its host picked out, a hash shortened with its algorithm beside it, a list written into one text field as separate entries. What changes is how the value is shown. The stored value stays as it is until you edit it.

A chevron (›) at the end of a value opens a view of the whole value under its row.

Value In the grid Under the row Long text (description, bio, a post) The first line, and how many lines follow (+3 lines). The whole text with its line breaks, Find and Copy. A list written into one text field (name_servers, open_ports, user_ids, tags) The first entries as chips, and how many there are. One entry per row, with the host of each URL. Copy, one per line, Copy defanged, and Edit as text. URL The URL as stored, its host highlighted. A badge marks a URL the browser cannot read (unreadable) and one with a user name or password before the host (credentials). Scheme, host (and its Unicode form when it is punycode), port, path, each query parameter decoded, fragment. Defanged shows it as hxxps://example[.]com, in the grid too. The other nodes with the same host. Hash The first and last eight characters, and the algorithm read from the property name or the length (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, mmh3, ssdeep, TLSH…). The algorithm is a label; nothing is computed. The whole hash, Copy, Lower case for a hex hash written in capitals, and the other nodes with the same value. IP address or CIDR block The value, v4 or v6, and a special-purpose range such as private, loopback or documentation. A block written from a host address is marked host bits set. The canonical form of an address, or a block's network, netmask, first and last address and size. The other nodes in the same /24 (IPv6: /64), or with an address in the block. E-mail address The domain highlighted. The local part, the tag after a +, and the domain (and its Unicode form). Size, count or amount (size_bytes, *_count, followers, balance) Digits grouped in thousands, a size also in KiB, MiB or GiB, an amount with the node's currency. — Code: a detection rule, an armored key, a raw record, a command line Monospace, the first line. Line numbers, highlighting for YARA, Sigma, PGP armor and WHOIS (up to 8,000 characters), Find, Wrap, Copy, Download, and Edit, a code editor that saves when you press Save. The editor is highlighted when the code is up to 8,000 characters as it opens, and plain otherwise; code that grows past that while you edit loses its colours and keeps the editor, the caret and undo. Cryptocurrency address The chain its format belongs to, and whether its checksum holds (EIP-55, Base58Check, Bech32 and Bech32m). Solana addresses and all-lowercase EVM addresses carry no checksum, and Monero's is not checked. A Base58Check address whose version byte names no chain Vineyard knows (Bitcoin Gold, Dash) shows checksum ok without a chain. The format, the chain, what the node's own currency or network field says, and a link to a block explorer: the one for the network the node names, or for the format's own chain when it names none. The link asks before it opens, because the explorer sees your IP address, the time and the address you looked up. JSON One line of JSON, with { } to edit it (JSON values). A tree: fold and unfold, click a key to copy its path (rdap.events[0].action), Find, and Raw for the indented JSON.

A legacy Bitcoin address is the same string on Bitcoin Cash and Bitcoin SV, and an EVM address the same string on every EVM chain, each a different account. So no explorer link is offered when the node names a network of another format, a network Vineyard has no explorer for (Ethereum Classic, Bitcoin Gold, Dash and others), or only evm or unknown for an address several chains share. The view under the row says which.

Which kind a value is, is read from its declared type, the property name and the value itself, so it can be wrong for an unusual value; a wrong reading changes only how the value is shown and, for a list written into one text field, how the agent's aggregate_values counts its entries. The list of other nodes appears in the node panel, not in the Review dialog.

docs.title: Times, choices and true or false
docs.text:
Values of these kinds are shown as they are stored, even when the type expects something else:

  • A date and time (datetime) is shown as written, and a line under it says what it reads as: the moment in UTC and how long ago (2026-11-14 09:02Z · 2h ago), the UTC time alone for a time more than a minute ahead, such as a certificate's expiry, or no timezone for a date and time that names no zone, an EXIF time (2021:12:14 11:58:18) included. A bare date, an epoch number and free text get no line. Nothing is converted when you save.
  • A date (date) has a date picker. A date field that holds a time, or a date the picker cannot show, is shown as written, like a date and time.
  • A choice (enum) is picked from the values its type lists; type to narrow the list. A stored value the type does not list stays on screen as itself, marked (not in type), and hovering it says Not one of the values this type lists. Only a field the type does not require has a × to clear it.
  • A boolean (boolean) is a switch. A field that holds nothing is not shown as false: it reads —, with a choice of true or false, and hovering it says Not collected. Nothing is stored here, which is not the same as false. A value that is neither, such as yes, is shown as stored. Choosing writes true or false.
  • A number field that holds text, such as AS13335 from an import, shows the text rather than the digits in it.
  • A value with a line break is never put in a one-line field, whatever its type declares, so no line is lost. It gets a field of several lines or, in a text field whose lines read as a list (name_servers written one per line), entries.

docs.title: Editing a value
docs.text:
• Click a value, or move to it with Tab, to edit it. Long text and code grow in place.
  • In a text field, a number field, a date picker, a date and time, long text and code, Esc puts the value back as stored and leaves the field. In a one-line field (text, a number, a date, a date and time) Enter saves; in long text and code Enter adds a line and ⌘Enter (Mac) or Ctrl+Enter saves. A value is also saved when you leave the field. The Enter or Esc that finishes a Korean syllable only finishes the syllable.
  • In a choice (an enum, or true and false), a list and the colour picker, Esc leaves the field too, and does not close a Run plugins or Skill pack panel open beside the panel. With a choice's list of options open, Esc closes only the list. In the colour picker, Esc puts the stored colour back over one half typed.
  • While you type, the field stays the one you clicked, even when what you have typed so far reads as a URL, an address or a list. It shows as that kind when you leave it.
  • While you edit a URL, an e-mail or IP address, a hash or a cryptocurrency address, a line under the field says what is wrong with it: a rule of its type, or a checksum that fails. The type's rules decide what is saved.
  • In a panel marked View only, values are shown and opened the same way and cannot be edited.

What you edit a value in depends on its declared type and on what it holds:

The field holds You edit it in Text A one-line field. Text its type declares text, or any value with a line break, unless it reads as a list (below) A field of several lines. Line endings stay as the value had them, so the CRLF endings of a raw WHOIS record are still CRLF after an edit. A number A number field. In one that holds text, what you type is saved as a number when it is written as one (13335), and refused otherwise, with the reason. A choice (enum) A list of the values the type lists. A boolean (boolean) A switch, or a choice of true and false when the field holds neither. A date (date) A date picker, or a text field when the picker cannot show the value. A date and time (datetime) A text field, with what it reads as under it. A colour (color) A colour picker, in hex. A list of text, numbers or true/false Entries (Lists). An object, or a list that holds objects One line of JSON and { } (JSON values).

A list written into one text field is edited as entries: type one and press Enter, or remove one with its ×. It is saved with the separator the value already used, one per line or ,. To fix an entry where it stands, without moving it to the end, open the row and choose Edit as text: the field is then the text as stored. Edit as entries turns it back.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
A list's entries are chips, with Add… after them. Type an entry and press Enter to add it, or press an entry's × to remove it. Each change is saved at once. An entry you have typed is also added when you leave the field, with a click elsewhere or Tab; Esc drops it and adds nothing. A list written in one text field behaves the same way. A field its type declares a list (array) is edited this way even before it holds anything.

The list keeps the kind of its entries:

  • In a list of numbers, such as open_ports holding [80, 443], an entry that reads as a number is stored as one, so 8080 joins as the number 8080. One that does not, such as 8080/tcp, is stored as text, and the list then holds both.
  • In a list of text, an entry stays text even when it is all digits: "01" stays "01" and does not become 1.
  • In a list of true and false, true and false are stored as true and false.
  • A list that mixes kinds has none to keep: after an edit, every entry in it is stored as text, so [80, "http"] becomes ["80", "http"]. Edit such a list in the JSON view to keep its numbers.
  • An empty list has no kind to keep, so what you add to it is text. To start a list of numbers, write it in the JSON view.
  • A whole number larger than 9,007,199,254,740,991 stays text, because as a number it would lose its last digits.

docs.title: JSON values
docs.text:
An object, or a list that holds anything other than text, numbers and true/false, shows as one line of JSON. Point at it to see it indented, or open the row (›) for a tree. { } at the end of the line opens it in a JSON editor, on the value as it is stored when you open it.

  • Save writes the value only when the text is valid JSON. Otherwise the editor stays open with the reason, and nothing is saved.
  • A whole number larger than 9,007,199,254,740,991, or one too large to be a number at all (1e400), is refused. JavaScript would already have rounded it, so 18446744073709551616 would be saved as 18446744073709552000. Put it in quotes, "18446744073709551616", to keep every digit.
  • Cancel, Esc or a click outside closes the editor without saving.
  • The editor highlights the JSON when it is up to 8,000 characters as it opens, and is plain otherwise. JSON that grows past 8,000 characters while you edit loses its colours but stays in the same editor, with the caret where it was and undo still working.
  • What you save is then checked against the type like any other value (Saving and checks).

The JSON view edits the node's whole data under the same two rules.

docs.title: Saving and checks
docs.text:
• Text, a number, a date and a date and time are saved when you leave the field or press Enter (⌘Enter or Ctrl+Enter in long text and code). A switch, a choice, a list entry and a colour are saved as soon as you change them, and a JSON value when you press Save in its editor.
  • Nothing is written when the value is what the node already holds, so clicking or tabbing through fields writes nothing.
  • The value you changed is checked against what the type declares for it: its kind, its allowed values, and any pattern or range. A value that fails is not saved, and a message names the field and what is wrong, for example country_code does not match the format its type requires: kr, followed by the type's description of the field when it has one. What you typed stays in the field, so you can correct it, or, in a field that takes Esc, put it back (Editing a value).
  • Only the fields you change are checked. An edit does not ask for the required (*) fields to be filled, so a node a plugin saved without one can still be edited. Fields the type does not declare, and every field of a node whose Type Pack is not installed, are not checked.
  • A save the server refuses because you cannot write to the project says Not saved: you do not have write access to this project., and the field goes back to what is stored. Any other refusal says Could not save this property. When the server cannot be reached, Unable to reach the server. In both, what you typed stays.

The checks are listed in full under What the app checks on node data.

docs.title: When others edit the same node
docs.text:
• The panel follows the node as it is stored. A change a collaborator saves, a review that is applied and a write by the AI agent show in the panel as they land, without selecting the node again.
  • A field you are typing in is left alone: a change to it that arrives meanwhile does not replace what you are typing. Once your save has landed, the field follows the node again. In a field that takes Esc, it puts back the value as it is stored now, a collaborator's change included.
  • A save writes only the fields you changed, laid over the node as this tab holds it when the save is sent. A change someone else made to another field is kept.
  • When two people change the same field, the later save wins, and the grid does not warn you. The JSON view asks before it replaces a field someone else changed.
  • One short window is left. The server replaces the node's whole data on each save, so a change someone else saves in the moment between your save being sent and the server applying it can be lost, even when it was to another field. Adding or removing a field, and saving from the JSON view, write the whole data the same way.

docs.title: The value menu
docs.text:
Point at a value and ⋯ appears at the end of its cell (on a touch screen it is always there). It opens a menu for that value:

  • Copy copies the value as stored, line breaks included, and a structure as indented JSON. Copy defanged appears when defanging changes the value: the scheme becomes hxxp, hxxps or fxp, the dots of a host and of a URL's path become [.], an e-mail's @ becomes [@] and an IPv6 address's colons [:], and a URL inside a URL (a redirect's target) is defanged too. A host name or an e-mail address is defanged whatever its top-level domain, dc01.corp and user@evil.zz included. Copy refanged appears when the value was stored defanged. Refanging a defanged copy gives back the value exactly.
  • Search the graph puts the value, refanged, in the canvas's search box and shows the results, so evil[.]example finds evil.example. It is offered for a value on one line of up to 256 characters, and for a number.
  • When the whole value is one indicator (an IP address or block, a domain, a URL with its scheme, an e-mail address, a phone number, a hash, a CVE id, a Bitcoin, TRON or EVM address), the menu offers the node it names:
    • Go to … when a node with that identity is already in the graph, and Select it and run plugins… when an installed plugin takes its type and you can edit the project. The graph is asked by the value as written too, and a hash in upper case as well, so a SHA-256 stored in upper case or an IPv6 address written in full is found as that node. A field that holds the node's own identity, such as a domain's domain_name, offers neither, however it is written.
    • Review the staged … when a change set waiting for review already creates it.
    • Otherwise New … node…. It stages the node, with a link from the node that holds the value labelled with the field's name (name_servers), and opens the Review dialog. Nothing is written until you apply it, and you can untick the link. The link is recorded as yours, and the Tasks pane keeps a row that reopens the review. When an installed plugin takes the node's type, Run plugins is shown greyed with it, and with Review the staged … too: a plugin runs on a node in the graph, so the new node has to be applied first.
    • A hash is read with its field's name, as the grid reads it: a 64-digit value under tx_hash is a transaction id, and a 32-digit one under imphash or ja3 a fingerprint, so neither is offered as a file's hash. Nor is a value in a field whose name says fingerprint or thumbprint (a certificate's fingerprint_sha256, a PGP key's fingerprint), or in a field declared hash that identifies its own node (a DOM hash's hash_value): each is the digest of that certificate, key or page, not of a file. A SHA-256 becomes a threat.file_hash, an MD5 or SHA-1 a threat.indicator.
    • A Bitcoin, TRON or EVM address becomes the Cryptocurrency pack's cryptocurrency.crypto_address, on the network its format settles: bitcoin for bc1…, tron for T…, evm for a 0x address, and unknown for a legacy 1… or 3… address, which is the same string on Bitcoin, Bitcoin Cash and Bitcoin SV. A project that has the Financial pack and not the Cryptocurrency pack is offered the legacy financial.crypto_address with its currency instead. With neither pack installed, the item is greyed and names cryptocurrency.crypto_address.
    • When no installed Type Pack defines the type, or the type's format refuses the value, the item is greyed with the reason.
  • Open in browser…, for a URL stored with http:// or https://, asks first and names the host the browser will connect to, with its Unicode form when it is punycode, which is how a look-alike host shows itself. That server sees your IP address and the time, and the page runs in your browser. In the desktop app it opens in your default browser, with that browser's own profile, cookies and fingerprint. A URL stored defanged is not offered: refang it on purpose first.
  • Remove field… ends the menu of a field the node's type does not declare, also when the field holds nothing (Adding and removing fields).
  • Esc closes the menu and nothing behind it. In the Review dialog, keys pressed in the menu or in its URL confirmation stay there: Space chooses the item rather than ticking the staged row, and Esc in the confirmation leaves the review open.

Each entry of a list written into one text field has its own ⋯ in the view under its row, so one name server can be copied, searched for or made a node of on its own.

The menu reads a value the way the grid badges it and the AI agent's extract_indicators reads text, so an address shown as private in the grid is reported as private there too.

In a panel marked View only the menu copies, searches, goes to nodes and opens URLs, and offers no new node. A link's stored data has the menu too, and a node made from it is not linked, since a link cannot end at another link. In the Review dialog the menu copies and opens URLs only.

docs.title: Adding and removing fields
docs.text:
A node can hold fields its type does not declare. Plugins write them, and you can add your own, such as notes or tags, without waiting for a new version of the Type Pack. The grid lists them under Added fields, after the fields the type declares (The grid).

  • + Field, under the last row, opens a form with a Name, a Kind and a Value. Add field writes the field to the node at once; it is not staged for review.
  • A name is lower-case letters, digits and _, starting with a letter, up to 31 characters. That is the rule a Type Pack's own field names follow, so a later version of the pack can declare the field under the name you gave it. A name such as First Seen is refused with Use first_seen beside it. A field the type declares is filled in its own row, and a field the node already has is changed in its row, so neither name is accepted here.
  • Under the name, Suggested offers notes (Text) and tags (Array), then the fields that other nodes of the same type carry and their type does not declare, most common first, so one field keeps one name across the graph. Clicking a name fills it in, with the kind the other nodes hold it as. A name the type declares or the node has is not suggested.
  • The kinds carry the names the Type Pack schema gives these values: Text (text, line breaks kept), Number (number), Boolean (boolean), Array (array of text entries: type one and press Enter) and Object (object, written in braces {…}). A list typed under Object is refused with a pointer to Array; a list of numbers can be written in the node's JSON view. A field is added with its value: an empty text, an array with no entries, and {} are refused, since a field with nothing in it reads as one the node does not have. A number too large to store exactly is refused; choose Text to keep every digit.
  • Enter in the name or in a number adds the field, and ⌘Enter (Mac) or Ctrl+Enter adds it from anywhere in the form, the JSON editor included (without adding a line break to the JSON), with a list entry you are still typing. Esc or Cancel closes the form and drops what you typed. If the panel moves to another node first, the form closes and a notice offers Copy the value.
  • Adding waits until a change you made in a row has been saved, then writes the node's data as it is at that moment with the new field in it, so a change saved just before, yours or someone else's, is kept. If someone else added a field of the same name meanwhile, the form says so and writes nothing.
  • A field the node's type does not declare has Remove field… at the end of its value menu (⋯), also when it holds nothing. Vineyard asks first and shows what the field holds. If the field changes before you confirm, you are asked again with its new value; if someone else has already removed it, nothing is written. Like adding, it waits for a change you made in a row to be saved. Like a removal in the JSON view, it writes the node's whole data, so a change someone else saves at the same moment can be lost.
  • A field the type declares keeps its row: clear its value instead, or, when the type does not require it, remove it in the JSON view. When the node's Type Pack is not installed or did not load, Vineyard cannot tell which fields the type declares, so Remove field… is not offered; the JSON view can still remove a field.
  • In a panel marked View only, + Field is not shown and no field can be removed.

docs.title: Document and JSON views
docs.text:
Under a node's name, Table, Document and JSON change how the panel shows it. The choice is remembered on this device. Table is the grid. Enter or F2 on the canvas, and G then P, open a field from Document or JSON too: the panel switches to Table for it, and the view remembered on this device stays the one you chose.

Document shows the node as one page to read:

  • Its title, its type, and the fields that identify it, then its one-line values, then each longer value under its field name: long text as paragraphs with its line breaks, a rule or a raw record as code, a list as entries, JSON folded to one line until you open it. Declared fields with nothing in them are named under Not collected. A value over 40 lines shows its start and Show all.
  • Source gives when the node was created and last changed (UTC). Who created and changed it reads the account that did each from the activity log. It is read when you click, not each time a node is selected. Agent and plugin writes are recorded under the account that applied them. In local mode, and for an account that opened the project through its public link, only the times are shown: the activity log is for project members. If the activity log cannot be read, the page says so and offers Try again, and the last writer seen since the tab opened is shown under In this session.
  • Links lists the node's outgoing and incoming links grouped by label, with how many carry each evidence grade. Click a node in the list to select it and centre it on the canvas.
  • Copy as Markdown copies the page for a report. Every value, and every name that comes from the data (the title, field names, link labels, account names), is written as code, so nothing in it turns into a link, an image or formatting where you paste it, and line breaks are kept. Times are in UTC, without "3h ago". Copied before Who created and changed it has answered, the Markdown says the names were not read from the activity log.

JSON shows the node's whole data as indented JSON; Tree folds it, finds in it and copies a key's path (whois.events[0]). Edit opens the data in the JSON editor, where a field can be changed, added or removed. A node that holds a WHOIS or RDAP record is often close to 8,000 characters: the editor is highlighted or plain from its size when it opens, as for a JSON value, so deleting or pasting a raw record does not cost you the caret or undo.

  • Saving writes only the fields you changed, added or removed. A field you left as it was keeps whatever the node holds when you save, so a change someone else made to it while the editor was open is kept. A line above the editor names the fields that changed since you opened it. If someone else already made every change you made, saving writes nothing.
  • Before a save removes a field, or replaces a field someone else changed since you opened the editor, Vineyard asks. A save that removes a field writes the node's whole data, so a change someone else saves at the same moment can be lost.
  • A field the type marks required (*) cannot be removed; give it another value instead. Changed values are checked against the type as in the table, and a number too large to store exactly has to be written in quotes.
  • Esc and a click outside close the editor only while you have typed nothing. Cancel discards your edit. Nothing closes the editor while a save is on its way. A save that is refused (you have no write access) or fails leaves the editor open with the reason, so your edit can be fixed or copied.
  • If the panel moves off the node while the editor holds an edit you have not saved (the agent selected another node, or someone deleted this one), the editor closes without saving and a notice offers Copy your JSON. A save that fails after the editor has closed is reported the same way.
  • In a panel marked View only, Edit is disabled.

docs.title: A link
docs.text:
Click a link (an edge) on the canvas to show it in the panel. The top says what the link is and how far to trust it:

  • Its two ends, from → to, by their names, and its ID.
  • Who wrote its label:
    • Edited here: a person, who drew the link, changed its label in this panel, or made it from a value's menu.
    • Written by the assistant: the AI agent.
    • Written by and a plugin's identifier, such as run.vineyard.plugins.crtsh_subdomains: that plugin.
    • Original label: nothing records who wrote it, as on links written before the app recorded it.
  • Evidence: its grade and who set it, and under them, in one line, what the grade says (Evidence grades). Who set it reads Graded here (a person, also for a link made from a value's menu), Graded by the assistant, Graded by and a plugin's identifier, Graded by a re-verification (a Re-verify you applied), Graded by a merge (raised because a merged node's writer drew the same link; see Merging nodes), Nobody graded this (copied in by an import from a file that carried no grade), or Grader not recorded (graded before the app recorded who did). A link written before grades were recorded has no Evidence line.
  • Re-verify, and beside it Re-collect with the agent (Re-verify).

Below them are the two values you can change when you can edit the project:

  • relation is the link's label: what connects the two, stated as the evidence rather than the conclusion. Saving it changes the label on the canvas and marks it Edited here. A label is kept to 1,024 characters, and an empty one is refused with A link needs a label saying what connects the two. While Stop and ask before anything is removed or overwritten is on, which it is unless you turned it off, AI agent changes that are applied automatically are held for your review when they would rewrite a label a person wrote (AI agent settings).
  • confidence is whether you vouch for the link: asserted or unassessed, the two grades a person can state. The other grades say that a check or a tool did something, so they are not offered. A link that holds one shows it in the list, and choosing it again writes nothing. The grade you choose reads Graded here. Changing the grade does not make the label yours, and changing the label does not change who graded the link.

There is no finder or Hide empty in a link's panel.

docs.title: Recorded with this link
docs.text: Under Recorded with this link is everything else the link stores, read-only for everyone. It is what the plugin or the agent that drew the link recorded with it, such as where and when the link was observed: OTX Passive DNS, for example, stores source, record_type, first_seen and last_seen. The list also holds corroborated_by, the other writers that drew the same link, which the evidence grade counts. A link that stores nothing more, such as one you drew yourself, shows Nothing else is stored with this link. The Review dialog shows the same list for a link that is waiting to be applied.

docs.title: Evidence grades
docs.text:
Every link carries one grade saying how far its evidence goes. The canvas draws each grade with its own line, and the legend's Evidence key lists the grades in the project (Legend). Strongest first:

Grade What it says Comes from assessed An independent check argued against this link and it held. The independent check, or a re-verification you apply asserted A person vouched for this link: an analyst's judgement, not a measurement. It says nothing about whether anything checked the link. A person. A link you draw starts here. recorded A tool recorded this: one end's own fields name the other, a collector linked what it found to a node it did not find (a DNS lookup's domain to the IP it resolved), or two independent collectors both drew it. Not a claim that it was verified. Applying a plugin's or the agent's changes, or a link made from a value's menu, which reads Graded here because you applied it circumstantial Checked, and consistent, but innocent explanations fit the same evidence. The independent check, or a re-verification contested The check refused this link. It is here because a person kept it. Drawn heavier, in amber. The independent check, or a re-verification unassessed Nothing on this link says it was checked. Applying changes nothing checked, or a person taking back asserted

A grade records what was known when it was set. It does not change by itself as the graph grows around the link, only when the link is written again: by a person, by the check, or by a later run that brings new evidence for it. Re-verify asks again on purpose. No grade stops you from editing, deleting or building on a link. The independent check is the AI agent setting Have an independent check test each inference (AI agent settings).

docs.title: Re-verify
docs.text:
Re-verify asks the independent check to judge the link again, as of now. It reads the label, what each end records, what else the graph holds at each end (not this link), who wrote the label, the grade on record and who gave it, the other collectors that drew the link, and how old it is. It asks your model provider, with the key set for the AI agent; without a key the button says so and does nothing.

The check writes nothing. Its verdict is staged as a change set named Re-verification and opened in the Review dialog, and the Tasks pane keeps a row for it. The review says what the check made of the link, such as supported — still valid or refuted — stale, and applying it sets the grade:

Verdict Grade still valid assessed stale contested inconclusive circumstantial not checked: the check could not run, and a notice says why Never lowered, and contested stays. As on any update, it can rise to recorded when one end's fields name the other or another collector drew the link (corroborated_by).

A re-verification never proposes deleting the link. The check is told that a link it cannot re-establish is not therefore false, and to call it inconclusive, not stale, unless the evidence now contradicts it: a dead page or one failed lookup is not staleness. Even a link the check refutes stays in the graph as contested, for a person to remove. When applying the re-verification changes the grade, the grade reads Graded by a re-verification; one that leaves the grade as it was leaves who graded it as well. A verdict is not applied to a link whose label has changed since it was checked. While one is waiting for review, the button reads Review re-verification and opens it.

The arrow beside the button holds Re-collect with the agent. It opens a new AI agent conversation with a request filled in, not sent, asking the agent to collect fresh evidence for the link and propose any change through review. Nothing runs until you read it and send it.

docs.title: Next / See also
docs.text:
• The canvas: selecting nodes and links, the node table and the legend
  • Working with Type Packs: the types that decide which fields a node has
  • Running plugins: the Review dialog, which shows staged values in the same grid
  • Tasks & runs: the AI agent and its review settings

docs.title: Running plugins
docs.text: Once a plugin is installed in a project, you open the Run plugins panel from a right-click on a node, a selection or empty canvas, from the ▶ button on the canvas toolbar, from Run ▸ Run plugins… in the top menu bar, or from the command palette (⌘K). You watch and cancel the run from the Tasks panel.

docs.title: Where a plugin shows up
docs.text:
Every installed plugin is listed in one panel, Run plugins. At the top, a scope switch picks Selected (N) — the plugins that read nodes, each seeing only the selected ones of the type it accepts — or Whole graph (N) — the plugins that take no node input at all. N counts nodes: in Selected the selected nodes this run keeps (a chip you drop leaves the count), in Whole graph every node in the project. A plugin that declares an input type (consumes) runs only on nodes you picked; there is no "run it over every node of that type" shortcut, the same way the agent's invoke_plugin refuses a call without node_ids. Every plugin declares its inputs, and that declaration decides which group it appears in:

  • Matches selection → plugins whose consumes types are in the selection, with an "N targets" badge.
  • Whole-graph / input via form → plugins that consume nothing (for example a query plugin that reads its form). They still receive your current selection, so select a node first when the plugin acts on the current selection.
  • Not applicable here → installed, but none of their input types are in scope (greyed out).
  • Desktop only → installed, but not runnable in a browser.

You can tick several plugins and press Run (N). Once there are more than 6 plugins, a filter box searches names, descriptions and types; its × clears it. Selection chips can be dropped from this run with their ×, which leaves the canvas selection unchanged.

A pack in which a plugin is not named as a plugin, or is named as one of the app's own writers (the AI agent, a merge, a re-verification, New node), is not loaded at all, and none of its plugins is listed or run. A red notice names it: 1 pack was not loaded — … so none of it was run. It needs a corrected release; tell the pack author or the registry maintainers.

Run plugins opened from a right-click on example.com: the scope switch, the selection chip, and the plugins that match it.

docs.title: Launch surfaces
docs.text:
Right-click a nodeThe Run menuThe command palette

Right-click a node, a selection, or empty canvas and choose Run plugins…. The panel opens scoped to that node/selection, or to the whole project from empty canvas.

The top menu bar's Run menu — Run ▸ Run plugins… — opens the same panel, scoped to your current selection, or to the whole project when nothing is selected. The ▶ button on the canvas toolbar does the same; its tooltip names the scope.

Press ⌘K (Ctrl+K) and type the plugin's name. Run WHOIS on the selection (for a plugin that reads no nodes, Run and its name) opens the panel on your selection with that plugin ticked. If the panel was already open, it becomes the only plugin ticked. Nothing runs from the palette: you check the panel and press Run. Run takes the focus, or, when the plugin has a required field that is empty, that field does. See Command palette.

docs.title: Running the same plugins again
docs.text:
A pivot runs the same plugins hop after hop. After a run, Run ▸ Run the last plugins again on the selection (also in the command palette) opens the panel on what is selected now, with the last run's plugins ticked and the parameters you typed for them filled in, and Run focused, so Enter runs them. Files you picked, list values, and anything a plugin marks as a password or a secret are not kept, so a run that needs a file asks for it again. A parameter you have already typed in an open panel is left as you typed it. The last run is forgotten when you leave the project.

The focus moves once, when the panel opens this way, and never while you fill it in. When a required field is empty, the cursor goes to that field instead of Run. When the panel was already open with other plugins ticked, they stay ticked and Run does not take the focus, so Enter never runs a plugin you did not choose here.

docs.title: The pre-run form
docs.text:
When you tick a plugin that takes input, its fields appear under it in the Run plugins panel — text, number, switch, dropdown, or a file drop zone. Required fields are marked * and Run stays disabled until they are filled. Esc in a dropdown's open list closes only the list, so the plugins you ticked and what you filled in stay; the next Esc closes the panel. The nodes a plugin runs on come from the panel's scope, not from these fields. File inputs accept at most 25 MB per file, 50 files and 250 MB per run.

Plugins that need stored settings (for example an API key or gateway URL) show a collapsible Settings (x/y set) block. These values are saved as you type and reused on later runs. Plugins of the same pack that call the same destinations share one value, so a key typed for one of them is filled in for the others that ask for it; a plugin published on its own, or one that declares no network destination, keeps its own. A secret field names the hosts its value is sent to and, when other plugins in the pack share it, how many (Sent to … · shared with N other plugins in this pack). Press Run (N) to start every ticked plugin.

Some packs connect to a server whose address only you know, such as a self-hosted sharing platform or an internal service. Their address field says where requests will go (Requests from this plugin go to …), or why the address is not used, for example This address is not used: it must start with https://. The plugin sends nothing there until the address is set. In the browser an http:// address is not used unless it is on this computer (localhost), because the browser blocks it from the https app: use an https address, or the desktop app. In the desktop app, a server on this computer or on your organisation's network can be read only once you trust it: press Trust … on this computer… under the field and confirm the dialog. The origin is added to Additional trusted origins in Desktop Settings…, applies in every project, and is removed there.

Values are kept separately for each account on this device — in the browser only in this tab, gone when it closes; in the desktop app encrypted and kept across launches (for the session only, on a computer that cannot encrypt them). This separates accounts inside Vineyard, not from someone with direct access to this computer. Manage Keys & Secrets, at the bottom of the panel, opens Settings → Keys & Secrets. Its Plugin keys table lists every plugin key stored for your account on this device, with Pack, Key, Sent to and Value columns; inside a project it also lists the keys the project's packs declare that are not set yet. From a row you can show a stored secret (Show), set or replace the value (Set, Replace) and remove it (Forget); Forget all… removes every stored plugin key.

docs.title: Reviewing a run's changes
docs.text:
A plugin never writes to the project directly. What it would add, change or delete is staged, and when the run ends you get a toast ("N change(s) staged — review to apply") and a needs review badge on its Tasks row. Click the row to open the Review dialog, untick anything you do not want, then press Apply (N) (or ⌘Enter / Ctrl+Enter) — or Discard all. / jumps to Filter by keyword. Nothing is written to the project until you apply; while the Review dialog is open, the changes are only previewed on the canvas. A run that stages nothing ends with a toast showing its summary (or "No changes"). A change that would leave an edge as it is, with its label and the fields it already stores, is not staged, so running a plugin again over the same data does not list those edges again.

The right side of the dialog shows the selected row's properties. For a node, they are what the node will hold once the row is applied: for a change, its stored values with the proposed ones merged in. A new node that is in the project by now, because a review you applied since this run staged added it, is merged into that node instead of being added twice; the pane then says This node is already in the project and shows the merged values, with the node's own spelling of the fields that identify it (Example.com stays Example.com when the run found example.com), as the apply keeps it. For an edge, Recorded with this link below them lists what the edge will store besides its label and grade once the row is applied: for a new edge, what the plugin recorded with it, such as where and when the link was observed; for a change, the edge's stored values with the proposed ones in their place; for a delete, what goes with the edge. The edge's Properties panel shows the same list (see Recorded with this link). Once the apply has finished, or when you reopen the run from Tasks as history, the list is headed Proposed by this change and shows only what the row itself proposed, since the edge may have changed since. The Status column says whether it landed, and the edge's Properties panel shows what it stores now.

Unticking a node also leaves out the edges that need it, and the footer says how many (N edges excluded — their endpoint nodes are not being created). If some links point at nodes from another run that is still waiting for review, the footer says so: apply that review first. Applied before it, those links stay staged in this run with the reason on each row, and they land when you apply this run again after the other one. If the other run is discarded instead, they are skipped. The optional Why reject? field beside Discard all gives your reason to the AI agent when the changes came from one of its conversations.

Closing the dialog with the X or Esc keeps the run waiting for review, and keeps your choices with it: what you unticked or ticked back on, and what you typed in Why reject?, are still there when you reopen the review, even after opening another project and coming back. Esc closes the dialog from anywhere in it, and also while nothing has focus, as right after Apply. That holds after an Apply from the keyboard too (Tab to Apply and Enter, or ⌘Enter / Ctrl+Enter in Why reject?), whatever you clicked last: the AI agent, Run plugins or Skill pack panel behind the review stays open. In the Filter by keyword field while it holds text, it clears the filter first, as the field's × does. An Esc right after a click in another panel, such as the AI agent's, is that panel's. While a review is open, an Esc pressed in Run plugins or the Skill pack panel, or right after a click in it, closes that panel and leaves the review open; an Esc from anywhere else leaves them open.

A run waiting for review is also kept on this device, under your account, so a reload, a restart, an app update or a crash does not lose it. The next time you open the project it is waiting for review again in Tasks, with your choices and your Why reject? text, even if the dialog was open when the page went away. A plugin run or AI turn that a reload or a crash cut short comes back with what it had staged by then. The Tasks row for what it staged is cancelled, as after Stop, and says Cut short by a reload, and the review says Cut short by a reload — this is what it had staged by then, not everything it would have found. A run whose apply was under way when the page went away comes back too, but the server may already have written some of its rows: its review says An apply of this set was under way when the page went away — some of these rows may already be in the graph, and a plugin run's Tasks row says so as well. Check the graph before you apply or discard it. If you discard it, each row the graph already holds, one that applying now would not change, is recorded as applied and the rest as discarded, as after a partial apply (below), so the AI agent is told what landed and that you rejected the rest. That needs the whole graph: discarded while the project is still loading, every row is recorded as discarded. A run is kept for 7 days after its last change, and longer while a tab has it open, and then deleted. The footer of the dialog says where the review is kept: Kept on this device only — a reload brings this review back, for 7 days after its last change, or Held in this tab only — a reload loses this review when no account is signed in or this device's storage refuses it. While the storage refuses it, a red notice also stays on screen (Changes waiting for review are not being kept on this device), and leaving the project while a plugin run or an AI turn is still working says the changes live in this tab only and a reload loses them (see Ephemeral by default). Nothing of a run waiting for review is sent to the Vineyard server. A run waiting in a tab that is still open stays with that tab: another tab shows it only once that tab has been closed, the next time it opens the project.

A change from the AI agent that edits a node's fields writes only the fields the agent changed. A field that someone else changed after the agent read the node, in this tab or another, keeps its new value, and the properties on the right show the node as it will be after the apply.

If some changes cannot be written, a Partly applied toast says how many. Those stay staged with the reason on each row and the run is still waiting for review: reopen it to try them again. Once a run is applied or discarded, clicking its row opens a read-only record of what was applied or discarded.

If you press Discard all after part of a run has been applied, only the changes still staged are thrown away; what was applied stays in the graph. The run is then recorded as applied, not discarded: its badge reads applied, its record lists what was applied and marks the discarded rows excluded, and when the run came from an AI agent conversation, the agent is told what landed and that you rejected the rest.

The Review dialog for one run: the staged nodes and edges, the selected row's properties, and Apply (4) / Discard all.

docs.title: Progress and cancellation
docs.text:
Every run you start becomes a task shown in the Tasks panel, with a live status badge, a progress bar where the plugin reports one, and a Stop control. Stop asks the plugin to wind down; if it has not finished within about 3 seconds, it is force-stopped. Any changes it had already staged are kept for you to review, not thrown away. A run that exceeds its time budget (10 minutes by default, at most 60) is stopped and marked failed. A run that fails discards anything it had staged: that includes a run stopped for exceeding its time budget, a sandbox that did not start, and a plugin error. Only Stop, or a reload that cuts the run short, keeps partial results. See Tasks & runs for states and controls.

Each request a plugin makes also has its own deadline, by default a minute at most unless the plugin sets another, so a host that does not answer fails that request instead of holding the run for its whole budget. If such a run still completes but stages nothing, its toast is yellow and names the hosts that did not answer (no answer from …). Read "No changes" there as "could not check", not "nothing found".

Plugin runs the AI agent starts have no Tasks row of their own. Each one that staged something appears as a change set in that conversation and is reviewed there, or applied at the end of the turn under Apply automatically. Stopping the turn, or deleting the conversation, stops them. See What the agent can do.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
A pivot is the same few steps again and again: select a node, widen the selection by a hop, run plugins on it, review what they found. Each of those steps has a key, so you can keep both hands on the keyboard while you work.

Press ? or ⌘/ (Ctrl+/ on Windows and Linux) anywhere you are not typing in a field, or choose Keyboard shortcuts at the foot of the sidebar, to see Vineyard's shortcuts. While another dialog such as Settings is open the keys do nothing until you close it, and opening Settings closes the list. The list shows the keys of the computer you are on: ⌘ on a Mac, Ctrl on Windows and Linux. Type in its search field to narrow it, by what you want to do (connect), by where (review) or by a key (esc, cmd, shift). Esc empties the search field first, and closes the list once the field is empty.

The list has the keys Vineyard gives you, on the canvas, in its panels and dialogs, and in its fields. It leaves out what every app shares: Tab between controls, Enter in a one-field form such as a project's name or an invitation, Enter and Space on a button, and the arrows in an open menu or drop-down.

docs.title: Command palette
docs.text:
Press ⌘K (Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux), even while you are typing in a field, or choose Command palette in the sidebar, and type what you want to do. The palette finds the commands of the project's menu bar, the canvas toolbar and the right-click menus by the name the menu gives them, so export finds Export graph (JSON) and grid finds Grid. Where two menus name one command differently, either name finds it: merge selected finds Merge nodes…, the Edit menu's Merge selected nodes…. The controls for hiding and saved views are commands too: Filter the canvas… opens the toolbar's Filter panel, Show all hidden clears its rules (greyed with Nothing is hidden on the canvas. while nothing is), and Save view… opens the Saved views dialog. Besides the commands it offers:

  • the Settings sections: keys finds Settings: Keys & Secrets;
  • the layouts, such as Layout: Stress (distance-preserving), with the one in use ticked;
  • the project's saved views on this device, such as Saved view: For the report, opened as View ▸ Saved views opens one. They are listed wherever views can be kept, so not on a project opened from its link while signed out;
  • a new node of any installed type, such as Add node: Domain, added and selected as the Types panel adds one;
  • a plugin to run, such as Run WHOIS on the selection, offered while a node it reads is selected; a plugin that reads no nodes is always offered. It opens Run plugins with that plugin ticked (the only one ticked, if the panel was open), and nothing runs until you press Run;
  • Run the last plugins again on the selection, once you have run plugins in the project (see Running plugins);
  • the skill packs and their starters, such as Infrastructure pivoting: Map the infrastructure. A starter with nothing to fill in puts its draft in a new AI agent conversation, where it waits for you to send it; one with blanks opens the skill pack on that starter's form;
  • a node, by any of its values, as the graph search finds it. Nodes come after the commands, and choosing one selects it and centres it.

With nothing typed, the commands you ran most recently come first; the palette remembers the last eight on this device, never a node or a saved view. ↓ and ↑ move, Enter runs the highlighted command, and Esc closes the palette. The Enter that finishes a Korean syllable only finishes the syllable. A command that cannot run right now is shown greyed with the reason the menu gives, for example Select something first to expand from. A command that cannot be undone never runs on Enter alone: Delete and Disconnect all open the same question as from the right-click menu, and Stop the AI agent's turn asks first, with Cancel focused; Esc there goes back to the list. Like the shortcut list, the palette does not open while another dialog such as Settings is open, and opening Settings closes it.

docs.title: Where the keys are shown
docs.text:
You do not have to learn the keys from this page. A menu item that a key also does shows the key on its right, and a toolbar button names its key at the end of its tooltip, for example Fit view · F. The keys are written for your computer: ⌘A on a Mac, Ctrl+A on Windows and Linux. In the Layout menus, ⇧L (Shift+L) is shown next to the layout in use, because picking that layout again is what the key does.

  • In the right-click menu, Connect to… shows its key and the click that links in one step (⌘-click, or Ctrl-click on Windows and Linux).
  • The edge menu shows no keys: a right-click on an edge does not select it, and the keys act on the selection.
  • While an AI agent conversation is open, Ask the AI agent on the toolbar and in the Run menu shows no key. Clicking it starts a new conversation, while A and G then A go into the open conversation's message box.
  • With the single keys turned off (see below), the menus, the tooltips and the command palette stop showing them, and show only the keys that still work. Keyboard shortcuts at the foot of the sidebar then shows ⌘/ (Ctrl+/) instead of ?.

docs.title: How shortcuts behave
docs.text:
• A key on its own, such as ?, works only when you are not typing in a field; in a field it types the character. The AI agent's message box locks while the agent works, so the keys you go on typing after sending a question are still typing: while the box stays locked they run no shortcut, however long you wait, until you click somewhere or move with Tab. Esc and the shortcuts with ⌘ or Ctrl still work.
  • When the agent is done, the caret goes back into its message box, unless you have clicked somewhere else in the meantime.
  • In a field, besides the field's own keys, only Esc, ⌘K (Ctrl+K), ⌘G (Ctrl+G) in the search field, ↑ in the AI agent's message box and ⌘↵ (Ctrl+Enter) in the Review dialog work.
  • The canvas keys need the canvas. Click the canvas, or press G then C, and the canvas keys act on it; a thin blue outline shows when the canvas has keyboard focus. They also work before you have clicked anywhere. A key pressed in the Properties panel, the menu bar, a floating panel or a dialog, or right after you clicked in one of them, leaves the graph alone: ⌫ (Backspace) after you edit a value in the Properties panel never deletes the selection.
  • Esc closes one thing per press, the one in front first, and once nothing is left open it clears the selection. An open menu of the menu bar (Project, Edit, View, Run) closes on its own, before the panel behind it, and an open drop-down list, such as a choice in the Properties panel or among a plugin's parameters, closes on its own before the panel it is in. Right-click menus gives the order.
  • ⌘C (Ctrl+C) copies the selected nodes' labels only while you are not typing in a field, no text on the page is selected and no dialog is open; otherwise it copies what it always does. See Copying labels.
  • With a Korean input source, the keys still work by their place on the keyboard: the key that types ㄹ is F, and G then A is the key that types ㅎ, then the one that types ㅁ.
  • A symbol key is the character it types, wherever your layout puts it. On German, French, Spanish, Italian, Nordic and Swiss layouts, [ and ] are typed with AltGr on Windows or Option on a Mac, and that is how they select inbound and outbound neighbors there.
  • Keys that switch the input source are never shortcuts, so typing Korean never runs one: 한/영, 한자, Caps Lock, Shift+Space, and Ctrl or ⌘ with Space. The key that finishes a Korean syllable only finishes the syllable.
  • Settings → General → Keyboard → Single-key shortcuts turns off every shortcut that is a single character (F, N, /, [ and the rest) and the G then a letter keys, for example if you use dictation. Esc, Enter, the arrow keys, Delete and the shortcuts with ⌘ or Ctrl stay on. The setting is This device only.
  • In a browser tab, the browser keeps some keys for itself before Vineyard sees them, such as ⌘N, ⌘T, ⌘W and ⌘Q on a Mac (Ctrl+N, Ctrl+T, Ctrl+W and Ctrl+Q elsewhere), so none of them is a shortcut here. The same goes for reload, the address bar, page zoom (⌘+, ⌘- and ⌘0 on a Mac) and the developer tools. On a Mac, ⌘, may open the browser's own settings instead of Vineyard's; Settings is also in the sidebar.

docs.title: What the default keys do
docs.text:
• Searching. ⌘F (Ctrl+F) or / goes to Search entities…. ⌘G / ⇧⌘G (Ctrl+G / Ctrl+Shift+G) jump to the next / previous search result, selected and centred. They work while something is typed in the search field: in the field itself, and anywhere outside another text field.
  • Going places. Press G, then the second key within a second. G then A goes to the AI agent's message box, and opens a new conversation if the panel is closed. G then P goes to the first field of the Properties panel, switching it to Table from Document or JSON, and G then T to the Types panel's search field, or to its first type when the panel is collapsed to icons. G then M opens the Marketplace when the Project menu offers it.
  • The view. F fits the whole graph in view, like Fit view, and ⇧F (Shift+F) fits the selection, centring a single node at 150%. = or + and - zoom like the toolbar buttons; hold one to keep zooming. 0 zooms to 100%. The arrow keys move the view, a longer step with Shift. L opens the Layout menu, where ↓ reaches the first layout and Enter picks one. ⇧L (Shift+L) lays the graph out again with the current layout, letting go of where nodes were left.
  • The selection. ⌘A (Ctrl+A) selects all nodes. N extends the selection to connected neighbors, and [ / ] inbound / outbound, one hop per press. Invert selection, Select isolated nodes and Clear selection have no key of their own; Esc clears the selection.
  • What is selected. R opens Run plugins on the selection, or on the whole project with nothing selected. A asks the AI agent about the selection: a new conversation opens with the question filled in, not sent. With a conversation already open, the key goes to its message box instead and fills in the question only if the box is empty, so a question you have started stays as it is. C is Connect to…: click the node to connect the selection to. Enter or F2 edits the selected node's value in the Properties panel, in the field its label shows; for an edge, its relation. From the panel's Document or JSON view the panel switches to Table for it, and the field opens even when the panel's finder or Hide empty leaves it out. ⌫ or ⌦ (Delete or Backspace on Windows and Linux) deletes the selection: the same confirmation as Delete (N) opens, with Cancel focused. Duplicate and stopping an agent turn have no key, so neither can happen by a stray keystroke.
  • The AI agent panel. ↑ in an empty message box brings back your last question to edit and send again. Esc closes the Setup drawer, then the panel; a running turn keeps going (see Tasks & runs).
  • The Review dialog. / goes to Filter by keyword. ⌘↵ (Ctrl+Enter) applies the ticked changes, also from the Why reject? field, but only while Apply is shown and has something to apply. Esc closes the dialog, also while nothing has focus, as right after Apply, and after an Apply from the keyboard even when your last click was in the AI agent, Run plugins or Skill pack panel, which stays open behind it; the run and your ticks stay (see Running plugins).
  • The Properties panel. Tab and Shift+Tab move to the next and previous field. In a one-line field, a number and a date included, Enter saves and Esc puts the value back as stored (see Editing a value).

docs.title: Working with Skill Packs
docs.text:
A Skill Pack is text: a reusable investigation playbook the AI agent can consult.

Where a plugin changes your graph, a Skill Pack changes how the agent works: it is guidance the agent follows. It requests no permissions of its own and executes nothing.

docs.title: What a Skill Pack contains
docs.text:
A Skill Pack is a single document with three parts:

Part Role overview What the playbook is for, and how to route through it — the agent reads this first. sections The actual steps, which the agent loads on demand, one at a time. starters Ready-made ways to start a run — a prompt template with blanks ({{handle}}, {{email}}…) you fill in before sending.

A pack also declares applies_to (the node types it is about) and triggers (keyword hints), so the agent and the UI know when it is relevant.

docs.title: Installing a Skill Pack
docs.text:
Skill Packs install from the Marketplace exactly like plugins:

  1. Open the Marketplace and find the pack (e.g. Account & identity pivoting).
  2. If the pack declares requires (plugin packs its steps call), the Marketplace offers them for co-install — the skill is not usable without them.
  3. Install once; the pack is now available to the agent in that project.

Availability is gated on dependencies

A Skill Pack is only available in a project when every plugin pack in its requires is installed there and can run on this platform. If you uninstall one later, or open the project in a browser when a required pack is desktop-only, the skill quietly stops being offered to the agent and is no longer listed in Run ▸ Skill packs. For example, Account & identity pivoting requires the WhatsMyName pack, which runs only in the desktop app, so this skill is available only there; in the browser it is missing from the menu.

The current catalog ships two Skill Packs:

Skill Pack applies_to Requires What it does Account & identity pivoting (run.vineyard.skillpacks.account_identity_pivot) identity.handle, identity.account, identity.email_address, identity.person run.vineyard.pluginpacks.whatsmyname (desktop app only) Turn one account or handle into the person's other accounts — and know when a shared username is not the same person. Infrastructure pivoting (run.vineyard.skillpacks.infra_pivot) infrastructure.ip_address, infrastructure.domain, infrastructure.certificate, infrastructure.autonomous_system — (none required; uses the graph tools plus whatever DNS/RDAP/certificate/ASN collection plugins the project has, and says which hops it cannot take without them) Expand one indicator (IP/domain/cert) into its connected footprint, one verifiable hop at a time.

docs.title: Using a Skill Pack
docs.text:
Open Run ▸ Skill packs in the top menu bar and pick a pack. The Skill pack panel lists the pack on the left — Overview (what it is about, which plugins it needs, and the text the agent reads first), every section, and the starters grouped by category (Find accounts, Corroborate, Report, …) — and shows the one you pick on the right. The Filter sections and starters… box above the list shows only the sections and starters that contain what you type. The panel opens on the first starter, and like the other panels it can be moved and resized while you keep working on the graph; Esc closes it, after first closing a comparison or going back from editing to reading. With a dialog open over the panel, such as Saved views or Settings ▸ Keys & Secrets, one Esc closes only the dialog, also right after you clicked a saved view's delete button or Keep, or edited a key, and the panel stays as it was. While a review is open, an Esc pressed in the panel, or right after you clicked in it, closes the panel and leaves the review open.

The Skill pack panel: overview, sections and starters on the left; the chosen starter, its blanks and the prompt preview on the right.

Then either:

  • start a run from it: pick a starter on the left, fill the blanks (required ones are marked), set Work without stopping to confirm and Answer language under How to run if you want (both are remembered on this device for your next run), check the preview, and press Ask the agent to follow this. The prompt is placed in the message box of a new AI agent conversation (one you already had open stays in Tasks); nothing is sent until you edit it as you like and send it; or
  • just ask in your own words — the agent decides a pack is relevant (via applies_to / triggers) and reads it on its own.

Skills are guidance, not commands

The agent may adapt a playbook to the project. If a pack's steps cannot proceed (say, the hop needs a plugin the project does not have), the agent says so and stops that branch rather than filling the gap from memory.

docs.title: Your project's own skill packs
docs.text:
Besides the packs installed from the Marketplace, a project can hold skill packs of its own: a copy of an installed pack that you change, one written from scratch, or one imported from a file. They are stored in the project rather than in the registry. In Run ▸ Skill packs they are listed after the installed packs, and in the Skill pack panel they carry a Custom badge.

Action Where What it does Make a copy Skill pack panel, beside the pack's name Saves an independent copy in the project and opens it in the editor. The copy is named Copy of …, gets an identifier such as local.project.skillpacks.account_identity_pivot_copy, version 1.0.0 and you as author. Updating or withdrawing the original does not change it. New skill pack Run ▸ Skill packs Opens an empty pack in the editor; the first Save creates it. Unavailable once the project has 32 packs of its own. Import skill pack… Run ▸ Skill packs Opens a skill pack JSON file of 1 MB or less in the editor, unsaved: it reaches the project only when you press Save. Fields that are not part of a skill pack are left out, and the panel names them. A file that is not a skill pack is refused, and so is one with problems, which are listed by their place in the file. An empty or missing author does not stop the import; the editor asks for one before Save. Edit Skill pack panel, own packs Opens the pack in the editor. Export JSON Skill pack panel, own packs Downloads the pack as a .skill.json file in the format published packs use. Delete Skill pack panel, own packs Shows Deleting this pack removes it from this project for everyone.; Delete pack confirms.

When the file you import has the identifier of one of the project's own packs, the import stops with A custom pack with this identifier already exists. Replace it opens that pack in the editor with the file's content, so saving replaces it; Import as a copy imports the file as a new pack; Cancel imports nothing. A file whose identifier is in the run.vineyard namespace, or already belongs to another pack in the project such as an installed one, is imported as a new pack the same way. Such a pack is re-keyed like a copy: it gets a new local.project.skillpacks.* identifier, a name another pack already uses becomes Copy of …, and an author of VINEYARD becomes your username.

The editor. The left column lists Details (identifier, name, description, author, version, Applies to, Triggers and Requires), Overview, Sections and Starters, with New section and New starter to add one. The bar at the bottom counts problems, which block Save, and warnings, which do not (for example a section the overview never mentions, or a required plugin that cannot run in this project); click a count to go to the first one. Nothing is written until you press Save. Discard changes drops your edits, and Done goes back to reading once there is nothing left to save. If the pack was changed in another session meanwhile, the save is refused with This pack changed elsewhere, so your changes were not saved., and Reload pack replaces your draft with the stored pack. In local mode there is no username, so Author starts empty and is listed as a problem until you fill it in; Export JSON stays unavailable until the saved pack has an author.

  • Who can see and change them. Everyone who can edit the project sees its own packs in Run ▸ Skill packs, can read them, start runs from them and export them, and their AI agent can use them. People who can only view the project do not see them. Only the project owner can make a copy, create, import, edit or delete one, and only the owner is shown the buttons and menu items for it.
  • Limits. A project keeps up to 32 packs of its own, each at most 256 KB. Signed in, they may also take at most 1 MB together. Each field has a length limit as well; the editor shows it and refuses text over it.
  • Reserved names. The run.vineyard namespace and the author name VINEYARD belong to the official packs, and the editor refuses both. New packs and copies start in the local.project.skillpacks.* namespace; you can change the identifier to another of the same form, such as org.example.skillpacks.my_pack, outside run.vineyard. An identifier or name that another pack in the project already uses is refused.
  • Not reviewed by the registry. The registry never sees these packs. The agent is told that such a pack was written in this project by its owner; not reviewed by the registry, and the app's own rules outrank it as they outrank any pack.
  • Packs whose plugins cannot run. One of the project's own packs whose required plugin packs cannot run in this project is not offered to the agent. It stays in Run ▸ Skill packs, dimmed and marked needs plugins, so you can still open it to fix, export or delete it. The panel says The agent does not use this pack while a plugin it needs cannot run in this project., and Ask the agent to follow this is unavailable.
