docs.title: Tasks & runs
docs.text: Every plugin run you start, and every AI agent conversation, is a task shown in the Tasks panel (one row per conversation; each new turn updates it).

docs.title: How tasks work
docs.text:
A running task shows a running badge and, when the plugin reports it, a progress bar.

Plugin runs the AI agent starts have no Tasks row of their own; they belong to the conversation's row. Each run that staged something becomes its own change set in that conversation and is reviewed there, or, under Apply automatically, applied at the end of the turn like the agent's own changes. Stopping the turn, or deleting the conversation, stops the plugins it started.

docs.title: Task states
docs.text:
State What it means running Actively executing. succeeded Finished successfully (terminal). failed Ended with an error (terminal). cancelled You stopped it before it finished (terminal). An AI turn you stopped usually comes back as incomplete when you reopen the project. A run a reload or a crash cut short comes back as cancelled too, holding what it had staged by then, with Cut short by a reload — what it had staged by then is waiting for review. under it, and Cut short by a reload. once you have applied or discarded that review. incomplete AI agent only — the turn ended before the agent finished (terminal): it was left with tool calls that never got an answer, or, when you reopen the project, you had stopped it, it had run out of steps, or it was cut off by the app closing. What it did is kept; open the conversation and press Continue.

A turn that runs out of steps keeps its succeeded badge, and a turn you stop shows cancelled, until the project is reopened; either way the conversation says why it stopped and offers Continue.

A running plugin task has a Stop button (stop an AI turn from the AI agent panel). Click a row to open it: an AI task reopens its conversation, a plugin task opens its review. After a run with changes, the badge shows the review state instead — needs review (or N to review), applied, or discarded — and an AI task with pending changes also has a Review staged changes button. A failed or cancelled badge shows in place of the review state, so a run you stopped usually stays cancelled even when it kept changes. A plugin run's row still opens the review of what it kept, and an AI task still has Review staged changes. A stopped plugin run that comes back after you open another project and return (see Ephemeral by default) shows needs review.

A plugin run waiting for review, and an AI conversation whose changes were applied.

Stop is cooperative

Stop asks the plugin to wind down cleanly. If it has not returned within about 3 seconds, it is force-stopped. Whether it winds down or is force-stopped, the changes it had already staged are kept and offered for review. A run that fails is different: it discards everything it had staged. That includes a run stopped and marked failed for exceeding its time budget (10 minutes unless the plugin declares its own, at most 60), a plugin whose sandbox or code did not load, and a plugin error. Only Stop, or a reload that cuts the run short, keeps partial results.

docs.title: Ephemeral by default
docs.text:
Plugin-run tasks live only in your browser tab's memory; close the tab and they are gone, except the runs still waiting for review. Opening another project drops the previous project's plugin rows; when you come back to it in the same tab, only the plugin runs still waiting for review return. AI conversations are saved on this device (per project) and come back as Tasks rows after a reload, so you can reopen them. Conversations are saved as they happen, so a turn cut short by closing the app is kept and can be continued. Staged changes still waiting for review are kept on this device too, for 7 days after their last change (longer while a tab has them open): after a reload or a restart they are waiting for review again, and the agent is told they are still waiting (see Reviewing a run's changes). A change set that is no longer kept — its 7 days are up, or this device could not store it — is lost on the reload. If an apply had already written part of it, that part stays in the graph: the conversation shows the set as N applied · M not applied, with K skipped between the two when some changes needed no write of their own, such as a duplicate of a node already in the graph. The agent is told what landed, that the rows you had unticked at that apply were refused, and which of the rest were lost, so it proposes only those again.

Leaving a project while a plugin run or an AI turn is still working asks first: Stop the running plugin and leave this project? or Stop the agent and leave this project? Stay in this project keeps you there; Stop and leave stops the work and leaves. When changes are already staged, the dialog says they are kept and will be waiting for review when you open the project again, and whether a reload loses them: They are kept on this device, so a reload does not lose them either while this device keeps them, or They live in this browser tab only — a reload loses them while no account is signed in or the device's storage refuses them.

In the desktop app, closing the window, quitting or reloading while a plugin run or an AI turn is still working asks too: Leave while an AI turn or plugin run is still in progress? Stay keeps everything as it is. Leave anyway closes, quits or reloads, and the rest of the turn is lost. What the turn or the plugin run had staged by then, and the changes already waiting for review, are kept on this device and are waiting for review the next time you open the project; a run cut short this way is marked Cut short by a reload. That is what the prompt says while this device keeps them. While it does not, because no account is signed in or the device's storage refuses them, the prompt says that leaving loses them too: This device is not keeping the changes waiting for review, or what the turn or plugin run has staged, so leaving loses them too. Stay, and apply or discard them before you leave. In a browser tab, the browser asks with its own dialog.

Neither task rows nor conversation content are sent to the Vineyard server; only applied changes are written to the project — the ones you apply in a review, and the ones the agent applies under Apply automatically. The agent's model calls go from the app straight to your AI provider. Where its web searches and the pages it reads go depends on your settings. With the defaults, when you are signed in, the queries the agent writes from the project pass through the Vineyard server on their way to Serper and Google. In a browser tab, the default page-reading mode sends each URL the agent opens to the reader service r.jina.ai; the desktop app does so only when its own fetch fails. See Web search and page reading.

AI conversations stay on this device, under your account

Conversations, messages, project memory, and each conversation's session scope and plan are kept on this device only and are never written to the server. Like your AI provider and web-search keys, they are kept separately for each account — this separates accounts inside Vineyard, not from someone with direct access to this computer. Set the AI provider, model and key in the AI agent panel under Setup → Settings; the web-search key is under Settings → AI agent. Both kinds of key are listed under Settings → Keys & Secrets (LLM keys and Search engine keys), where you can show, replace or forget them. The desktop app encrypts them with the computer's keychain (on a computer that cannot encrypt, they last for the session only); the web app keeps them only until you close the tab.

docs.title: The AI agent panel
docs.text:
The AI agent panel's header shows AI Agent, the conversation's title and its model (click the model to change it), then Setup, ⋯ and Close. Setup opens a drawer with three tabs:

  • Session scope — your boundaries for this conversation only: Rules, Already allowed, Hosts nothing may collect from (each with its subdomains) and Tools ruled out. A new chat starts without a scope, so a boundary set in one conversation does not apply to the project's other conversations. Rules and permissions are told to the agent; hosts and tools are also enforced, and a call that crosses one is refused (see What the agent can do). While a scope is in force, a teal dot shows on the Setup button.
  • Project memory — the agent's notes, shared by every conversation on the project.
  • Settings — provider, model and key, and under Advanced, Temperature, Max output tokens, Context window and Seed. Temperature, max output tokens and seed set here win over the defaults in Settings → AI agent on this browser; a blank field falls back to them. Context window is the window size compaction plans against; set it when Vineyard does not know the model's (see Conversation compaction).

⋯ holds Export this conversation as HTML, Open the agent's working folder (desktop app only) and Delete conversation…. The exported page reads on its own; its Save as JSON button saves the same record as JSON.

The AI agent panel with Setup open on Session scope. The chips above the message box show the apply mode, commands and follow-up turns for the next message.

A row of chips above the message box shows what your next message will run under. The apply and Commands chips open a menu that applies to this conversation only, with Follow my settings to return to your account settings; Follow-up applies to your next message only:

  • The first chip says who applies the agent's changes: Review everything, Review everything (AI-assisted) (the same review, with the agent's suggestions already unticked) or Apply automatically. It turns amber while changes land without review. The menu also holds Stop and ask before anything is removed or overwritten and Have an independent check test each inference. When the check has run, the Review dialog adds a Check column with its verdict on each row (supported, weak, unresolved, refuted, not checked, check failed, or dropped for a change the agent withdrew), and an Independent check pane under the list shows the focused row's claim, the case against it and what would settle it. Drag the pane's top edge to resize it.
  • Commands (desktop app only) — whether the agent may run commands on this machine: Do not run commands, Ask every time, Ask only for risky commands or Never ask. The chip is red while commands run without asking.
  • Follow-up — switch on Keep working after this turn, on its own and the agent carries on for up to the number of turns you set, without asking. It needs Apply automatically, and it switches off again after the message you send.
The first chip's menu, here set to Apply automatically with the independent check on.

Other things to know:

  • While changes wait for review you cannot send. The line above the message box says N change(s) across M change sets need review, with Review and Discard all. This Discard all works like the Review dialog's: a change set part of which was already applied is recorded as applied, with the rest rejected.
  • When the agent works from a plan, a Plan strip sits above the conversation. Add a lead, raise or lower a lead's priority, or drop it; the agent is told at its next plan update, or when the next turn starts.
  • A turn with several tool calls is folded into one line. It counts the calls, names the skill pack the agent read behind a book icon (the first by name, +N for more), and flags notes, errors and staged changes; click it to unfold.
  • An image in an answer is shown as its description and address, and is never loaded.
  • While a turn runs, a bar between the conversation and the message box says what it is doing and counts the seconds. It is teal for the steps the app reports itself, such as Planning…, Checking staged changes…, Applying staged changes… and Finishing the turn…, and violet otherwise: Thinking…, Running and a tool name, or Working….
  • With Show token usage on (Settings → AI agent), each answer shows the tokens its turn used.
A run in progress: the Plan strip on top, an automatic follow-up turn, and 18 tool calls folded into one line that names the skill pack the agent read.

docs.title: Closing and deleting a conversation
docs.text:
In an empty message box, ↑ brings back your last question, to edit and send again. G then A puts the cursor in the message box from anywhere outside a text field, and opens a new conversation when the panel is closed (see Keyboard shortcuts).

Closing the panel — the close button, or Esc — never stops the agent: a running turn keeps working and its row stays in Tasks, so you can reopen it from there. If the Setup drawer is open, Esc or a click outside it closes the drawer first; press Esc again to close the panel. Esc closes the panel when it is meant for it: pressed while you are typing or working inside the panel, or right after you last clicked in it (for example while a turn is running and the message box is locked). An Esc that closes a dropdown or a dialog inside the panel closes only that, and an Esc pressed on the canvas or in another panel leaves the AI agent panel alone.

Deleting a conversation (⋯ → Delete conversation…) asks for confirmation first; Cancel has the focus, so pressing Enter by reflex does not delete. Once you confirm:

  • the conversation, its Tasks row, its session scope and its plan are removed from this device — this cannot be undone;
  • if the agent is still working, its turn is stopped first, along with any plugin runs it started;
  • change sets proposed in the conversation and not yet applied are discarded (the dialog says how many); changes already applied to the graph stay;
  • the panel closes.

Delete conversation… is greyed out, marked Nothing to delete yet, until there is something to delete.

docs.title: What the agent can do
docs.text:
The agent works through tools and calls them on its own as it works, within the limits in the last column; of these, only running a command can stop to ask you first. Whatever it changes in the graph goes through the apply mode: staged for your review, or, under Apply automatically, applied at the end of the turn. Each tool call is listed by its tool name when you unfold a turn's tool-call line.

What it can do Tools What limits it Read the project list_node_types, graph_stats, read_nodes, find_nodes, get_node, read_edges, node_neighbors, similar_hashes, get_selection Read only. similar_hashes compares perceptual hashes, such as a favicon's phash and dhash, by how many of their 64 bits differ — 10 by default, 16 at most. It does not compare a hash at or near a blank icon's, as a blank, single-colour or symmetric icon's is, and a hash from outside the graph must name the one field it was computed as. Trace how two nodes connect find_paths Read only. Like the other reads, it sees only what is already in the graph, not what is staged. Returns up to 10 paths of at most 6 links each, shortest first. By default no path passes through a node with more than 50 links, such as a shared name server, registrar or hosting provider that connects unrelated things; the agent is told which nodes it skipped, and whether the two nodes connect through one of them or by a longer route. It is told they are not connected only when no chain of links of any length joins them and no filter narrowed the search. While the project is still loading (for example while it re-syncs after a reconnect), it waits for the rest of the graph; if the graph has still not finished, it is told its answer covers only what has arrived. See what surrounds a node neighborhood Read only. Like the other reads, it sees only what is already in the graph, not what is staged. Counts the nodes one, two or three links away (two by default) by type, and lists up to 50 of them at each distance, taking from every type in turn so that a few e-mail addresses are not crowded out by hundreds of IP addresses. By default it does not follow the links of a node with more than 50 links, such as a shared name server, registrar or hosting provider: that node is counted, and the agent is told it was not passed through, how many nodes the count would reach if it passed through every such node, and which setting counts them in one call. It is told a node has nothing around it only when the node has no link to another node. While the project is still loading, it waits for the rest of the graph; if the graph has still not finished, it is told its answer covers only what has arrived. Find what nodes have in common common_ground Read only. Like the other reads, it sees only what is already in the graph, not what is staged. Compares 2 to 20 nodes and returns the nodes several of them link to, the values they hold in the same field (any field; true/false values are not compared, and one value under two different field names, such as a WHOIS record's registrant email and an email address node's email, is not compared), and the links between them. Values that differ only in case, spacing, full-width letters or a host name's trailing dot count as the same value. A field that an installed type pack gives its own rule follows that rule instead, on every node that has the field: with the Cryptocurrency pack installed, crypto addresses and transaction hashes are compared by its rule, the Financial pack's legacy ones included, so two addresses that differ only in case on a chain where case matters are two values. Without that pack, a legacy address ignores case like any other value. For each shared value the agent is told how many nodes in the project hold it and how many different values that field has. A shared node with more than 50 links, or a value more than 50 nodes hold, is marked and listed last: something that common links nothing. Count how one field's values are spread aggregate_values Read only. Like the other reads, it sees only what is already in the graph, not what is staged, and while the project is still loading it waits for the rest. For the nodes of one type it counts how many hold a value in a field, how many different values there are and what share of them only one node holds, and lists the values most held first, each with how many nodes hold it; without a field it summarises every field those nodes hold. Values count as the same when common_ground would call them the same. True/false values are counted, and a list written into one text field, such as open_ports, is counted entry by entry: the entries the Properties panel shows. The counts are of this project only, and the agent is told so: nodes collected because they are related share their operator's values, so a value many nodes hold here is not therefore common elsewhere. Asked to classify, it labels a field specific (at least 100 different values, at least half of them held by one node each), quasi-specific (at least 10) or non-identifying (fewer than 10), following Operation MIDAS (Black Hat Europe 2024). It does not classify a field that fewer than 100 nodes hold while it has fewer than 100 different values and at least half of them are held by one node each: with more nodes it could be specific, so at that size the thresholds would measure the project rather than the field. A list field can have 100 different entries among fewer nodes, and a field whose few values many nodes share is categorical at any size, so both are classified. Nothing is classified while the project is still loading. Pull indicators out of text extract_indicators Reads only the text it is given and the nodes it names. Nothing leaves the app and nothing is staged: what it finds are candidates, which the agent stages with create_node like any other node. See what the graph's connections hang on graph_structure Read only, and like the other reads it sees only what is already in the graph. Returns the graph's connected components, the clusters inside them, and the links and nodes that alone join two groups: a link that is the only one between two groups, and a node every connection between groups runs through. If such a link is wrong, the groups are not connected at all, so links come in the order to check them: the weakest grade first, so those graded below asserted or not graded come before the rest, and links of the same grade by how many nodes hang on them. By default, like find_paths, it does not count a route through a node with more than 50 links, such as a shared name server, as a second connection between two groups: a link or node that is the only one between them apart from such a node is listed too, with that node named. A link that holds a single node to the rest is counted, not listed. Given nodes, it looks only at the parts of the graph that hold them and puts first what their connection to each other depends on. A node with more than 50 links at such a junction is marked as shared infrastructure that does not show the groups are related. Clusters are computed in the background so the canvas does not freeze; where that is not possible and the graph has more than 15,000 links, or if clustering fails, the agent is told they were not computed. While the project is still loading, it waits for the rest of the graph, as find_paths does. Rank nodes by their links rank_nodes Read only, and like the other reads it sees only what is already in the graph. Ranks nodes by how many links they have (all of them, or only those recorded as pointing to or leaving the node), or by how many of the shortest connections between other nodes run through them, and returns up to 100 at a time. Every answer tells the agent that a high rank says where to look, not that anything is related: the most-linked nodes are usually shared infrastructure, such as a name server, and a node with more than 50 links is marked as such. For connections through a node, like find_paths it does not pass through a node with more than 50 links by default. That ranking is computed in the background so the canvas does not freeze. Where a part of the graph that stays connected without passing through such a node is too large to count in full, its scores are estimated from a sample of starting nodes, and the agent is told which scores are estimates. Groups that connect to each other only through such nodes are counted one by one, so small groups are counted exactly. Where the background is not available and the graph is too large to rank this way without freezing, or if the computation fails, the agent is told it was not computed. While the project is still loading, it waits for the rest of the graph, as find_paths does. Select nodes by their values filter_nodes Read only, and like the other reads it sees only what is already in the graph. Selects the nodes whose fields meet every condition it is given: a number or date before or after a bound (a date such as 2026-12-31, or one counted from now, such as 30 days from now), an exact value or one of a list, text a field contains or a regular expression it matches, whether a field is set, or a perceptual hash within some bits of another (10 by default, 16 at most). Text comparisons ignore case unless the agent asks otherwise. A text field that holds a list one per line or comma-separated, such as a domain's name servers or a host's open ports, is compared item by item, so a domain with two name servers matches either of them. A date without a time counts as that whole day. Returns up to 100 nodes at a time, each with the values the conditions read. A node whose value cannot be compared, such as a follower count written as 12.3K, a date without a time on the very day a condition falls in, or a value where it is unclear whether a comma separates two items, is left out, and the agent is told how many were left out, with examples, so that it does not report the rest as all of them. As with similar_hashes, a hash at or near a blank icon's is not compared; the agent is told how many nodes held only such a hash, and that this is not a gap in the answer. A condition on a field no node holds is refused, and the agent is told the fields the nodes do hold. A regular expression is tested in the background, on values of up to 4,096 characters, and is stopped after 3 seconds, so a pattern that would run without end cannot freeze the app; a pattern of a shape known to do so is refused outright. Where nothing can run in the background, regular expressions are refused. While the project is still loading, it waits for the rest of the graph, as find_paths does. Find and merge duplicates find_duplicates, merge_nodes find_duplicates is read only. It groups nodes of one type that the type packs' identity rules call the same entity (see Duplicates and merging), largest group first, and names the best-linked member as the one to keep, or, once part of a group is merged, the node that merge keeps. It returns up to 25 groups a call; each names up to 5 members with their label and number of links, the one to keep first, then the next members by id, up to 21 in all, which is one merge_nodes call. Members a staged merge already takes are left out and counted, so a second call after a merge lists the rest of a large group, and a group whose members are all being merged is counted, not listed. merge_nodes changes the graph like the tools below: one call folds up to 20 duplicates into the node kept, and only live nodes of one type, unless the agent says it is replacing an older type's node. Parallel workers can find duplicates but not merge them: a worker reports the groups it found to the lead agent, which merges them. Change the graph create_node, update_node, delete_node, create_edge, update_edge, delete_edge; read_staged and drop_staged for what it has staged The apply mode (the first chip, or Apply the agent's changes automatically in Settings), with Stop and ask before anything is removed or overwritten and the independent check on top. Run installed plugins list_plugins, invoke_plugin It needs no approval to start a run, and the plugin makes its usual network requests; what it collects is handled like the agent's own changes. It cannot start a plugin this build cannot run, such as a desktop-only plugin in the browser. A run is refused when a target names a host in Hosts nothing may collect from, or when invoke_plugin is in Tools ruled out. When the app refuses a plugin's code, the agent does not run that plugin, or another plugin from the same pack that runs the same code, again in that turn, and is told to report which one was refused with the reason the error gives, such as code that does not match the registry's digest or code that could not be checked. It does not call a refusal tampering unless the error says the code did not match. Search the web and read pages web_search, fetch_page Allow web search, Search provider and Reading a page (see Web search and page reading). A query or URL that names a ruled-out host is refused. Work several leads at once investigate_in_parallel; read_findings recalls this turn's worker findings and challenge verdicts Up to 5 workers per call, each up to 8 steps, with the same read and collection tools but no fan-out, challenge, plan or memory writes of their own. Challenge a claim before asserting it challenge_claim A separate model call, up to 8 per turn, judging by the Independent review prompt. Keep a plan update_plan, prove_goal Shown in the Plan strip. Keep project memory remember, consolidate_memory Project memory size. It may merge or retire its own notes without asking. Read skill packs list_skills, load_skill Offered only when the project has a skill pack whose plugins are installed and can run here. Show you nodes, or a path between them select_node View only; changes no data. Selects one node, or up to 200 nodes and 200 links at once, such as every node and link of a path find_paths found, in place of what you had selected, and moves the view onto them. When they do not fit the part of the canvas that floating panels such as the AI agent panel leave uncovered, it zooms out until they do, and centres them there. It never zooms in, so one node, or nodes already in view, keep your zoom. If you zoom, drag the canvas or show something else while the view is moving, your move wins and the rest of the agent's is dropped. One node or link also opens in the Properties panel. A node your canvas filter hides is shown on its own, and the agent is told so. A link it shows whose ends the filter hid brings those ends back onto the canvas with it, not selected, and the agent is told which ones. While the canvas is still drawing or laying out the graph, the agent waits for it first, for up to 8 seconds. Stop ends the wait and changes nothing: a node the filter hid goes back under it, unless you selected it meanwhile. When the canvas takes longer than the wait, a node the filter hid still appears once it is drawn, and the agent is told the filter was hiding it. A node staged this turn, or one the canvas has not drawn yet, cannot be shown; the agent is told which ids it could not show and why, and the rest are still shown. Run commands (desktop app) run_command The Commands chip, or Run commands on this machine in Settings. Runs as you, in the project's working folder, for up to 2 minutes by default (10 at most). A command line that names a ruled-out host is refused. Work with files (desktop app) list_files, read_file, write_file, edit_file, delete_file Only inside the project's working folder (⋯ → Open the agent's working folder), whatever the Commands setting. Writing over a file keeps a copy, and deleting moves the file to .vineyard-trash/; a file removed by a command is not kept.

extract_indicators finds IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and ranges, domains, URLs, e-mail addresses, phone numbers, MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, CVE ids, Bitcoin, Ethereum-format and TRON addresses, and Telegram handles, including defanged spellings such as hxxp and [.]. A domain must end in a real top-level domain, so a file name such as invoice.pdf is left out, and so is sentence.It, two sentences with the space after the full stop missing. An @handle counts as a Telegram handle only where the text puts it on Telegram: in Telegram: @a | X: @b, only @a does. A wallet whose checksum fails (Base58Check, Bech32, or the mixed case of an EVM address, EIP-55) is left out too, with the reason. A result also carries the node it would be, ready to stage, when the project has that type and the value fits it. For a Bitcoin, Ethereum-format or TRON address that is the Cryptocurrency pack's cryptocurrency.crypto_address on the network its format settles, as the value menu offers it: bitcoin for bc1…, tron for T…, evm for a 0x address, and unknown for a legacy 1… or 3… address, which is the same string on Bitcoin, Bitcoin Cash and Bitcoin SV. Only a project that has the Financial pack and not the Cryptocurrency pack gets the legacy financial.crypto_address instead, with its currency. Each result says how often it appears and how it was written, and marks private and documentation addresses, hosts under Hosts nothing may collect from, and a node of the same type that already has the value. Addresses are read as the Properties panel reads them, so a range is named the same way in both (Reading values); a Teredo, 6to4 or NAT64 address carries a public IPv4 address and is not marked. A node of another type with that value, such as a threat.indicator holding a domain, is not the same node, so the agent can still create the domain.

docs.title: Duplicates and merging
docs.text:
One entity recorded twice splits its links between two nodes, and a pivot through it stops at whichever one it reached. find_duplicates finds them two ways:

  • The same identity. Nodes whose identifying fields are the same value once the type pack's identity rules fold it. From Infrastructure 4.3.0 that includes a domain, host or DNS record name written with a trailing dot or in Unicode (Bücher.de. and xn--bcher-kva.de), an IPv6 address with and without zero compression, an IPv4 address padded to three digits per part where each padded part is 000 to 007 (192.000.002.001; a part such as 010 is read as octal by browsers, so that address is compared as written), and a URL that differs only in the case of its scheme or host, its default port or its percent-encoding. A URL path keeps its case. Two nodes can share an identity because one was made before its type pack folded the spelling, by hand, by import, or by two collections at once.
  • The same canonical form. Phone numbers are identified as written, so +82 10-1234-5678 and 010-1234-5678 stay two nodes when they are written. Once a pack has filled their e164, they are found as one number. This is reported, not done by itself: nothing merges them until a merge is applied.

A rule a type pack adds reaches a project only after you update that type pack in the project.

merge_nodes keeps one node and folds the others into it, staged like any other change:

  • Fields the kept node has no value for are filled from the duplicates. A field it already has is never replaced: a different value on a duplicate is reported to the agent and listed on the duplicate's row as not kept, and is not written. There are two exceptions, both as an import has them, and the agent is told of each:

    • tlp is raised to the strictest TLP label among the kept node and the duplicates, and never lowered, also from a duplicate of an older type that lends no other field. One label spelled two ways, such as TLP:AMBER and amber, or TLP:WHITE and TLP:CLEAR, is one value and no conflict; a label with a note beside it, such as TLP:RED (Case 7 only) against TLP:RED, still differs. A duplicate you keep by unticking its delete lends no label, and the next strictest one still counts.
    • The source fields source_report, created_by, tags, markings and references are combined: the kept node's parts stay and each duplicate's other parts are added (fields_unioned). A duplicate whose parts the kept node already holds is no conflict; a value that is not a list, such as an object, still is.

    The fill is applied to the node as it is when you apply, so a value written on it in the meantime stays.

  • Each link of a duplicate moves to the kept node with its own wording and record: who wrote it, its evidence grade and who gave it, and the fields its writer recorded, as the link stands when you apply. A link you drew yourself is still yours on the kept node. The moved link is a new edge, so the edge's own history in the activity log does not carry over.

  • Where the kept node already has a link to the same node, the duplicate's link is not added again. With the same wording, a different writer's link is recorded as corroboration on the kept link; the same collector drawing it from two spellings, or the agent, adds nothing. If the duplicate's link is yours (you wrote it or gave it its grade) and the kept link is not, the kept link takes your record instead, and its own writer is listed as corroborating it. With different wording, the kept link stays and the duplicate's is deleted with it; the agent is told both wordings.
  • Where two duplicates link the same node in different words, the first one's link moves and the agent is told both wordings. If you keep the first duplicate, the second one's link moves instead, in its own words.
  • A link the agent staged in the same turn on a pair a duplicate already links does not take the place of the duplicate's link. The duplicate's link moves and is applied first, and the agent's adds nothing.
  • A link between two of the merged nodes is deleted.
  • Where links are folded into one, the link that stands takes the strictest TLP label among them and is never lowered, also when the kept link takes your record (links_tlp_raised). That covers a duplicate's link folded into the kept node's same link, by another writer or by the same one, and the same link on two duplicates that moves as one.

In the review every row of a merge says so: the update of the kept node (fields filled from …, tlp raised from … to … when the label rises, and source_report combined, adding … for a source field), each moved link (moved from …), each corroborated link, and the duplicate's delete (merged into …, with the fields that are not kept). A moved or corroborated link whose label rises ends with ; tlp raised from TLP:CLEAR to TLP:RED (none when the link had no label), and one folded in only for its label reads (merge: the same link on …, by the same source; tlp raised from …). The Tasks row's summary says, for example, source_report combined. Unticking a duplicate's delete keeps that node as it is: the links that would move off it, the fields it would fill and the corroboration it would lend are unticked with it. A link or a field that two duplicates both carry stays ticked while either of them is deleted, and is taken from the one that is.

When you apply, a duplicate is deleted only after every link and field moving off it has landed. If one of them is refused, for example at the project's link limit, the delete waits in the review with the reason, and applying again retries the rest first. If the kept node has been deleted in the meantime, nothing is merged and the duplicates stay. A duplicate deleted in the meantime lends the merge nothing: its fields are not filled onto the kept node, and what would have come only from it is skipped with the reason. If a reload cuts a merge's apply short, applying it again completes it: a link already moved is recognised as the move's own, and the delete goes ahead. A link on the same pair in the same words but with another record still holds the merge, because deleting the duplicate would lose that record.

A merge carries the links and fields the duplicate had when it was staged, so a duplicate that has changed since is not merged. That is the case when a link was drawn to it or one of its links was relabelled, a field was written on it, another change in the same set touches it, or a link of the kept node that the merge relied on was removed, relabelled or added. Nothing moves off that duplicate, its delete is skipped with the reason, and the agent can merge again from the graph as it now is. When an earlier apply of the same change set already landed the fill and the moved links and only the delete failed, the reason says what is already on the kept node (blank fields filled from the duplicate, links copied, links folded into the same link), that the duplicate still has its own, and that merging again finds those on the kept node rather than adding them twice. While a merge is waiting, a collection that writes a duplicate's value does not add it to the duplicate. It goes to the kept node when that node has the same identity, and is a new node otherwise. Once the agent has merged duplicates, its own later writes to a merged duplicate or to one of that duplicate's links (editing it, linking to it, relabelling or deleting one of its links, deleting it again) are refused, and it is told the node to write on instead. That holds for a merge in another change set still waiting for review too, your own merge included, so a merge the agent reports is not skipped at apply over a stray write of its own.

You can merge nodes yourself from the canvas as well (see Merging nodes). That is the same merge, planned and staged by the same code, under its own change set named Merge for your review; the apply mode and the independent check below are the agent's and do not apply to it. When the agent finds duplicates it does not merge, because a parallel worker cannot merge or because it is not certain the nodes are one entity, it tells you why and where to merge them yourself.

A merge deletes nodes, so under Apply automatically with Stop and ask before anything is removed or overwritten on, it stops for your review; raising a label or combining a source field on the kept node would stop it there too, as a plugin's change to a value does. The independent check, when it runs, judges a merge once, as the claim that the nodes are one entity; the moved links and the filled fields are not new claims and are not checked. If the check refuses that claim, the whole merge waits for your review, not only the delete.

When the agent reads edges (read_edges, node_neighbors, and the edges in get_selection), each edge comes with what the project records about how far to trust it: its evidence grade (the one the canvas draws and the legend's Evidence key lists), who gave that grade, who wrote its label, which other writers drew the same link, and when a collector first and last saw it. Anything that is not recorded is left out. Other fields a plugin stored on an edge come back only when the agent asks for them. The agent is told what each grade means, including that recorded means a tool recorded the link, not that anyone verified it, that an unassessed you set may have replaced a check's grade, and that a grade from Re-verify came from the re-verification you ran, not from a plugin, and that a grade a merge you made raised came only from the merged nodes' writers drawing the same link. It cannot set a grade itself.

Every turn is bounded by the Step budget. The model calls a turn hands to parallel workers and to challenge_claim come out of a separate allowance of five times the step budget. Any of web_search, fetch_page, invoke_plugin, run_command and investigate_in_parallel can be put under Tools ruled out for a conversation, and parallel workers are held to the same session scope.

docs.title: Web search and page reading
docs.text: What happens when the agent searches or opens a page is set under Settings → AI agent, by the settings below. A change applies from your next question. The choices are stored with your account when you are signed in, and on this device in local mode (Signed in or local).

docs.title: Allow web search
docs.text: On by default. It offers the agent web_search and fetch_page. Off, the agent and its parallel workers have neither tool, so nothing from the project goes to a search provider or a page reader. Search provider and Reading a page are dimmed while it is off.

docs.title: Search provider
docs.text:
Where the agent's queries go. A query is written by the agent from the project, so it can name the domains, accounts and people under investigation. Each option in the list says who sees the query, and badges mark no key, desktop only and unreliable. An option this app cannot use is greyed out; in local mode the two server options are marked needs the Vineyard server.

Provider Where the query goes Key Where it works Serper, through the Vineyard server (default) Vineyard server (auxiliary.vineyard.run) → Serper → Google None (the operator's) Signed in, in the browser or the desktop app; not in local mode Brave, through the Vineyard server Vineyard server (auxiliary.vineyard.run) → Brave None (the operator's) Signed in, in the browser or the desktop app; not in local mode Brave, with your own key Desktop app → Brave Yes Desktop app only Mojeek App → Mojeek Yes Browser and desktop app SearXNG (self-hosted) App → the address you set → the engines it aggregates None; needs your instance's address, with its JSON output turned on (formats: [json]) and CORS headers that let the app call it Browser and desktop app Jina App → Jina Optional; without one, searches are heavily rate-limited Browser and desktop app Exa App → Exa Yes Browser and desktop app Serper, with your own key App → Serper → Google Yes Browser and desktop app DeepSeek, with your own key App → DeepSeek Yes (your DeepSeek API key, billed per call; queries of up to 128 characters) Browser and desktop app Kimi (Moonshot), with your own key Desktop app → Moonshot Yes (your Moonshot API key, billed per call) Desktop app only DuckDuckGo Desktop app → DuckDuckGo None Desktop app only; marked unreliable, since DuckDuckGo blocks datacenter and VPN addresses with a CAPTCHA

When the chosen provider cannot run where you are, the agent searches with another one instead of failing:

  • In a browser tab, a desktop-only choice (made in the desktop app, which shares your account's settings) falls back to Serper, through the Vineyard server.
  • In local mode, a server option, including the default, falls back to DuckDuckGo.

The two server options run on the operator's key, so they can run out; for work that has to be reliable, pick a provider you supply your own key for. Choosing a provider that takes a key adds a key field below the list, and choosing SearXNG adds an address field. Both are This device only: what you enter stays on this device and is never sent to the Vineyard server. The key is kept like the agent's other keys, encrypted by the desktop app or until the tab closes in the web app; the address stays until you change it.

docs.title: Reading a page
docs.text:
How the agent turns a link into text. No mode needs a key or a sign-in.

Mode Where the URL goes Whichever works (default) In the desktop app, Vineyard fetches the page itself and falls back to the reader service r.jina.ai only when that fails. In a browser tab, every URL goes to r.jina.ai first, and a direct fetch is the fallback. HTML is converted to Markdown either way. Reader service (r.jina.ai) r.jina.ai fetches the page and returns clean text. It handles almost any site, and sees every URL the agent opens. Direct, converted to Markdown Vineyard fetches the page itself and reduces the HTML to Markdown, keeping its links. Nobody else is involved. In a browser tab this works only for sites that allow cross-origin requests; the desktop app has no such limit. Direct, exactly as served The same fetch, with no conversion. Costs far more context on an HTML page; meant for JSON or plain-text endpoints, or for keeping a source exactly as it was served.

In the desktop app, a direct fetch refuses your own machine and private-network addresses, and follows each redirect itself, so a hop onto a host in Hosts nothing may collect from is refused before it is requested. In a browser tab, a page that redirected onto a ruled-out host is discarded after it arrives. The reader service follows redirects on its own servers, where they cannot be checked.

docs.title: Allow non-standard ports
docs.text: Off by default, under Desktop app. A direct fetch in the desktop app uses only ports 80 and 443; this lets it use other ports, while your own machine and private network stay closed. It has no effect on the reader service or in a browser tab, and it is greyed out while web search is off or the reader service is chosen.

docs.title: AI agent settings
docs.text:
Settings → AI agent (⌘, on a Mac or Ctrl+, opens Settings) holds the agent's defaults. They are stored with your account when you are signed in, and on this device in local mode; rows marked This device only stay in this browser. Changes apply from your next question. A conversation can override the apply mode and the Commands setting from its chips.

Provider and Model are shown here read-only: you choose them in the AI agent panel under Setup → Settings, and they are kept on this device only.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Step budget 50 (1–200) How many steps the agent may chain in one turn before it has to stop and report. Parallel workers and challenge_claim draw on a separate allowance of five times this many model calls. Project memory size 50 notes (10–200) How many notes the project memory holds before the agent is refused and has to ask you to prune. Every note is re-read into each turn. Compaction threshold 70% (30–75%, in steps of 5) When older messages are summarized; see Conversation compaction. Allow web search On Offers the agent its search and page-reading tools. Show reasoning On Shows the model's thinking, folded under each answer, where the provider sends it. Show token usage Off Shows the tokens each turn used under its answer, with the cached share and a breakdown by call. Re-arrange the graph after each turn Off Runs the current layout again over the whole graph each time an agent turn's changes are applied.

docs.title: Web search
docs.text: This group holds Search provider (default Serper, through the Vineyard server), a key field for a provider that takes one and an address field for SearXNG, both This device only, and Reading a page (default Whichever works). See Web search and page reading for what each choice does.

docs.title: Review and apply
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Apply the agent's changes automatically Review everything (AI-assisted) Review everything (every change waits, all ticked), Review everything (AI-assisted) (the same review, with the changes the agent advises against already unticked) or Apply automatically. Stop and ask before anything is removed or overwritten On With Apply automatically only: holds a change set for your review when it deletes something, rewrites a link label you wrote or overwrites a field that already has a value. Have an independent check test each inference, and collect what would settle it Off A second model tests each relationship, overwrite and removal. A link the agent draws or rewords is tested together with the fields it records on the link. Under review it puts its verdict on the row; under Apply automatically it holds back what it refutes. Verification limit 50 (1–500) The most items the independent check examines in one change set.

docs.title: Desktop app
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Run commands on this machine Ask every time Do not run commands, Ask every time, Ask only for risky commands or Never ask. Set in the browser, it configures the desktop app the next time you open it. Allow non-standard ports Off Lets a direct page fetch in the desktop app use ports other than 80 and 443, while your own machine and private network stay closed. Greyed out with web search off or with the reader service chosen.

docs.title: Generation
docs.text: Temperature (0–2), Top-p (0–1), Maximum output tokens (up to 1,000,000) and Seed are all blank by default, which leaves the provider's own default. Temperature, maximum output tokens and seed set in the AI agent panel under Setup → Settings → Advanced take precedence on that browser.

docs.title: System prompt and Independent review prompt
docs.text: Each box shows the built-in text. Edit it and press Save to replace that prompt completely; Reset to default goes back to the built-in. The system prompt (up to 40,000 characters) is what the agent follows on your turns, with the open project's type catalog appended. The independent review prompt (up to 20,000 characters) is what the independent check and challenge_claim judge by.

docs.title: On this device
docs.text: Three rows, all This device only: API keys (entered in the AI agent panel under Setup → Settings), Self-hosted model address (where your own Ollama or compatible runtime lives) and Chat history (kept per project).

docs.title: Conversation compaction (token compression)
docs.text:
Long AI conversations are compressed automatically — there is no manual /compact command. When the conversation history would exceed the model's context window, Vineyard folds the oldest turns into a single dense summary so the agent keeps working on the whole project instead of forgetting its start.

How it works:

  1. Trigger. At the start of each turn, Vineyard estimates the size of the request and compacts once the instructions, tools and conversation together would fill the share of the model's context window set in Settings → AI agent → Compaction threshold (30–75%, default 70%) — before the window is full, because the turn's tool results and the model's answer need the rest. When Vineyard does not know the model's window, it assumes 64,000 tokens; set the real one under Setup → Settings → Advanced → Context window.
  2. What survives verbatim. The most recent 4 turns (two analyst exchanges) are always kept as-is, so immediate context is never summarized.
  3. What gets compressed. Everything older is sent to the LLM (the same model you configured, so the summary is written in the same language and register as the conversation) with instructions to produce a dense factual summary of at most 200 words: indicators and entities discussed (domains, IPs, accounts, hashes), what was established about each and on what evidence, decisions made, what was rejected and why, and open questions. No speculation is added.
  4. The replacement. The summary replaces the older turns only in the request sent to the model, as a single message prefixed [earlier conversation, summarized]. The conversation you see, the saved transcript and the export stay whole. Each compaction summarizes the original older turns, and the summary is reused while those turns are unchanged.
  5. Failure is silent-safe. If the summarization call fails, the history is left unchanged — compaction never silently drops the earlier half of an investigation. You would see the provider error instead.

docs.title: Collaborator presence
docs.text: When you share a project, participants see collaborator badges next to the project title, each with the collaborator's avatar and colour and what they currently have selected; click a badge to jump to it. Presence is sent only to project participants — people viewing through a public link see no roster or headcount. If you are signed in, opening a project through its public link puts your name, avatar and colour on the participants' roster, though you do not see theirs and your selection is not shared. The live roster is not stored, but each signed-in connection is recorded as a session (who, when it started and ended) so that edits in the audit log can be attributed to it.

docs.title: Next / See also
docs.text:
• Running plugins — how a run becomes a task.
  • Task lifecycle (internals) — the developer-facing mechanics behind these states.
  • Getting started — orientation for the rest of the guide.

docs.title: Working with Type Packs
docs.text: A Type Pack is a small JSON bundle that defines the kinds of entities your graph can hold — IP addresses, domains, malware families, threat actors, and so on. Installing one in a project makes those types available when you create nodes, and tells the canvas how each node should look.

docs.title: What a Type Pack gives you
docs.text:
A Type Pack declares entity (node) types. Edges carry no type: each edge has a free-text label, written by you when you draw it or by the plugin that found the link. Each entity type carries:

  • A label_property — the property whose value is shown as the node's name on the canvas. For an IP address that is the address itself; for a vulnerability it's the CVE id. Some types build the label from several properties instead (a label_template), and fall back to the label_property until all of them are filled.
  • A set of properties — the named fields you can fill in (e.g. country_code, asn, registrar). These appear in the Properties panel when a node is selected, each shown by the kind of value it holds (Reading values). When you edit one, the value is checked against what the type declares: its kind, its allowed values, and any pattern or range (for example, country_code must be two capital letters and asn a whole number from 1 to 4294967295). A value that fails is not saved, and a message says why. A node can also hold fields its type does not declare: plugins write them, and you can add your own (Adding and removing fields).
  • An icon and a color — the visuals that drive how the node renders on the canvas and in the Types and Properties panels.

docs.title: Installing a Type Pack
docs.text:
Install a Type Pack the same way you install anything else (see Browse & install). Once it is installed, its types show up in the Types panel and become selectable when you create a node. Until at least one Type Pack is installed, there are no entity types to choose from.

In the Types panel, types are grouped by category, not by pack, so one pack can fill several groups (the Infrastructure pack appears under both Infrastructure and Web), each with a count. Hover a type to see its description, its Category: and the Type pack: it comes from. Click a type to create a new node of that type (a placeholder labelled New <type>), which is selected right away so you can fill in its properties. A type whose nodes are hidden on the canvas is dimmed here; hide or show a type from the canvas legend or Filter (see Hiding nodes and edges). The Search types… box at the top filters the list by type name, category, description or pack name; a panel too narrow for it shows only the type icons. With no Type Pack installed, the panel says so and offers Browse the marketplace, except to a visitor reading a shared project without signing in.

The Types panel groups types by category; hovering one shows its description, category and type pack.

When you create a node, you pick a type from an installed Type Pack. Vineyard stores that choice as a qualified string in the form category.name — for example infrastructure.ip_address or threat.malware. Plugins reference the same form when they declare what they consume and produce.

docs.title: The reference packs
docs.text:
Vineyard ships several official Type Packs. Each is self-contained — install the ones your investigation needs — and they are designed to be used together: an edge can join nodes from different packs (a threat.malware that communicates with an infrastructure.ip_address, a cryptocurrency.crypto_address controlled by an identity.person, and so on).

Pack (identifier) Category Types Models Infrastructure (…typepacks.infrastructure) infrastructure, web 15 The network you map during recon, plus the web resource (URL), web-fingerprint (header, favicon, DOM hash) and tracking-ID entities observed on it Threat (…typepacks.threat) threat 10 Threat-intelligence (STIX-aligned) Identity (…typepacks.identity) identity 7 People, orgs, and online personas Financial (…typepacks.financial) financial 4 Exchanges and other virtual-asset service providers, bank accounts, and two legacy crypto types Cryptocurrency (…typepacks.cryptocurrency) cryptocurrency 4 Addresses, transactions, tokens and non-custodial services on every chain, identified by network Endpoint (…typepacks.endpoint) endpoint 6 Host / DFIR artifacts Geospatial (…typepacks.geo) geo 3 Places and physical context Social Media (…typepacks.social) social 5 Platform-agnostic accounts, posts, hashtags, groups, and media Telegram (…typepacks.telegram) telegram 4 Accounts, channels, supergroups, and posts, collected without joining

docs.title: Financial — bank accounts
docs.text:
An account number is unique only within its bank, so financial.bank_account is identified by bank_code and account_identifier together: the same number at two banks is two nodes, and the label names the bank (123456789012 · KB Kookmin). Write both without spaces or hyphens. A value such as 123-456-789012 is refused, and the message says what form to write. bank_code is the country's own bank code where it has one (Korea's three digits, such as 004, 088 or 090), otherwise the SWIFT/BIC, never the bank's name: KB or SHINHAN is refused. Leave it empty for an IBAN, which already names its bank.

The AI agent is told which fields identify a bank account and how to write the bank code. An account written without one still shares a node with any other account of the same number and no code, whichever bank holds it, so check that the agent's bank accounts carry a bank code when you review them.

The status of a reported account has its own fields:

Property What it records fraud_registration registered as a fraud-use account (in Korea, 사기이용계좌), not_registered when checked and not found, or released after a registration was lifted payment_suspended_at When payments from the account were suspended (in Korea, 지급정지) report_channels Where the account was reported, one per line (112, 1332, the holding bank…) status_checked_at, status_source When the status was last confirmed, and by whom

account_holder is the holder of record, who is often not the person who used the account. Record whoever operated it as an identity.person linked by an edge. The AI agent reads a bank account's properties like any other node's, so its number and holder name go to your AI provider when the agent reads the node. Leave account_holder empty when the case does not need the name.

Bank accounts created before Financial 2.0.0 have no bank code, so a new write of the same account becomes a separate node. Give an old node its bank code and remove any hyphens from its number, and later writes of that account land on it; a duplicate already written stays separate. The agent can still record the status of an old account whose number has hyphens: an edit is checked only on the values it changes.

docs.title: Infrastructure — a closer look
docs.text:
run.vineyard.typepacks.infrastructure models the network-side entities you map during reconnaissance, in the infrastructure category:

Type (category.name) Label shown Notable properties infrastructure.ip_address the IP address version, country_code, asn, reverse_dns infrastructure.domain the domain name registrar, created_date, name_servers infrastructure.host the hostname operating_system, open_ports, hosting_provider infrastructure.autonomous_system the ASN autonomous_system_name, registry infrastructure.netblock the CIDR network_name, asn infrastructure.dns_record name, type and value (e.g. www.example.com A 93.184.216.34); the record name until type and value are filled record_type, record_value, ttl infrastructure.whois_record the subject (domain/IP) registrant, registrar, created_at infrastructure.certificate the SHA-256 fingerprint fingerprint_sha1, subject_common_name, issuer, not_after infrastructure.ssh_host_key the SHA-256 of the key (hex) key_type infrastructure.technologies the technology name kind, vendor, version, cpe

The same pack also ships five types in a separate web category:

Type (category.name) Label shown Notable properties web.url the URL domain (the hostname as plain text; an edge links a domain node), http_status web.hhhash the HTTP header hash header_count, server_hint web.favicon_hash the Shodan-style MMH3 hash (signed decimal) mmh3_hex, md5, sha256, phash, dhash, favicon_url web.dom_hash the DOM structure hash tag_count web.tracking_id the identifier as the page carries it (e.g. G-SXM8TFRYSW); identity is provider + value provider, kind

web.favicon_hash holds one favicon in every form the search services index it under: hash_value for Shodan, FOFA, Censys and ZoomEye, mmh3_hex for Criminal IP, md5 for Censys, ZoomEye, 360 Quake, Hunter.how, ONYPHE and VirusTotal, sha256 for Censys, Netlas and urlscan.io, and the perceptual phash and dhash, which are compared by how many of their bits differ. The AI agent compares them with similar_hashes, and the Shared-Attribute Clustering pack links favicons whose phash or dhash differ in at most 10 of 64 bits (adjustable per run) with a similar favicon edge. A blank or single-colour icon hashes the same whatever its colour, and a symmetric logo's phash lies within a few bits of that value, so neither compares a hash at or near it; the favicon's other hash is still compared.

infrastructure.certificate is identified by its SHA-256. When the source reports the SHA-1 too (Shodan, Censys and VirusTotal do), it goes in fingerprint_sha1: blocklists such as abuse.ch SSLBL list certificates by SHA-1 alone, and a SHA-1 cannot be computed from the SHA-256. The abuse.ch pack's SSLBL Certificate Check reads it.

infrastructure.domain takes a name under an internationalised top-level domain, such as .한국 (xn--3e0b707e) or .рф (xn--p1ai), from Infrastructure 4.3.0. Write it in Unicode (사이트.한국) or in punycode (xn--vf4b27jhrk.xn--3e0b707e): the two spellings are one domain. From 4.3.1 the punycode prefix may be in capitals too (EXAMPLE.XN--P1AI), as the rest of the name always could. The AI agent's extract_indicators writes a name it reads in text in punycode. A project on an earlier version refuses these names until the pack is updated (Update on its card in the marketplace).

Each type ships its own icon and color.

docs.title: Endpoint — host artifacts
docs.text:
run.vineyard.typepacks.endpoint holds what an incident responder finds on a machine. The Host Artifacts plugin pack fills it from exports you already have: its Process Activity Import plugin reads Sysmon events 1, 3 and 22, or ECS process, network and DNS events, from files you pick in the Run plugins panel (JSON, JSON lines, CSV or Windows event XML, parsed on your device) and draws these links:

From → to Label Edge data endpoint.process → endpoint.process spawned none endpoint.process → endpoint.file executed from none endpoint.process → infrastructure.ip_address connected to, or accepted connection from when every connection was inbound source, events, direction, first_seen, last_seen, ports, port_count, protocols, remote_hostnames endpoint.process → infrastructure.domain queried source, events, first_seen, last_seen, answers, failed_events, statuses

A process is identified by its process GUID, image name and PID, so a record without a Sysmon ProcessGuid or an ECS process.entity_id is skipped: without it, the same name and PID on two hosts would become one node. The process type has no host field, so the plugin writes the computer name to an extra hostname field, which the Properties panel shows. All events between one process and one destination are one link, and its events counts connections or lookups rather than records: Elastic Defend logs a connection when it opens and again when it closes, and that is one event. A new link carries that summary from the first import. Importing a later export replaces it rather than adding to it, and a key the later export has no value for becomes empty. The review lists only the links whose summary changed, so importing the same export again stages nothing. A link that is already in the project keeps its label, including one you renamed, and only its summary is written: a spawned or executed from link you renamed is left as it is. A command line too long for one node (Linux allows megabytes of arguments) is cut, keeping its start, and the node says so in command_line_truncated and command_line_length. Loopback and link-local traffic never comes in, and private-network addresses and internal names only when you turn that on. A DNS query for a name under an internationalised top-level domain, such as update.example.xn--p1ai, is a queried link to its Domain. A project still on Infrastructure 4.2 does not take such a name: the summary counts it with the names no Domain type takes (… names this project's Domain type does not accept (Infrastructure 4.3 or later takes internationalised names)), and it is not a failed write.

Host data on a server

Host names, user names and command lines become node fields. In a project on a Vineyard server they are stored on that server. For a case whose host data must stay on your computer, use the desktop app in local mode (Signed in or local).

The other packs follow the same shape — for example the Threat pack adds threat.malware, threat.threat_actor, threat.indicator, and threat.operation (a bounded operation within a campaign — one campaign can contain several operations), while Identity adds the people and personas behind the activity.

docs.title: Cryptocurrency — a closer look
docs.text:
run.vineyard.typepacks.cryptocurrency covers every chain with one set of types, in the cryptocurrency category, and says which chain with network. The same string is a different account on another network — a 1… address on Bitcoin and on Bitcoin Cash, one 0x… address on Ethereum and on BSC — so network is part of the identity, and two such nodes never merge.

Type (category.name) Label shown Identity Notable properties cryptocurrency.crypto_address the address and its network network + address + memo address_kind, balance, first_funder, public_label, sanctioned cryptocurrency.crypto_transaction the hash and its network network + tx_hash block_height, block_time, status, fee cryptocurrency.crypto_token the symbol and its network network + contract_address standard, decimals, issuer cryptocurrency.crypto_service the name name service_type (mixer, bridge, gambling, merchant, defi)
  • Letter case. Hex, bech32, CashAddr and TON raw values match whatever their case, so an EIP-55 checksummed address and its lower-case form are one node, and a 64-hex hash matches with or without 0x. Base58 values (legacy Bitcoin, TRON, Solana, Monero, XRPL) are compared exactly.
  • evm and unknown are networks not established yet: a 0x… address whose chain the source did not give, and any other address whose network neither the source nor its format settles. They stay separate nodes: once the network is established, the evm or unknown node links to the node on that network with same address on.
  • Exchanges and anything else that holds customers' funds (OTC desks, custodial wallets, payment processors) are financial.exchange; crypto_service is for services that do not.
  • Amounts (balance, fee) are decimal strings in the network's native unit: full precision, but they do not sort as numbers.
  • The Financial pack's crypto_address and crypto_transaction remain for older nodes and are shown as "(legacy)". They do not merge with the new types. With both packs installed, the short name crypto_address means the Cryptocurrency pack's type.

Most network values have a CAIP-2 chain id, the form other tools exchange: some only as a draft or a proposal, and a few have none registered. The ids are not part of the identity, so a correction to one never splits a node.

network CAIP-2 bitcoin bip122:000000000019d6689c085ae165831e93 bitcoin_cash bip122:000000000000000000651ef99cb9fcbe bitcoin_sv bsv:mainnet (draft) bitcoin_gold none registered litecoin bip122:12a765e31ffd4059bada1e25190f6e98 dogecoin bip122:1a91e3dace36e2be3bf030a65679fe82 dash none registered zcash none registered monero monero:418015bb9ae982a1975da7d79277c270 (draft) verge none registered ethereum eip155:1 ethereum_classic eip155:61 bsc eip155:56 polygon eip155:137 arbitrum eip155:42161 optimism eip155:10 base eip155:8453 avalanche_c eip155:43114 evm none: the chain is not established tron tron:728126428 solana solana:5eykt4UsFv8P8NJdTREpY1vzqKqZKvdp xrpl xrpl:0 ton tvm:-239 cardano proposed: cardano:1-764824073 bnb_beacon cosmos:Binance-Chain-Tigris (draft) unknown none: the network is not established

Edges carry no type, so the Cryptocurrency pack fixes the labels and data keys that collectors use. A pair of nodes has one link: a collector adds its data keys to a link that is already there rather than relabelling it, and figures from different sources go under keys of their own.

From → to Label Data address → address sent to network; per source summary_<source> (asset, symbol, count, total, first, last, window_from, window_to, complete); recent, the latest 20 (tx_hash, asset, amount, time); first_funding; deployment address → address deployed deployment (tx_hash), when the pair has no link yet address → transaction input to amount, inputs (index, amount, prev_txid, prev_vout) transaction → address output to amount, outputs (index, amount) contract address → token token contract — address → exchange, service or organization attributed to per source attribution_<source> (label, label_kind: verified, prediction or public_tag, as_of) evm or unknown address → address same address on how the network was decided. For a contract it does not mean the same owner person or organization → address listed address list (e.g. OFAC SDN), uid, program (the entry's programmes), listed_as (the codes the list gives the address, e.g. USDT), as_of; listed, the value as the list wrote it, when it differs URL or domain → address accepts payment to where the payment address was found legacy financial.crypto_address, or a payment web.tracking_id → address same as why they are the same

sanctioned, sanctions_programs and sanctions_as_of are a screening's answer for the list dated sanctions_as_of: false means not on that list, not cleared. The Sanctions Screening plugin pack writes them from OFAC's SDN list, with sanctions_list naming the list, and draws the listed address links. It leaves an address alone that is already marked sanctioned from another list or by hand.

The Chain Explorer plugin pack fills these types without an account or a key. It reads an address's history and counterparties, a transaction's inputs and outputs, TRON and XRP Ledger first funders, contract deployers and tokens, explorer labels, and USDT and USDC freezes. Its Identify Crypto Network plugin decides the network of an evm or unknown address, a legacy Financial address or a payment tracking ID, and draws the same address on and same as links above. An address whose format several networks share is placed on each network where it has activity, once every one of those networks has answered: while an explorer is not answering, the address is left for the next run. An EVM address that has never sent a transaction and holds no coin or code stays undecided. The pack covers Bitcoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin, Dash, Zcash, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain (the last 30 days), OP Mainnet, Avalanche C-Chain, Ethereum Classic, TRON, Solana, the XRP Ledger and TON. History on Polygon, Arbitrum and Base needs a keyed pack.

The Blockchair plugin pack writes the transaction rows of the table above, input to and output to, and same address on, for Bitcoin and six chains built like it.

The Blockscout PRO plugin pack fills these types and links on Ethereum, OP Mainnet, Ethereum Classic and Arbitrum One with your own free key, and on Polygon PoS and Base with a paid Blockscout plan.

Solana through Helius. The Helius plugin pack needs a Helius API key, and its free plan covers history and first funder. A Solana wallet holds SPL tokens in token accounts it owns, so a plain Solana RPC history leaves out a USDC payment to it; this pack's history includes the transactions that change those token accounts. It writes sent to links with summary_helius and recent, the latest 20 transfers merged into the list a link already holds. SOL a wallet wraps into its own wSOL account is not counted as a payment. On the address it writes balance, last_seen, history_examined and history_complete, with first_seen only when the whole history was read. Its first-funder plugin writes first_funder, first_funding_tx and activated_at, and adds first_funding to the funder's sent to link. That key's source says how the funder was found: helius funded-by is Helius's own lookup, which needs a paid Helius plan (Developer or above); helius earliest SOL deposit is the SOL transfer in the transaction where the address's balance first rose from zero, the definition funded-by itself uses. A free key gets that method, and so does an address funded-by has no record of. An address first credited by a program rather than a transfer gets no funder. Helius's identity labels (public_label, helius_category, and attributed to an exchange, service or firm) need a paid plan too. Token transfers before December 2022 are not found through token accounts.

Mixing Type Packs

Install as many Type Packs as you need — they share one qualified-type namespace and interlink by design. You might link a threat.malware to the infrastructure.ip_address it beacons to, attribute a threat.campaign to an identity.organization, and trace a ransom cryptocurrency.crypto_transaction.

Identity & de-duplication

When a plugin or AI task adds a node, Vineyard de-duplicates by type + the type's identity fields — its identity_properties when it declares them (e.g. identity.account → username + platform; endpoint.file → SHA-256, file name, path, host; endpoint.process → process GUID, name, PID; financial.bank_account → bank code + account number), otherwise its label_property value. Two nodes with the same type and identity are merged and their properties combined. Fields the pack marks case-insensitive (domains, hostnames, emails, handles…) match regardless of case. A crypto address or transaction hash matches whatever the case of its hex or bech32 form, while a Base58 address is compared exactly and the network is part of its identity. From Infrastructure 4.3.0 a domain, host or DNS record name matches without its trailing dot and in its punycode form, an IP address in its standard form (IPv6 as RFC 5952 writes it), and a URL however its scheme, host, default port or percent-encoding is written; a URL path keeps its case. The node keeps the spelling it already has: a matching write in another spelling adds its other fields and leaves the identity as it was. The most useful label is therefore one that is both readable and identifying. Most types key on a naturally-unique field (an IP, a CVE id, a tx hash, a WHOIS subject). Where a type's label is inherently non-unique — a identity.person's name, an identity.organization's name — distinct entities sharing that label will merge, so give them a distinguishing label (e.g. John Smith (DOB 1990)). These two types are identified by the label alone, so filling another property, such as a date of birth or a registration number, does not keep them apart. Phone numbers are identified as written, so +82 10-1234-5678 and 010-1234-5678 are two identity.phone_number nodes; the Phone Numbers plugin pack writes the E.164 form they share as e164 (Identity 2.4.0 and later), with region and a line_type estimated from the number's range, and leaves the label as it is; nodes that share an e164 are found as duplicates (Identity 2.5.0 and later). Nodes you add manually are never auto-merged. Nodes that are one entity but are already two in the project are found and merged by the AI agent's find_duplicates and merge_nodes, through your review (see Duplicates and merging), or you merge them yourself (see Merging nodes).

docs.title: In the Properties panel
docs.text:
Selecting a node shows its fields in the Properties panel. Its Type Pack decides much of what the panel can say about them:

  • The fields the type declares are listed first, in the pack's order, and a required one is marked *. The fields the node holds that its type does not declare come after them, under Added fields.
  • Each declared field is edited the way its type calls for, as long as its value fits: a choice from the listed values, a switch for true or false, a date picker, a number field (Editing a value).
  • A value you change is checked against the declared type, allowed values, and pattern or range before it is saved (Saving and checks). Added fields are not checked.

When the node's Type Pack is not installed or did not load, the panel still shows every field the node holds, but marks none as required and checks no value.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: Type Packs use semantic versioning. A MAJOR-version bump signals a breaking change to the type definitions — a renamed or removed type, for example — which can mean updating the nodes that already use the old type. Minor and patch updates (new optional properties, visual tweaks) do not break existing nodes.
