docs.title: Investigation recipes
docs.text: Each recipe follows one investigation from what you start with to where it stops: the packs it needs, what you click or ask the AI agent at each step, what to look for in the result, and the mistakes that are easy to make on the way. The controls themselves are described on the other pages of this guide, and the recipes link to them instead of repeating them.

docs.title: From a phishing domain to its infrastructure
docs.text: One reported domain: its records and registration, the address it sits on, and which neighbours share an operator rather than only a provider. → Phishing domain to infrastructure

docs.title: Pivoting on an account or handle
docs.text: One handle and an e-mail address: the accounts that carry the name, and the evidence that ties two of them to one person or keeps them apart. → Account or handle

docs.title: Reading the review and evidence grades
docs.text: What a review shows before anything is applied, what a link's grade and its corroboration say afterwards, and how to ask again. → Review and evidence grades

docs.title: About the examples
docs.text:
Every name, address and result on these pages is made up for them:

  • domains under the reserved top-level domains .example and .test;
  • IP addresses from the documentation ranges 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24 and 2001:db8::/32, and AS numbers from the documentation range AS64496–AS64511;
  • handles, e-mail addresses, organisations and crypto addresses coined for these pages. The crypto addresses contain characters their network does not allow, so they belong to nobody.

None of them resolves, so a plugin run on them finds nothing: follow the steps on your own case.

docs.title: Before any recipe
docs.text:
• A project you can edit. Only the project owner installs packs (Browse & install); the type packs a plugin pack writes, and the plugin packs a skill pack requires, are installed with it.
  • For the steps that ask the AI agent: a provider, model and key in the AI agent panel under Setup → Settings (The AI agent panel).
  • While you learn, keep the agent's first chip on Review everything, or on Review everything (AI-assisted), the default, so that every change it proposes waits for you (Review and apply).
  • Nothing a plugin or the agent finds reaches the project until you apply it in a review. If you have not applied one before, start with Reading the review and evidence grades.

docs.text:

docs.title: Pivoting on an account or handle
docs.text: The phishing page from the previous recipe gives a Telegram contact, @vardelmoth_ops, and the kit's configuration file names an e-mail address, vardelmoth@quillpost.test. You want the other accounts of whoever uses them, and you want to know which of the accounts that carry the same name are someone else's. The names here are made up (About the examples).

docs.title: What you start with
docs.text:
• A handle, vardelmoth_ops, and where you saw it.
  • An e-mail address, vardelmoth@quillpost.test. A profile URL is as good a start (starter Start from a profile page).

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Work in the desktop app. Install from Project → Add from Marketplace…:

Pack What it adds Needs Account & identity pivoting (Skill Pack) The playbook the AI agent follows for this kind of question It requires WhatsMyName, which is installed with it WhatsMyName Whether a handle is registered on about 700 sites The desktop app GitHub Repositories, commit identities, GPG keys and activity hours of a GitHub account A GitHub token PGP Key Lookup Public keys whose user IDs name an address, from four key directories The desktop app Disposable Email Whether an address's domain is a throwaway-mail service No key Telegram The profile a Telegram username resolves to, read without joining A Vineyard account (signed in) X (Twitter) An X account's public profile and recent posts The desktop app

The type packs these plugins write (Identity, Infrastructure, Social Media, Telegram) are installed with them.

Account & identity pivoting is offered only where WhatsMyName can run, so it is missing from Run ▸ Skill packs in a browser. The sweep requests a profile page from each site, from your computer.

docs.title: 1. Put the handle and the address on the canvas
docs.text: In the Types panel, click Handle and, in the Properties panel, type vardelmoth_ops into handle, and where you saw it into first_seen_context. Click Email Address and type vardelmoth@quillpost.test into email.

docs.title: 2. Judge the crowd before you sweep
docs.text: Before anything runs, ask how many unrelated people could carry the same handle. A common word, a first name or a fandom reference is used by thousands, and an exact match on one of them groups nobody. vardelmoth_ops is unusual; shadow would not be. The starter Deep-dive one handle (step 7) has the agent make this estimate first and say what it rests on.

docs.title: 3. Sweep the handle
docs.text:
Select the Handle, press R, tick WhatsMyName Account Search and press Run. Review and apply.

Look for:

  • One Account node per site where the handle was found (username, platform, profile_url), linked same handle from the Handle. The summary counts the likely false positives it left out as blocked.
  • What these are: candidates. Their links are graded recorded, which says the tool recorded that an account of this name exists on that site, not that it belongs to the same person.

WhatsMyName also takes the Email Address: it sweeps the part before the @ and links a Handle to the address by uses handle.

docs.title: 4. Read the e-mail address
docs.text:
Select the Email Address and run Disposable Email Check and PGP Key Lookup.

Look for:

  • is_disposable on the address. A throwaway address was made for the occasion and leads nowhere further.
  • PGP Key nodes linked key bound to, with their user IDs. user_id_sources says, for each user ID, which directories served it and whether one of them verifies addresses. A key on a directory that does not verify can carry anyone's address.
  • The other addresses in the key's user IDs, each a new Email Address to read the same way.

docs.title: 5. Read each profile for its own pivots
docs.text:
Take the candidates one at a time:

  • A GitHub account: GitHub GPG Keys gives its keys and the addresses GitHub has verified on the account (registered email on this account (GitHub GPG key)). GitHub Account Repositories lists its repositories, and GitHub Commit Identities on a repository URL gives the names and addresses its commits were made with. GitHub Activity Timeline writes activity_hours_utc, the account's recent activity per hour of the day.
  • An X account: X Profile writes its bio, location, website and join date, and X Posts its recent posts.
  • The Telegram handle: Telegram Resolve on the Handle creates the Telegram user it currently resolves to, with its bio.

Look for what ties two accounts together: one profile's website or bio naming another account, the same PGP key fingerprint on both, the same verified address. A display name, an avatar style or the handle itself does not.

docs.title: 6. Decide each pair
docs.text:
Choose Run ▸ Skill packs, pick Account & identity pivoting, and choose the starter Are these the same person?. Fill First account and Second account, press Ask the agent to follow this, and send the prompt. Rule out a false match asks the opposite question, and Sort candidates by how well they hold up takes a whole list.

Look for, in the answer:

  • How many people share each attribute the pair has in common, and what that figure rests on.
  • Whether two shared attributes are independent or came from one act: a profile copied from another carries its bio, its avatar and its links all at once.
  • For a pair still open, the one check that would settle it. The playbook has the agent challenge a same-person claim before it stages a link for it, and never stage one on a shared handle alone.

docs.title: 7. Let the agent run the whole sweep (optional)
docs.text: The starter Deep-dive one handle (Handle or username, and What you already know (optional)) runs steps 2 to 6 as one investigation: it judges the crowd, sweeps, reads the profiles it found and sorts the candidates. Start from an email address does the same from the address. Its changes wait for your review turn by turn.

docs.title: 8. Record your own conclusion
docs.text:
When the evidence ties two accounts, draw the link yourself: select one, ⌘-click (Ctrl-click) the other, and name the link for the evidence, such as same PGP key fingerprint or bio links this account, not for the conclusion (Drawing edges). A link you draw is graded asserted and marked Edited here.

Keep two accounts on two platforms as two nodes. Merge nodes… is for one entity recorded twice, and it deletes the nodes it folds in (Merging nodes).

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
The pivot ends when a pass adds no account and settles no pair, or when the leads left need a check nothing installed can run. The starter Summarise what the project establishes (Who or what the summary is about) reports in five parts: what is corroborated as one owner and on what evidence, what is still a candidate and the check that would settle it, what was ruled out and why, what was run and came back empty, and what nothing installed can reach. What would settle the open questions? turns the open pairs into a list of checks.

When a lead turns into infrastructure, such as a personal domain or a mail server, go back to From a phishing domain to its infrastructure.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• A shared handle is not a shared person. Neither is a near-variant: vardel_moth is another string, not a match.
  • An account found by name can be anyone's. A squatter, a namesake or an account renamed since: read the profile before you count it.
  • Telegram usernames change hands. A username can be released and claimed by an unrelated account, so currently resolves to is who holds it now. No result from Telegram Phone Lookup is not evidence that a number has no account.
  • A commit address is what the committer typed. An address GitHub verified on the account, as in its GPG keys, is a stronger tie.
  • People are identified by name. Two identity.person nodes of the same name become one; give a person a label that tells them apart (Working with Type Packs).
  • Where the data goes. In a project on a Vineyard server, what you collect about people is stored on that server and seen by its collaborators, and the agent sends the nodes it reads to your AI provider. A case that must stay on your computer belongs in local mode, where the Telegram pack does not run (Signed in or local).

docs.title: From a phishing domain to its infrastructure
docs.text: A text message impersonating a parcel service, Kestrune Post, sends its recipients to hxxps://kestrune-redelivery[.]example/redeliver. You have that one URL. The question is what else the same operator runs, so that it can be blocked or taken down together, and what the domain only shares with thousands of unrelated sites. The names and addresses here are made up (About the examples).

docs.title: What you start with
docs.text:
• One domain, kestrune-redelivery.example, and the URL on it.
  • When the message was seen, if you know: here 2026-11-03.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Install these from Project → Add from Marketplace…:

Pack What it adds Needs Infrastructure pivoting (Skill Pack) The playbook the AI agent follows for this kind of question Nothing; it works with whatever collection plugins the project has Domain Recon DNS records, RDAP registration, Certificate Transparency subdomains No key IP Recon RDAP IP (netblock and organisation), Shodan InternetDB (ports, tags, names), IP Geolocation No key IP to ASN (Team Cymru - DoH Based) The autonomous system that announces an address No key CDN / WAF Detection (cdncheck) Whether an address or a name is a CDN or WAF front No key Shared-Attribute Clustering Links nodes already in the graph that share a registrar, a name server, an ASN, a certificate or a similar favicon No key; reads only the graph AlienVault OTX Passive DNS: the names an address served in the past, and when A free OTX API key Web Recon, Ad Tags The page's favicon, header and DOM hashes, and the tracking IDs in its markup The desktop app

The type packs these plugins write (Infrastructure, Threat and Geospatial, and for Ad Tags also Identity and Cryptocurrency) are installed with them.

Where the requests go: Domain Recon, IP to ASN and CDN / WAF Detection ask public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers (Cloudflare and Google); RDAP goes to rdap.org, Certificate Transparency to crt.sh, InternetDB to Shodan and Passive DNS to AlienVault. None of them contacts the phishing site. Web Recon and Ad Tags do: they request the page from your computer, so its server sees your address and the time. They come last here, for a case where that is acceptable.

docs.title: 1. Put the domain on the canvas
docs.text:
In the Types panel, click Domain. The new node is selected: in the Properties panel, type kestrune-redelivery.example into domain_name and press Enter. Write the value refanged; [.] and hxxps belong in a report, not in a node. To fingerprint the page later (step 7), add a URL node for https://kestrune-redelivery.example/redeliver the same way.

When the report holds many indicators, paste it into the AI agent panel and ask the agent to put them on the graph. It reads defanged spellings, and the nodes it finds wait for your review.

docs.title: 2. Resolve the domain
docs.text:
Right-click the domain and choose Run plugins… (or select it and press R). Tick DNS Lookup (A Record), DNS Lookup (AAAA Record), DNS Lookup (NS Record), DNS Lookup (MX Record), RDAP Domain and Certificate Transparency Subdomains, then press Run (6).

Each plugin is a run of its own: six rows appear in Tasks, and each reads needs review when it ends. Click a row, check what it staged and press Apply; the review recipe shows what to read on the way.

Look for:

  • RDAP Domain fills the domain's registrar, created_date, expiration_date, status and name_servers, and creates no node. A created_date a few days before the message was seen, here 2026-10-30, is what a domain registered for one campaign looks like.
  • The A and AAAA records become IP Address nodes linked resolves to: 203.0.113.47 and 2001:db8:4f2::47. The Properties panel badges them documentation; on a real case, a badge such as private or loopback in that place marks an address that is not on the internet.
  • The NS and MX records become DNS Record nodes linked has record, here ns1.dovrapark-dns.test and ns2.dovrapark-dns.test.
  • Certificate Transparency Subdomains adds the names certificates were issued for, up to 150, linked subdomain: track.kestrune-redelivery.example, pay.kestrune-redelivery.example.

docs.title: 3. Ask whose address it is
docs.text:
Select both addresses (click one, Shift-click the other) and open Run plugins…. Tick IP → ASN, RDAP IP, Shodan InternetDB and Detect CDN/WAF (IP), then Run (4).

Look for:

  • Detect CDN/WAF (IP) sets an address's organization to the provider when the address is in a known CDN or WAF range, such as cloudflare (WAF). The domain then sits behind a front, and every other name on that address is another customer of the same provider. Stop pivoting on the address; the Infrastructure pivoting starter Find the origin behind a CDN goes on from there.
  • IP → ASN creates the Autonomous System, linked announced by, and sets the address's asn. RDAP IP creates the Netblock, linked within netblock, and fills organization and country_code when they are empty. Here: 203.0.113.0/24, announced by AS64500, a small hosting company.
  • Shodan InternetDB creates a Host with the open ports (exposes), the CVEs it knows of (affected by), the names that point back at the address (resolves to, from the address), and writes shodan_tags such as cdn, cloud or self-signed.

docs.title: 4. Find the names the address served
docs.text:
Select 203.0.113.47 and run OTX Passive DNS. The first time, paste your OTX key into the plugin's Settings block in the Run plugins panel. It is kept on this device for your account, in a browser tab only until the tab closes (Running plugins).

Look for:

  • The Domain nodes that resolved to the address, each linked with the dates in its label: resolved to (2026-09-14 → 2026-11-02). The link also stores first_seen and last_seen.
  • Names built like the seed and seen in the same weeks: kestrune-parcel-fee.test, kestrune-customs.example. They are candidates. A shared address says only that both names were served from it at some time.
  • How many names there are. Dozens of unrelated names on one address, such as ombrisel-florist.example, mean shared hosting, which groups nobody.

OTX draws resolved to (…) from the seed domain too, where DNS Lookup already drew resolves to. One pair of nodes holds one link, so that row is an Update proposing the OTX wording in place of the current one. Untick it to keep resolves to.

docs.title: 5. Compare the candidates' registration
docs.text:
Select the candidate domains and run RDAP Domain on them. Then select them together with the seed and run Shared-Attribute Clustering, which is listed under Whole-graph / input via form and works on the selection (on the whole graph when nothing is selected).

Look for:

  • One link between two domains, naming every value they share, such as shared registrar: …; shared nameserver: ns1.dovrapark-dns.test, ns2.dovrapark-dns.test. Up to four values of each attribute are named, then and N more. The plugin uses only what the nodes already hold and sends no request.
  • Run it again after the graph has grown, and a link it drew is relabelled in place when what the two domains share has changed. A link between them that you or another plugin drew is left as it is, and the summary counts those pairs (already linked under another label, left as they are).
  • What the shared values are. Read every value the label names, not the first one: the registrar comes first, and it is often the weakest. One small DNS host's name server, shared by three brand-like domains registered in the same week, narrows the field. A mainstream registrar or a large DNS provider's name servers group nobody. The plugin skips a value that more than 30 of the nodes it compares share, and leaves it out of the label, but a value that is rare among them can still be common on the internet.
  • The links' grade. They join nodes that were already in the graph and state a shared value, not an observation, so they are applied as unassessed and drawn dotted, also when one domain lists more name servers than the other. That is the honest reading of them.

docs.title: 6. Ask the agent to weigh it
docs.text:
Choose Run ▸ Skill packs and pick Infrastructure pivoting. Under the starters, choose Related, or just shared hosting?, fill First indicator (kestrune-redelivery.example) and Second indicator (kestrune-parcel-fee.test), and press Ask the agent to follow this. The prompt is placed in the message box of a new conversation: read it and send it.

Other starters fit other moments: Expand one indicator from the start, Find the origin behind a CDN after step 3, Strip out shared-hosting noise on a graph that has grown, and Fingerprint a URL and What did it look like before? in the desktop app.

Look for, in the answer:

  • An estimate rather than a bare verdict: how many unrelated parties share each attribute, what that figure rests on, and the check that would settle the question.
  • Its changes, waiting for review as change sets. Each link it stages is labelled for what was observed (resolves to, shares certificate), not for a conclusion such as "same operator".
  • The hops it could not take. A hop that needs a plugin the project does not have is named, not filled in from memory.

docs.title: 7. Fingerprint the page (desktop app, optional)
docs.text:
This step requests the page from your computer. Select the URL node and run Favicon Hash, HTTP Header Hash (HHHash), DOM Structure Hash and Ad Tag Extract.

Look for:

  • A Tracking ID that another site in the project carries too. Both sites link to the same Tracking ID node by carries tracking ID, a strong lead and still a candidate: a cloned kit keeps the analytics ID of the site it was cloned from.
  • Favicon hashes. The URL node is still selected, and Shared-Attribute Clustering compares only the selected nodes, so first clear the selection (Esc, or a click on empty canvas) to compare every favicon in the project, or select the Favicon Hash nodes. Then run Shared-Attribute Clustering again, and favicons whose perceptual hashes differ in at most 10 of 64 bits are linked similar favicon: …. A blank or single-colour icon is not compared.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
A branch stops when the next hop would reach only background values (a CDN front, shared hosting, a mainstream registrar), when it reaches someone who can act (the registrar RDAP names, the organisation behind the netblock), or when no installed plugin can take it. Ask for the summary with the starter Summarise the footprint (Starting indicator): it walks the chain hop by hop with the evidence for each, names the branches that stopped and why, and lists what was run and came back empty.

For a briefing, View ▸ Saved views keeps the arrangement (Saved views), a node's Document view has Copy as Markdown (Document and JSON views), and Edit ▸ Copy labels, defanged copies the selected indicators for a ticket.

When a page or a registration record names a person, an e-mail address or a handle, go on with Pivoting on an account or handle.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• A front is not the operator. The addresses of a domain behind a CDN belong to the CDN, and so do the names that share them.
  • Shared is not related. A registrar, a name server or an ASN that thousands use links nobody. Shared-Attribute Clustering's limit of 30 counts the nodes it compares, not the internet.
  • Passive DNS is history. A name that resolved to the address two years ago does not share it now; read the dates in the label.
  • Certificate logs list names, not live hosts. A subdomain from crt.sh had a certificate issued for it once.
  • "No changes" can mean "could not check". A run whose hosts did not answer ends with a yellow toast that names them (Progress and cancellation).
  • Several plugins, several reviews. A link in one run to a node another run has not created yet waits until that review is applied, and the footer of the review says so.
  • Some steps touch the site. Web Recon and Ad Tags fetch the page from your computer. To keep the agent off a host altogether, such as the impersonated brand's own kestrunepost.example, add it in the AI agent panel under Setup → Session scope → Hosts nothing may collect from.

docs.title: Reading the review and evidence grades
docs.text: Whatever a plugin, the AI agent, a merge or a re-verification proposes waits in a review before it reaches the project, and every link it applies carries an evidence grade. This recipe takes one plugin run through its review, then reads the grades of the links it drew, and asks again with Re-verify. The example continues From a phishing domain to its infrastructure; its names and addresses are made up (About the examples).

docs.title: What you start with
docs.text:
A change set waiting for review. It shows as one of these:

  • a needs review badge (or N to review) on a row in Tasks, after a toast such as Certificate Transparency Subdomains: 14 change(s) staged — review to apply;
  • in an AI agent conversation, the line N change(s) across M change sets need review above the message box, with Review;
  • a Merge or a Re-verification row in Tasks.

docs.title: 1. Open the review
docs.text: Click the Tasks row, or Review in the AI agent panel. The dialog's title names the run, such as Review: Certificate Transparency Subdomains. Nothing is written while it is open: the canvas previews the changes, and what they would change or delete is drawn even when your canvas filter hides it (Hiding nodes and edges).

docs.title: 2. Read the list
docs.text:
• The tabs All, Add, Update and Delete count the rows of each kind, and the line beside them how many of the rows shown are ticked (12 of 14 selected).
  • Each row has Op (Add, Update or Delete), Kind (node or edge), Label and Type. When the independent check ran, a Check column gives its verdict; after an apply, Status says what happened to the row.
  • Filter by keyword (label, type, data…), or /, searches what the rows hold, not only their labels: cloudflare finds every row whose data names it, so that you can untick those.
  • A row you untick is left out of the apply. Unticking a node leaves out the links that need it too, and the footer counts them (N edges excluded — their endpoint nodes are not being created).

Look for Update rows on links. An Update on a link means the pair already has one. When the new writer used other words, the row proposes its wording in place of the current one: in the step 4 run of the phishing recipe, OTX's resolved to (2026-09-14 → 2026-11-02) over DNS Lookup's resolves to. Untick the row to keep the wording you have. An Update that keeps the wording adds what the new writer stored with the link, and when the new writer is another collector drawing the same link in the same words, it adds that writer to corroborated_by (step 6).

docs.title: 3. Read the focused row
docs.text:
Click a row, or move with ↑ and ↓. The pane on the right shows what the row will write:

  • A node: its fields as they will be once the row is applied, an Update's proposed values merged over the stored ones. This node is already in the project means a node of the same identity has reached the project since this run was staged, for example through a review you applied in the meantime: applying adds these fields to it, and the values shown are what it will hold.
  • A link: from, relation and to, and under Recorded with this link what the writer stored with it, such as the first_seen and last_seen OTX keeps. For an Update that rewords a link, the pane shows current_relation, who wrote it (current_relation_written_by) and proposed_relation. Edited here there means the words about to be replaced are yours.

docs.title: 4. Read the check, when it ran
docs.text:
The independent check runs on the AI agent's change sets while Have an independent check test each inference is on, and on every re-verification. Its verdict is in the Check column:

Verdict Reads as If you apply the link supported The check argued against it and it held assessed weak, unresolved Consistent, but thin circumstantial refuted The check argued it down contested: it stays because you kept it not checked, check failed Nothing judged the row The grade it would have had without the check dropped The agent withdrew the change —

The Independent check pane under the list gives, for the focused row, the Claim, the Case against, Prevalence (how common the attribute the claim rests on is) and what it Would be settled by. Drag its top edge to make it taller. Under Review everything (AI-assisted), the default, the rows the agent advises against arrive unticked.

docs.title: 5. Apply, or say why not
docs.text:
Press Apply (N) (⌘Enter, or Ctrl+Enter). The footer counts the rows as they land and ends with Done N/N. A row that could not be written stays staged with its reason, and the run is still waiting for review: reopen it to try again. Discard all throws away what is still staged. When the change set came from an AI agent conversation, Why reject? (optional — the agent is told) gives the agent your reason, so that it does not propose the same thing again.

Closing the dialog with × or Esc keeps the run, what you ticked and what you typed; reopen it from Tasks. Once a run is applied or discarded, its row opens a read-only record (History — N applied, M skipped, K failed) with a Status for every row.

docs.title: 6. Read a link's grade
docs.text:
Click one of the links the run drew. The Properties panel shows (A link):

  • its two ends, from → to, and who wrote its label: Written by run.vineyard.plugins.crtsh_subdomains;
  • Evidence: the grade, who set it (Graded by the same plugin), and one line on what the grade says;
  • under Recorded with this link, what the writer stored, and corroborated_by, the other writers that drew the same link.

How a link gets its grade when it is applied, without any model:

The link Its grade A plugin's link between the node you ran it on and a node the run found: DNS Lookup's resolves to, Certificate Transparency's subdomain, IP to ASN's link from an address to its AS recorded A link where one end's own fields name the other in a field of its own, such as an account whose profile_url holds the URL the link points at, or a bio that quotes the other account's address recorded The same link in the same words, drawn by a second collector: OTX Passive DNS's subdomain where crt.sh already drew one recorded, and OTX's plugin is added to corroborated_by. The same plugin running again adds nothing, and nor does the AI agent agreeing. A plugin's link between two nodes already in the graph, stating a shared value: Shared-Attribute Clustering's shared registrar: …; shared nameserver: … unassessed An AI agent's link that nothing checked and whose ends do not name each other unassessed An AI agent's link that the check judged From its verdict (step 4) A link you draw yourself asserted

A value both ends hold in the same field is a shared attribute, not one end naming the other, also when one end's value is longer or contains the other's: one domain listing ns1 and ns2 against one listing only ns1, Ostrel Hosting against Ostrel Hosting Ltd, an RDAP status that adds add period to the other's, a handle against the same handle with a suffix. A link that rests on such a value is not recorded. With no check it is unassessed and drawn dotted, and the AI agent's link of that shape is an inference that the independent check, when it is on, judges.

recorded says a tool recorded the link, not that anyone verified it. A grade records what was known when the link was written: it does not change by itself as the graph grows, only when the link is written again with new evidence, by a person, or by a re-verification you apply. All six grades are in Evidence grades.

docs.title: 7. Read the canvas by grade
docs.text:
Each grade has its own line on the canvas: assessed a plain line, asserted long dashes, recorded shorter dashes, circumstantial short dashes, unassessed dots, and contested a heavier amber line. The legend's Evidence key lists the grades in the project with a count; click one to hide its links (Legend), or untick it under Filter → Evidence.

To see what a conclusion rests on, ask the AI agent, for example: Which links does the connection between kestrune-redelivery.example and kestrune-parcel-fee.test rest on, weakest first? The agent reads each link's grade, who gave it, who wrote its label and who corroborated it, and is told that a conclusion is as strong as its weakest link. Infrastructure pivoting's starter Check a link the project already draws audits one link against its evidence.

docs.title: 8. Ask again with Re-verify
docs.text:
Click a link and press Re-verify in its Properties panel (Re-verify). It needs the model key set in the AI agent panel, and it writes nothing: the verdict arrives as a change set named Re-verification, opens in the Review dialog and keeps a row in Tasks. Its one row is an Update of the link. The pane shows relation, relation_written_by and re_verified, such as supported — still valid, and the Check column and the Independent check pane give the reasoning.

Applying it sets the grade: still valid assessed, inconclusive circumstantial, stale contested. A re-verification that could not run never lowers the grade, and none proposes deleting the link. The arrow beside the button holds Re-collect with the agent, which opens a new conversation with a request to collect fresh evidence for the link, filled in and not sent.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text: The review ends when every row is applied or left out on purpose. The reading ends when you can say, for each link a conclusion rests on, how far its evidence goes and what would raise it. For a report, a node's Document view lists its links grouped by label with how many carry each grade, and Copy as Markdown copies the page (Document and JSON views).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• recorded is not verified. A DNS answer recorded today says nothing about who controls the domain.
  • asserted is a judgement, not a measurement. It says that a person vouched for the link, and nothing about whether anything checked it.
  • No grade is a gate. Nothing stops you from editing, deleting or building on a link, whatever its grade, and a contested link stays until a person removes it.
  • Inconclusive is not false. A dead page or one failed lookup is not staleness, and the check is told so.
  • "No changes" can mean "could not check". A run whose hosts did not answer ends with a yellow toast that names them.
  • A partly applied run stays applied. Discard all after a partial apply throws away only what is still staged; the run is recorded as applied.
  • Label and grade are separate. Rewording a link does not change who graded it, and grading it does not make the words yours.

  • Running plugins — the Review dialog in full
  • Tasks & runs — the apply mode and the independent check

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: The normative reference for VINEYARD's plugin and Type Pack formats: the JSON-Schemas that define each document (registry CI validates registry entries against theirs, but neither registry CI nor the app validates a pack document against its schema), the permission scope vocabulary, and the shared terminology used across the docs. Use these pages when you need exact field names, allowed values, and constraints rather than narrative guidance.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page What it documents Plugin manifest schema The vineyard:plugin manifest — identifier, version, platforms, io, scopes, lifecycle. Type Pack schema The vineyard:typepack document — type definitions in the qualified category.name form (e.g. infrastructure.ip_address). Registry entry schemas One row of community-pluginpacks.json / community-typepacks.json / community-skillpacks.json — the metadata-only catalog rows the browser reads. Scopes The complete permission vocabulary: the graph verbs (node:read, edge:delete, …), network, network_configurable, web_probe, services, and config.

docs.title: Where the canonical artifacts live
docs.text:
The authoritative JSON-Schemas are not duplicated here — they live in the registry repository (Vineyard-Intelligence/registry) under schemas/:

File Schema for schemas/plugin.schema.json A vineyard:plugin manifest. schemas/pluginpack.schema.json A vineyard:pluginpack manifest — the schema itself is the reference. schemas/typepack.schema.json A vineyard:typepack document. schemas/registry-plugin-entry.schema.json One community-pluginpacks.json row. schemas/registry-typepack-entry.schema.json One community-typepacks.json row. schemas/registry-skillpack-entry.schema.json One community-skillpacks.json row — the schema itself is the reference.

The reference pages summarize and explain these files; when the prose and the schema disagree, the schema in the registry's schemas/ wins. There is no schema for a Skill Pack document; its contract is described in Skill Packs.

docs.title: The Marketplace catalog the browser reads
docs.text: The static Marketplace browser loads its catalog live from https://registry.vineyard.run/registry/ — one metadata-only array per kind: community-pluginpacks.json, community-typepacks.json, community-skillpacks.json. These hold only listing metadata (identifier, name, version, repo, ref, scopes_summary, and similar); they never contain plugin bytes. Plugin Pack, Type Pack, and Skill Pack content is fetched from the author's GitHub repo through jsDelivr, pinned to the entry's commit, each time a project opens (and a plugin's code each time it runs), not from the registry.

docs.title: Naming, at a glance
docs.text:
• Identifiers are reverse-DNS under the author's own namespace: <your-namespace>.plugins.<name>, <your-namespace>.pluginpacks.<name>, <your-namespace>.typepacks.<name>, and <your-namespace>.skillpacks.<name> (first-party packs use run.vineyard).
  • Every document carries a content_type discriminator: vineyard:plugin, vineyard:pluginpack, vineyard:typepack, or vineyard:skillpack.
  • version is a SemVer string everywhere.
  • Types are referenced in qualified category.name form (e.g. infrastructure.ip_address).

docs.title: Next / See also
docs.text:

  • Build something: Plugin manifest · Type Packs
  • Real examples: Marketplace

docs.title: Plugin manifest schema
docs.text:
The authoritative, field-by-field reference for plugin.schema.json — the JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) that defines the vineyard:plugin manifest format. It is the format contract, not a gate: neither registry CI nor the app validates pack documents against plugin.schema.json or pluginpack.schema.json. For the prose walkthrough and authoring guidance, see the manifest guide.

Schema identity

  • $schema: https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema
  • $id: https://vineyard.run/schemas/plugin.json
  • title: VINEYARD Plugin Manifest
  • Root: type: object, additionalProperties: false — the schema allows no unknown top-level keys.

The manifest is the single source of truth for a plugin; there is no separate server-side plugin record.

docs.title: Top-level properties
docs.text:
additionalProperties: false. Required: identifier, content_type, name, version, description, platforms, io, scopes, lifecycle.

Property Type Req. Allowed / constraints Default Meaning identifier string yes pattern ^(?:[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*\.){2,}plugins\.[a-z0-9_]+$ — Reverse-DNS unique id, e.g. run.vineyard.plugins.rdap_ip. content_type string yes const: vineyard:plugin — Document discriminator; must be exactly this value. name string yes minLength 1, maxLength 128 — Human-readable display name. version string yes pattern ^\d+\.\d+\.\d+(?:[-+].+)?$ — SemVer string, e.g. 1.0.0, 2.1.0-beta.1. description string yes minLength 1, maxLength 1024 — One-paragraph summary. author object no see author — Authorship metadata. license string no — — SPDX license id, e.g. MIT. icon string no — — Icon (lucide name) shown next to the plugin in the Marketplace pack detail. thumbnail_url string no maxLength 512; repo-relative path, no leading slash or ./.. — Card thumbnail, e.g. assets/thumbnail.png. Resolved only at the pinned commit: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/{repo}@{ref}/{path}, falling back to https://raw.githubusercontent.com/{repo}/{ref}/{path}. Absolute URLs are rejected. 1:1 PNG/WebP, 256×256 recommended, ≤256KB, shown at 40–56px. marketing_url string no format: uri — Landing / marketing page URL. Accepted but not read by the app. latest_url string no format: uri — Designed as a per-author pointer to the newest manifest. Accepted but not read: the update check compares the registry catalog's version (see Updates). platforms object yes see platforms — Per-platform execution flags. io object yes see io — Consumed/produced Type Pack entity types. params object no see params — JSON-Schema for the pre-run form. scopes object yes see scopes — The plugin's authority surface. lifecycle object yes see lifecycle — Task execution model.

docs.title: author
docs.text:
type: object, additionalProperties: false. All properties optional.

Property Type Req. Constraints Meaning name string no — Author or organization name. url string no format: uri Author homepage. contact string no — Contact handle, email, or URL.

docs.title: platforms
docs.text:
Per-platform execution flags. type: object, additionalProperties: false, minProperties: 1 — at least one property, and primary counts, so { "primary": "web" } alone satisfies the schema. The host needs a web block (see the warning below). primary is preferred.

Property Type Req. Allowed values Default Meaning primary string no web, desktop — Platform contract. desktop makes the plugin desktop-only: the web build lists it greyed out ("Desktop only — …") and will not run it. web or absent runs everywhere. web object no see platforms.web — Web execution block. desktop object no see platforms.desktop — Desktop execution block.

What actually ships today

Plugins execute from platforms.web (runtime: "sandbox-js", entry) in both the browser and the desktop Electron shell. A plugin without one is not runnable (a pack member without its own entry inherits the pack's). The host does not read platforms.desktop (runtime, entry, fallback) or platforms.web.fallback, and the web-proxy runtime and native/subprocess desktop runtimes are valid in the schema as forward-looking design but are deferred — not built yet. Treat those fields as reserved, not as shipped behavior.

docs.title: platforms.web
docs.text:
type: object, additionalProperties: false. Required: runtime, entry.

Property Type Req. Allowed values Default Meaning runtime string yes sandbox-js, web-proxy — sandbox-js = author JS in the browser worker; web-proxy = thin client calling ONE author endpoint (deferred). entry string yes repo-relative path: /-separated segments of ASCII letters, digits, ., _ and -, none of them . or .. (so no URL, leading slash, backslash or %) — The module the plugin worker imports: a path inside the repository at the pinned commit, relative to the repo root, e.g. dist/pack.mjs. Not a URL: the app does not load a published pack whose entry does not resolve to such a path inside the pinned commit. Registry CI refuses inline, which names no module. proxy_endpoint string conditional format: uri — Required when runtime: web-proxy. The single endpoint; MUST equal the one scopes.network entry. fallback string no desktop, none none Where to fall back if web cannot run the plugin.

docs.title: platforms.desktop
docs.text:
type: object, additionalProperties: false. Required: runtime, entry. (Deferred — see warning above.)

Property Type Req. Allowed values Default Meaning runtime string yes sandbox-js, native, subprocess — Desktop execution mode. entry string yes repo-relative path, as platforms.web.entry — Entry path within the bundle. fallback string no web, none none Where to fall back if desktop cannot run the plugin.

docs.title: io
docs.text:
Entity types the plugin references from Type Packs. type: object, additionalProperties: false. Required: consumes, produces. An empty consumes array means a whole-graph plugin (global launch rather than a per-node right-click action).

Property Type Req. Items Meaning consumes array yes typeRef Node types the plugin reads as input. produces array yes typeRef Node types the plugin emits.

docs.title: typeRef (io.consumes / io.produces items)
docs.text:
$defs.typeRef. type: object, additionalProperties: false. Required: typepack, category, name. At runtime, Node.type = "<category>.<name>" (e.g. infrastructure.ip_address).

Property Type Req. Constraints Meaning typepack string yes pattern ^(?:[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*\.){2,}typepacks\.[a-z0-9]+(?:[._-][a-z0-9]+)*$ The owning Type Pack identifier. category string yes — Type category, e.g. infrastructure. name string yes — Type name within the category, e.g. ip_address. as string no — Designed as a binding alias to pre-bind the consumed node's value into params under this key. Accepted by the schema; no shipped plugin declares it and the run form does not read it yet.

Open issue

typeRef does not yet carry a Type Pack version — type compatibility is resolved by identifier + qualified name only.

docs.title: params
docs.text:
JSON-Schema (draft 2020-12) describing the pre-run form. The submitted object is passed to run as ctx.params (and kept on the run's task row). type: object. Note this object is not additionalProperties: false — it is itself a JSON Schema and may carry any standard schema keywords; only the three keys below are explicitly modeled.

Property Type Req. Constraints Meaning type string no const: object The params form is always an object schema. properties object no — Per-field JSON Schema definitions. required array no items: string Names of required fields.

No secrets in params

params MUST NOT contain secrets. Use a scopes.config entry with secret: true for API keys and credentials instead.

docs.title: File fields
docs.text:
A field declared "format": "file" renders as a drop zone — drag files onto it, or click to browse. Declaring it "type": "array" makes it multi-select; anything else takes a single file, and dropping two on it is refused rather than silently truncated. A dropped folder is expanded recursively.

Property Type Req. Meaning format string yes file. Without it the field is an ordinary input. type string no array for many files; omit (or use any other type) for one. accept string no MIME filter, e.g. image/*. Unlike a bare file input's accept, this also rejects non-matching files during the drag. No filter when omitted.

The value your run(ctx) receives is the File object itself (or an array of them) — not a data: URL, not a path. Read it with await file.arrayBuffer(), and take the file name from file.name. There is no companion "file name" field.

"params": {
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "images": { "type": "array", "format": "file", "accept": "image/*",
                "title": "Image files",
                "description": "One or more JPEG photos, read locally (never uploaded)." }
  },
  "required": ["images"]
}

One run, one batch

A multi-file field hands the whole selection to a single run — the host does not fan out one run per file. Loop over them yourself and report progress with ctx.progress.set({ percent }); check ctx.signal.aborted each iteration so Stop works.

The host caps a pick at 25 MB per file, 250 MB per run, and 50 files. Files cross into the sandbox as blob handles, so the memory cost is whatever your plugin materialises — read one file at a time rather than Promise.all-ing the batch.

docs.title: scopes
docs.text:
The plugin's authority surface. type: object, additionalProperties: false. ctx members are absent unless granted, and graph writes are held for the analyst's review before they are applied. See the scopes reference for verb semantics.

Property Type Req. Items / constraints Meaning graph array no uniqueItems; enum items (below) Fine-grained node/edge verbs. Backed by the project graph_edit tier. web_probe object no { purpose?: string } — an object, not an array Desktop only. One anonymous request to an arbitrary public host. Backs ctx.net.probe, which is absent in the web build. network array no items: networkScope External XHR targets. network_configurable array no items: configurableNetworkScope Endpoints whose address the analyst sets in a url setting, for a self-hosted MISP, OpenCTI or other TIP. See the scopes reference. services array no uniqueItems; enum: rdap, telegram Vineyard-operated services called by name through ctx.service — never by URL. See the scopes reference. config array no items: configValue Install-time values injected at runtime only.

scopes.graph enum values (each may appear at most once):

Value Meaning node:read Read nodes. node:create Create nodes. node:update Update node fields. node:delete Delete nodes. edge:read Read edges. edge:create Create edges. edge:update Update edge fields. edge:delete Delete edges.

Network fan-out rule

For a web-proxy plugin, scopes.network must contain exactly one entry, equal to platforms.web.proxy_endpoint (no fan-out). A sandbox-js plugin's entries are checked instead against the host's egress allowlist — see security. A sandbox-js plugin may declare several entries, in the browser and in the desktop app alike.

docs.title: networkScope (scopes.network items)
docs.text:
$defs.networkScope. type: object, additionalProperties: false. Required: endpoint, methods.

Property Type Req. Constraints Meaning endpoint string yes format: uri Exact origin/path prefix; no cross-host wildcards. methods array yes uniqueItems; items enum: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE Allowed HTTP methods. An empty list allows every method: the schema sets no minItems, and the host treats an empty list as no restriction. purpose string no — Human-readable reason, shown at install time.

docs.title: Sending a credential
docs.text:
ctx.net.fetch passes your request headers through unchanged, including Authorization. If your endpoint needs a key, put it there:

await ctx.net.fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${ctx.config.api_key}` } });

A request that carries a header or a body does not follow a redirect: a 3xx answer rejects the call with an error that begins redirect not followed, and the plugin does not see the 3xx response. So a key in Authorization or in a custom header (X-Api-Key, api-key, …) only reaches the endpoint you declared. A request with neither header nor body still follows redirects. Avoid a key in the query string, because it ends up in logs.

Cookie cannot be set, and no cookies are sent with plugin requests.

docs.title: configurableNetworkScope (scopes.network_configurable items)
docs.text:
$defs.configurableNetworkScope. type: object, additionalProperties: false. Required: config_key, methods.

Property Type Req. Constraints Meaning config_key string yes pattern ^[a-z0-9_]+$ A scopes.config key of type: url in the same plugin. The analyst's value for it is the endpoint: scheme, host and optional path, with no user name, password, query or fragment. Registry CI refuses an entry whose key is not such a setting. methods array yes uniqueItems; items enum: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE Allowed HTTP methods, as for networkScope. Registry CI refuses any other spelling, such as post. purpose string no — Human-readable reason, shown at install time. schemes array no uniqueItems, minItems: 1; items enum: https, http; default ["https"] Schemes the address may use. List http only for a server that cannot serve TLS; the install screen then says the traffic may be unencrypted. An http address works in the desktop app; the web app uses one only on localhost, because the browser blocks it from the https page.

docs.title: configValue (scopes.config items)
docs.text:
$defs.configValue. type: object, additionalProperties: false. Required: key, type. Config values are entered by the analyst in the plugin's Settings section of the Run plugins dialog, or under Settings → Keys & Secrets, and read by the declaring plugin as ctx.config. Members of the same pack that declare a key and call the same set of network origins (scheme, host and port of their scopes.network endpoints, plus one destination per network_configurable setting) share one value, entered once; a plugin published on its own, or one with no scopes.network or network_configurable entry, keeps its own. Each plugin still receives only the keys its own manifest declares — see scopes → config. Values are kept per signed-in account — in the OS keychain on desktop (only until the app quits on a computer that cannot encrypt them), for the tab session in the browser. secret: true masks the field. Values are never recorded in a task or conversation.

Property Type Req. Allowed values Default Meaning key string yes pattern ^[a-z0-9_]+$ — Stable config key. label string no — — Field label in the Run plugins Settings section and in Settings → Keys & Secrets. type string yes string, number, boolean, url, enum — Value type. enum array no items: string — Allowed choices when type: enum. secret boolean no — false BYOK-style secret: masked field. Never written to any record. scope string no plugin, project, user user Where the value is stored/shared. Accepted but not read; values are stored and shared by the pack and network-origin rule above. optional boolean no — false Whether the user may leave it blank. Not enforced: a non-optional field is only marked "required by this plugin", and the run proceeds without it.

docs.title: lifecycle
docs.text:
Task execution model. type: object, additionalProperties: false. All properties optional with defaults.

Property Type Req. Allowed values Default Meaning long_running boolean no — false Designed to have the runtime manage the task continuously (status/pause/resume/cancel/retry/progress). Accepted but not read. controls array no uniqueItems; enum: pause, resume, cancel, retry, progress — Controls exposed to the user. progress string no none, determinate, indeterminate none Progress reporting style. persistence string no ephemeral, opt-in, always ephemeral ephemeral = no Task DB row, in-memory only. states array no enum: queued, running, waiting, paused, cancelled, succeeded, failed all 7 states Canonical 7-state machine.

What the host actually reads

long_running, controls, progress, persistence, and states are accepted here but not read by the host today — the Tasks panel's only control is Stop, and a task's real terminal states are succeeded / failed / cancelled (plus incomplete for AI turns). See Lifecycle.

The host does read lifecycle.timeout_ms, a wall-clock budget per run (default 10 minutes, capped at 60). Past it, the sandbox is terminated and the task fails. It is not in plugin.schema.json yet; since nothing validates manifests against the schema, a manifest can declare it. See Lifecycle.

docs.title: Complete annotated example
docs.text:
A real, shipped plugin manifest — RDAP IP, a member of the IP Recon pack. It consumes an infrastructure.ip_address node and adds the owning infrastructure.netblock.

ip-recon.manifest.json (rdap_ip member)
{
  "identifier": "run.vineyard.plugins.rdap_ip", // (1)!
  "content_type": "vineyard:plugin",            // (2)!
  "name": "RDAP IP",
  "version": "1.1.1",                           // (3)!
  "description": "Looks up each selected IP Address in RDAP. Creates a Netblock node (CIDR, network name, country) linked \"within netblock\" and fills the IP's organization and country_code if empty.",
  "icon": "boxes",                              // (4)!

  "platforms": {
    "primary": "web",                           // (5)!
    "web": { "runtime": "sandbox-js", "entry": "dist/pack.mjs" }
  },

  "io": {
    "consumes": [
      { "typepack": "run.vineyard.typepacks.infrastructure",
        "category": "infrastructure", "name": "ip_address" }
    ],
    "produces": [
      { "typepack": "run.vineyard.typepacks.infrastructure",
        "category": "infrastructure", "name": "netblock" }
    ]
  },

  "scopes": {                                    // (6)!
    "graph": ["node:read", "node:create", "node:update", "edge:create"],
    "network": [
      { "endpoint": "https://rdap.org/", "methods": ["GET"],
        "purpose": "Look up each selected IP's netblock and owner in RDAP." }
    ]
  },

  "lifecycle": {                                 // (7)!
    "persistence": "opt-in",
    "controls": ["progress", "cancel"],
    "progress": "determinate"
  }
}

This manifest ships as one of four members inside the IP Recon pack, so its platforms.web.entry names the pack's bundle (see Plugin Packs).

  1. Reverse-DNS identifier matching ^(?:[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*\.){2,}plugins\.[a-z0-9_]+$.
  2. The const discriminator — must be exactly vineyard:plugin.
  3. SemVer — MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, optionally with a pre-release or build suffix.
  4. Icon shown next to the plugin in the Marketplace pack detail — here a lucide name.
  5. primary: web with the sandbox-js runtime, the only web runtime that actually executes today.
  6. graph verbs plus one network endpoint, checked against the host's egress allowlist at runtime.
  7. persistence/controls/progress are declarative only — see the warning above.

docs.title: Registry entry schemas
docs.text:
Reference for the registry entry schemas — one row in community-pluginpacks.json, one row in community-typepacks.json, and one row in community-skillpacks.json. Each entry is a lean, denormalized pointer that lets the static browser render a card without fetching every upstream manifest. This page covers all three.

The schemas live at:

  • schemas/registry-plugin-entry.schema.json
  • schemas/registry-typepack-entry.schema.json
  • schemas/registry-skillpack-entry.schema.json

docs.title: What a registry entry is (and is not)
docs.text:
The registry repo (Vineyard-Intelligence/registry) stores path and metadata only — no code, no copies. The full plugin manifest or Type Pack JSON, the README, and the bundle all stay in the author repo at the pinned ref.

A registry entry is therefore a catalog projection: enough fields to search, filter, and badge an item in the browser, plus the repo@ref/path pointer that the detail page uses to hydrate the real thing.

Denormalized — the manifest is the source of truth

platforms, scopes_summary, services, plugin_count, desktop_only, icon, type_count and section_count are derived fields. You write them in the entry, and CI recomputes each one from the pinned document and rejects the entry if any disagree. categories and applies_to are also projections of the document, but CI does not recompute them, so copy them from your document yourself. typepacks and requires are not derived: you declare them, and CI checks them. They can drift from the live manifest between updates. When in doubt, the manifest wins.

docs.title: Plugin entry
docs.text:
A row in community-pluginpacks.json. The schema sets additionalProperties: false, so unknown keys are rejected by registry CI.

Required: identifier, content_type, name, author, summary, repo, ref, path.

Field Type Required Meaning identifier string yes Reverse-DNS primary key, ^(?:[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*\.){2,}(?:plugins|pluginpacks)\.[a-z0-9_]+$ (plugins.* = single plugin, pluginpacks.* = bundle). Equals manifest.identifier. Unique across the whole registry (all three catalogs). content_type string yes vineyard:plugin (a single plugin) or vineyard:pluginpack (a bundle: one file → many plugins). name string yes Display name, 1–128 chars. author string yes Author handle, matched against verified-authors.json; for an author listed there, the pack repository's owner GitHub id must equal that author's github.id. summary string yes The card's one line: ≤250 chars, sentence case, ends with a period, no emoji. It must equal the pinned document's summary. The pack's page is not in the catalog (A pack's line and its page). repo string yes owner/name GitHub path (^[^/]+/[^/]+$). The only pointer to code. ref string yes Immutable commit SHA (40-hex SHA-1 or 64-hex SHA-256), captured at PR time. Tags and branches are rejected (both re-pointable). The commit must be on a branch or tag of repo itself; a commit that exists only in a fork is refused. version carries the human-readable release. path string yes Path to manifest.json within repo@ref. version string no SemVer mirror of manifest.version at this ref (^\d+\.\d+\.\d+(?:[-+].+)?$). platforms string[] no Derived: the platform keys the pack's plugins declare under platforms (web, desktop), without primary; unique. The schema's enum also allows web-proxy, but CI never derives it, so an entry that lists it fails. scopes_summary object no Derived filter facets (see below). scopes_summary.network boolean no true if scopes.network or scopes.network_configurable is non-empty, or the plugin declares web_probe. scopes_summary.graph_write boolean no true if any node:/edge: create/update/delete verb is present. scopes_summary.secret_config boolean no true if any scopes.config entry has secret: true (a key the analyst must supply). plugin_count integer no Derived: number of plugins bundled when the identifier names a pack (one file → many plugins). Omitted or 1 for a single-plugin entry. The card installs all contained plugins together. Minimum 1. desktop_only string no Derived: all when every plugin in the pack runs only on the desktop app, some when at least one but not all do. Omitted when none do. icon string no Derived: the manifest's icon when it is a kebab-case lucide icon name. Omitted otherwise. typepacks string[] no Declared by you and checked by CI: the Type Pack identifiers the pack's plugins consume/produce (io.consumes/io.produces), unique. Every type an io entry references must come from a Type Pack listed here, and each listed pack must be in the catalog. The marketplace offers these for co-install the same way a skillpack's requires offers pluginpacks; a plugin that writes a type from a pack the project never installed fails at node-create time. services string[] no Derived: Vineyard services the pack's plugins call by name (rdap, telegram). Its own field, not a scopes_summary flag. See scopes. thumbnail_url string no Repo-relative card-image path (e.g. assets/thumbnail.png), mirrored from the pinned manifest and checked by CI. Resolved only at the pinned commit via cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/{repo}@{ref}/{path} / raw.githubusercontent.com/{repo}/{ref}/{path}. Absolute URLs are rejected. verified boolean no true only when the identifier's namespace is claimed in verified-authors.json by the handle in author and the repository owner's numeric GitHub id matches github.id. Set by CI, not self-asserted. Default false. status object no Present only on a delisted pack: { state: "deprecated" | "withdrawn", reason, since, replacement? }. The row stays in the catalog; deleting it would signal nothing to projects that already installed the pack. deprecated still loads and warns; withdrawn is refused at install and dropped at load. See Publishing → Taking a pack down.

docs.title: Example plugin row
docs.text:
This is the real Chaos reference pack — a single identifier that bundles six graph-manipulation plugins (Korean Roulette, Russian Roulette, Thanos Snap, Black Hole, Dumb AI Optimizer, Schrödinger's Node), so plugin_count is 6.

{
  "identifier": "run.vineyard.pluginpacks.chaos",
  "content_type": "vineyard:pluginpack",
  "name": "Chaos Reference Pack",
  "author": "VINEYARD",
  "summary": "Six graph-manipulation plugins for demos and validation.",
  "repo": "Vineyard-Intelligence/pluginpack-chaos",
  "ref": "024c36cf17011abb4a7fc6004ced208751c13473",
  "path": "plugins/chaos-pack.manifest.json",
  "version": "1.0.3",
  "platforms": ["web"],
  "scopes_summary": { "network": false, "graph_write": true, "secret_config": false },
  "plugin_count": 6,
  "icon": "boxes",
  "typepacks": [],
  "verified": true
}

Reading the facets

scopes_summary.graph_write is true because the Chaos plugins mutate the graph (deleting and reshuffling nodes/edges). network is false — these plugins run entirely client-side and call no endpoints — so the card shows a "graph-write" facet and no network badge. The browser surfaces these as filters.

docs.title: Type Pack entry
docs.text:
A row in community-typepacks.json, symmetric with the plugin entry. Type Packs carry no scopes — no code executes — so the scopes_summary facet is replaced by categories, which drives the category filter. Again additionalProperties: false.

Required: identifier, content_type, name, author, summary, repo, ref, path.

Field Type Required Meaning identifier string yes Reverse-DNS primary key, ^(?:[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*\.){2,}typepacks\.[a-z0-9]+(?:[._-][a-z0-9]+)*$. Equals typepack.identifier. content_type string yes Constant vineyard:typepack. name string yes Display name, 1–128 chars. author string yes Author handle. summary string yes ≤250 chars (same rules as the plugin entry). repo string yes owner/name GitHub path. ref string yes Immutable commit SHA (40-hex SHA-1 or 64-hex SHA-256), captured at PR time. Tags and branches are rejected (both re-pointable). The commit must be on a branch or tag of repo itself; a commit that exists only in a fork is refused. version carries the human-readable release. path string yes Path to the Type Pack JSON within repo@ref. version string no SemVer (^(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)$). categories string[] no Derived: distinct types[].category values (each ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$, unique). Drives the category facet. type_count integer no Derived: types[].length. Minimum 1. icon string no Derived: the first type's icon when it is a kebab-case lucide icon name. Omitted otherwise. thumbnail_url string (uri) no Optional card icon. verified boolean no Same as the plugin entry — CI-set mirror of verified-authors.json, including the repository-owner id check. Default false. status object no Present only on a delisted pack: { state: "deprecated" | "withdrawn", reason, since, replacement? }. The row stays in the catalog; deleting it would signal nothing to projects that already installed the pack. deprecated still loads and warns; withdrawn is refused at install and dropped at load. See Publishing → Taking a pack down.

docs.title: Example Type Pack row
docs.text:
The real Infrastructure base pack, defining fifteen infrastructure and web entity types:

{
  "identifier": "run.vineyard.typepacks.infrastructure",
  "content_type": "vineyard:typepack",
  "name": "Infrastructure",
  "author": "VINEYARD",
  "summary": "Network-infrastructure and web OSINT entities (IPs, domains, URLs, hosts, ASNs, netblocks, DNS/WHOIS records, TLS certificates, SSH host keys, technologies, web fingerprints and tracking/ad-account identifiers) and their relationships.",
  "repo": "Vineyard-Intelligence/typepack-basic",
  "ref": "721e3fdab2bdcace019cd9329b47b1014d8acdbb",
  "path": "typepacks/infrastructure.json",
  "version": "4.0.0",
  "categories": ["infrastructure", "web"],
  "type_count": 15,
  "icon": "network",
  "verified": true
}

The companion Threat pack is the same shape with categories: ["threat"] and type_count: 10.

docs.title: Skill Pack entry
docs.text:
A row in community-skillpacks.json, the same pointer shape as the two above. A Skill Pack is text, so it carries no scopes; its only dependencies are the Plugin Packs in requires. Again additionalProperties: false.

Required: identifier, content_type, name, author, summary, repo, ref, path.

Field Type Required Meaning identifier string yes Reverse-DNS primary key, ^(?:[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*\.){2,}skillpacks\.[a-z0-9_]+$. Equals the skill document's identifier. content_type string yes Constant vineyard:skillpack. name, author, summary, repo, ref, path string yes Same rules as the plugin entry; path is the skill JSON within repo@ref. version string no SemVer mirror of the document's version at this ref. applies_to string[] no Derived: node types (category.name) the playbook is about, shown in the detail view. Not recomputed by CI — copy it from your document. section_count integer no Derived: number of sections in the document. Recomputed by CI. Minimum 0. requires string[] no Plugin Pack identifiers the playbook's steps call. Each must be a live pack in the catalog. The marketplace offers them for co-install. thumbnail_url string (uri) no Optional card icon. verified boolean no Same as the plugin entry. Default false. status object no Same as the plugin entry.

The real row for Account & identity pivoting is shown on Skill Packs.

docs.title: How entries are validated and merged
docs.text: Submission is a fork-and-PR that adds one packs/<identifier>.json file — the catalogs are generated from it — gated by blocking CI checks plus a human merge. CI checks the entry against its schema, that ref is an immutable commit SHA on a branch or tag of repo, that the pinned document matches the entry (identifier, content_type, version and the derived fields), that a Plugin Pack's bundle declares the manifest's version and licence, and that declared dependencies and typeRefs resolve. It does not validate the pinned document against its own schema. See What CI enforces for the full list, and Publishing for the walkthrough.
